readme: The Lean library for Computer Science.
CSLib aims at formalising Computer Science theories and tools, broadly construed, in the Lean programming language.

folders.Cslib/Algorithms: This directory hosts **algorithms and their properties**. These properties concern functional correctness, complexity, and other relevant results. The directory also includes dedicated facilities for reasoning about algorithms written in Lean.
folders.Cslib/Computability/Distributed/FLP:
This directory contains a formalization of Völzer's proof [Volzer2004] of the famous result in
distributed computing, first proved by Fischer, Lynch and Paterson [FLP1985], that asynchronous
distributed consensus is impossible in the presence of even a single crash fault.
folders.Cslib/Computability: This directory hosts **formal developments in computability and neighbouring areas**. Its scope includes automata, complexity classes, formal languages over finite and infinite words, and other machine models.
folders.Cslib/Crypto: This directory hosts **cryptographic definitions, primitives, protocol models, and related security metatheory**. Its scope includes both basic cryptographic notions and larger developments such as security protocols.
folders.Cslib/Foundations: This directory covers **common foundations** for the rest of CSLib and downstream developments. As such, it acts as its fulcrum of integration through common concepts and APIs. This directory includes also additional results about foundational data objects defined in Mathlib, such as `Nat` and `Set`.
folders.Cslib/Languages:
This directory hosts **modelling and programming languages** formalised in CSLib and their properties. Their components can include syntax, semantics, typing and other reasoning disciplines, execution facilities (compilers, interpreters, etc.), behavioural theories, supporting metatheory, etc.
We are interested in many kinds of languages, from foundational calculi to applied programming frameworks.
folders.Cslib/Logics: CSLib offers **formal logics** for defining specifications and reasoning about programs and systems. Each subdirectory focuses on a specific logic or framework.

modules.title: Milner's Vending Machine
modules.doc:
This file formalises Milner's vending machine example for CCS.

We formalise two versions:
- A machine with a deterministic LTS: `coin.(tea.VM + coffee.VM)`.
- A machine with a nondeterministic LTS: `coin.tea.VM + coin.coffee.VM`.

We then prove the classical example that the two are not bisimilar.
We also show the distinction with HML: only the deterministic machine offers the choice of drink
after a coin is inserted.

Future work on proving that the two vending machines are trace equivalent would be welcome.

modules.title: MergeSort on a list
modules.doc:
In this file we introduce `merge` and `mergeSort` algorithms that returns a time monad
over the list `TimeM ℕ (List α)`. The time complexity of `mergeSort` is the number of comparisons.

--
## Main results

- `mergeSort_correct`: `mergeSort` permutes the list into a sorted one.
- `mergeSort_time`:  The number of comparisons of `mergeSort` is at most `n*⌈log₂ n⌉`.

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.ret_mergeM
items.doc: `TimeM.ret` passes through `List.mergeM` into the comparator.
items.statement:
theorem ret_mergeM {T} [AddMonoid T] (xs ys : List α) (le : α → α → TimeM T Bool) :
    ⟪List.mergeM xs ys le⟫ = List.merge xs ys (fun x y => ⟪le x y⟫)

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.ret_mergeSortM
items.doc: `TimeM.ret` passes through `List.mergeSortM` into the comparator.
items.statement:
theorem ret_mergeSortM {T} [AddMonoid T] (xs : List α) (le : α → α → TimeM T Bool) :
    ⟪List.mergeSortM xs le⟫ = List.mergeSort xs (fun x y => ⟪le x y⟫)

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.merge
items.doc:
Merges two lists into a single list, counting comparisons as time cost.
Returns a `TimeM ℕ (List α)` where the time represents the number of comparisons performed.
items.statement: abbrev merge (xs ys : List α) : TimeM ℕ (List α)

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.mergeSort
items.doc:
Sorts a list using the merge sort algorithm, counting comparisons as time cost.
Returns a `TimeM ℕ (List α)` where the time represents the total number of comparisons.
items.statement: abbrev mergeSort (xs : List α) : TimeM ℕ (List α)

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.ret_merge
items.doc: Our merge computes the one already in mathlib.
items.statement: theorem ret_merge (xs ys : List α) : ⟪merge xs ys⟫ = xs.merge ys

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.IsSorted
items.doc: A list is sorted if it satisfies the `Pairwise (· ≤ ·)` predicate.
items.statement: abbrev IsSorted (l : List α) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.MinOfList
items.doc: `x` is a minimum element of list `l` if `x ≤ b` for all `b ∈ l`.
items.statement: abbrev MinOfList (x : α) (l : List α) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.mem_either_merge
items.statement: theorem mem_either_merge (xs ys : List α) (z : α) (hz : z ∈ ⟪merge xs ys⟫) : z ∈ xs ∨ z ∈ ys

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.min_all_merge
items.statement:
theorem min_all_merge (x : α) (xs ys : List α) (hxs : MinOfList x xs) (hys : MinOfList x ys) :
    MinOfList x ⟪merge xs ys⟫

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.sorted_merge
items.statement:
theorem sorted_merge {l1 l2 : List α} (hxs : IsSorted l1) (hys : IsSorted l2) :
    IsSorted ⟪merge l1 l2⟫

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.mergeSort_sorted
items.statement: theorem mergeSort_sorted (xs : List α) : IsSorted ⟪mergeSort xs⟫

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.merge_perm
items.statement: lemma merge_perm (l₁ l₂ : List α) : ⟪merge l₁ l₂⟫ ~ l₁ ++ l₂

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.mergeSort_perm
items.statement: theorem mergeSort_perm (xs : List α) : ⟪mergeSort xs⟫ ~ xs

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.mergeSort_correct
items.doc: MergeSort is functionally correct.
items.statement: theorem mergeSort_correct (xs : List α) : IsSorted ⟪mergeSort xs⟫ ∧ ⟪mergeSort xs⟫ ~ xs

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.timeMergeSortRec
items.doc:
Recurrence relation for the time complexity of merge sort.
For a list of length `n`, this counts the total number of comparisons:
- Base cases: 0 comparisons for lists of length 0 or 1
- Recursive case: split the list, sort both halves,
  then merge (which takes at most `n` comparisons)
items.statement: def timeMergeSortRec : ℕ → ℕ

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.clog2_half_le
items.doc: Key Lemma: ⌈log2 ⌈n/2⌉⌉ ≤ ⌈log2 n⌉ - 1 for n > 1
items.statement: lemma clog2_half_le (n : ℕ) (h : 1 < n) : clog 2 ((n + 1) / 2) ≤ clog 2 n - 1

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.clog2_floor_half_le
items.doc: Same logic for the floor half: ⌈log2 ⌊n/2⌋⌉ ≤ ⌈log2 n⌉ - 1
items.statement: lemma clog2_floor_half_le (n : ℕ) (h : 1 < n) : clog 2 (n / 2) ≤ clog 2 n - 1

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.T
items.doc: Upper bound function for merge sort time complexity: `T(n) = n * ⌈log₂ n⌉`
items.statement: abbrev T (n : ℕ) : ℕ

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.timeMergeSortRec_le
items.doc: Solve the recurrence
items.statement: theorem timeMergeSortRec_le (n : ℕ) : timeMergeSortRec n ≤ T n

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.merge_ret_length_eq_sum
items.statement:
theorem merge_ret_length_eq_sum (xs ys : List α) :
    ⟪merge xs ys⟫.length = xs.length + ys.length

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.mergeSort_same_length
items.statement:
theorem mergeSort_same_length (xs : List α) :
    ⟪mergeSort xs⟫.length = xs.length

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.merge_time
items.statement: theorem merge_time (xs ys : List α) : (merge xs ys).time ≤ xs.length + ys.length

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.mergeSort_time_le
items.statement:
theorem mergeSort_time_le (xs : List α) :
    (mergeSort xs).time ≤ timeMergeSortRec xs.length

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.mergeSort_time
items.doc: Time complexity of mergeSort
items.statement:
theorem mergeSort_time (xs : List α) :
    let n := xs.length
    (mergeSort xs).time ≤ n * clog 2 n

modules.title: Arithmetic Queries and Complex Multiplication
modules.doc:
A simple example showing how to use `FreeM.cost` with variable/parametrized query costs.

`ArithQuery α` supports addition, subtraction, and multiplication, each with
independently parametrized costs. Complex number multiplication provides a toy example
where two algorithms (naive and Gauss's trick) trade multiplications for additions,
and the optimal choice depends on the cost ratio.

items.name: Cslib.Query.ArithQuery
items.doc: Arithmetic queries: addition, subtraction, and multiplication.
items.statement:
inductive ArithQuery (α : Type) : Type → Type where
  | add (a b : α) : ArithQuery α α
  | sub (a b : α) : ArithQuery α α
  | mul (a b : α) : ArithQuery α α

items.name: Cslib.Query.ArithQuery.doAdd
items.doc: Lift `ArithQuery.add a b` into a `FreeM` that returns the sum.
items.statement: abbrev doAdd (a b : α) : FreeM (ArithQuery α) α

items.name: Cslib.Query.ArithQuery.doSub
items.doc: Lift `ArithQuery.sub a b` into a `FreeM` that returns the difference.
items.statement: abbrev doSub (a b : α) : FreeM (ArithQuery α) α

items.name: Cslib.Query.ArithQuery.doMul
items.doc: Lift `ArithQuery.mul a b` into a `FreeM` that returns the product.
items.statement: abbrev doMul (a b : α) : FreeM (ArithQuery α) α

items.name: Cslib.Query.ArithQuery.honest
items.doc: An honest oracle interprets arithmetic queries using the actual ring operations.
items.statement: def honest [Add α] [Sub α] [Mul α] {ι : Type} : ArithQuery α ι → ι

items.name: Cslib.Query.ArithQuery.weight
items.doc:
Weighted cost model for arithmetic queries. Subtraction costs the same as addition
(both are linear-time on bignums).
items.statement: def weight (c_add c_mul : Nat) {ι : Type} : ArithQuery α ι → Nat

items.name: Cslib.Query.complexMulNaive
items.doc:
Naive complex multiplication: `(a + bi)(c + di) = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i`.
Uses 4 multiplications, 1 subtraction, 1 addition.
items.statement: def complexMulNaive (a b c d : α) : FreeM (ArithQuery α) (α × α)

items.name: Cslib.Query.complexMulGauss
items.doc:
Gauss's trick for complex multiplication: computes `(a+b)(c+d)` to save one
multiplication, at the cost of extra additions and subtractions.
Uses 3 multiplications, 2 subtractions, 3 additions.
items.statement: def complexMulGauss (a b c d : α) : FreeM (ArithQuery α) (α × α)

modules.title: Complex Multiplication: Correctness and Cost Analysis
modules.doc:
A simple example showing how to use `FreeM.cost` with variable/parametrized query costs.

We prove that both `complexMulNaive` and `complexMulGauss` correctly compute
complex multiplication when given an honest oracle, and compute their exact
costs under a parametric weight function. The cost theorems hold for *any* oracle
(not just honest ones), because both algorithms are straight-line (no branching
on query results).

items.name: Cslib.Query.complexMulNaive_eval_honest
items.statement:
theorem complexMulNaive_eval_honest [Add α] [Sub α] [Mul α] (a b c d : α) :
    (complexMulNaive a b c d).eval ArithQuery.honest = (a * c - b * d, a * d + b * c)

items.name: Cslib.Query.complexMulGauss_eval_honest
items.statement:
theorem complexMulGauss_eval_honest [CommRing α] (a b c d : α) :
    (complexMulGauss a b c d).eval ArithQuery.honest = (a * c - b * d, a * d + b * c)

items.name: Cslib.Query.complexMulNaive_cost
items.statement:
theorem complexMulNaive_cost (oracle : {ι : Type} → ArithQuery α ι → ι)
    (c_add c_mul : Nat) (a b c d : α) :
    (complexMulNaive a b c d).cost oracle (ArithQuery.weight c_add c_mul) =
      4 * c_mul + 2 * c_add

items.name: Cslib.Query.complexMulGauss_cost
items.statement:
theorem complexMulGauss_cost (oracle : {ι : Type} → ArithQuery α ι → ι)
    (c_add c_mul : Nat) (a b c d : α) :
    (complexMulGauss a b c d).cost oracle (ArithQuery.weight c_add c_mul) =
      3 * c_mul + 5 * c_add

items.note: ## Crossover: Gauss beats naive when multiplication costs at least 3× addition

items.name: Cslib.Query.gauss_le_naive
items.statement:
theorem gauss_le_naive (oracle : {ι : Type} → ArithQuery α ι → ι)
    (c_add c_mul : Nat) (a b c d : α) (h : 3 * c_add ≤ c_mul) :
    (complexMulGauss a b c d).cost oracle (ArithQuery.weight c_add c_mul) ≤
      (complexMulNaive a b c d).cost oracle (ArithQuery.weight c_add c_mul)

items.name: Cslib.Query.gauss_le_naive_iff
items.statement:
theorem gauss_le_naive_iff (oracle : {ι : Type} → ArithQuery α ι → ι)
    (c_add c_mul : Nat) (a b c d : α) :
    (complexMulGauss a b c d).cost oracle (ArithQuery.weight c_add c_mul) ≤
      (complexMulNaive a b c d).cost oracle (ArithQuery.weight c_add c_mul) ↔
        3 * c_add ≤ c_mul

modules.authors: Sebastian Graf, Kim Morrison, Shreyas Srinivas
modules.title: Upper and Lower Bounds for Query Complexity
modules.doc:
Definitions of upper and lower bounds on the number of queries a program makes,
quantified over oracles.

items.name: Cslib.Query.UpperBound
items.doc: Upper bound: for all oracles, inputs of size ≤ n make at most `bound n` queries.
items.statement:
def UpperBound (prog : α → FreeM Q β)
(size : α → Nat) (bound : Nat → Nat) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.Query.LowerBound
items.doc:
Lower bound: for every size n, there exists an input of size at most n and an oracle
making the program perform ≥ `bound n` queries.
items.statement:
def LowerBound (prog : α → FreeM Q β)
(size : α → Nat) (bound : Nat → Nat) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.Query.UpperBound.of_pointwise
items.doc:
To prove an `UpperBound` with a monotone bound function, it suffices to bound the
query count of each input by `bound` at its own size.
items.statement:
theorem UpperBound.of_pointwise {prog : α → FreeM Q β} {size : α → Nat} {bound : Nat → Nat}
    (hmono : Monotone bound)
    (h : ∀ (oracle : {ι : Type u} → Q ι → ι) (x : α),
      (prog x).countQueries oracle ≤ bound (size x)) :
    UpperBound prog size bound

items.name: Cslib.Query.LowerBound.le_upperBound
items.doc:
A lower bound for a program never exceeds an upper bound for the same program and
size function.
items.statement:
theorem LowerBound.le_upperBound {prog : α → FreeM Q β} {size : α → Nat} {l u : Nat → Nat}
    (hl : LowerBound prog size l) (hu : UpperBound prog size u) (n : Nat) : l n ≤ u n

modules.authors: Sebastian Graf, Kim Morrison, Shreyas Srinivas, Eric Wieser
modules.title: FreeM: query/cost interpreters and lower-bound lemma
modules.doc:
This file adds query-complexity interpreters to `FreeM F α`, where the type constructor
`F : Type u → Type v` represents a query type mapping each query to its response type.

The key operations are:
- `FreeM.eval oracle p`: evaluate `p` by answering each query using `oracle`
- `FreeM.countQueries oracle p`: count queries along the oracle-determined path
- `FreeM.cost oracle weight p`: weighted query cost in any additive monoid

The program `p` must be fixed independently of `oracle`. Arbitrary pure computation embedded
in `p` is uncharged, so `countQueries` and `cost` measure query complexity rather than total
runtime. However, pure code cannot inspect oracle responses: those enter only through
`FreeM.lift`.

This provides an alternative to the `TimeM`-based cost analysis in
`Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.MergeSort.MergeSort`: here query counting is structural (derived from
the `FreeM` tree) rather than annotation-based.

The combinatorial lower-bound lemma `FreeM.exists_countQueries_ge_clog` says: if `n` distinct
oracles produce `n` distinct evaluation results from a program whose every response type has
cardinality at most `r`, then some oracle makes at least `⌈log_r n⌉` queries. The proof uses
the adversarial/partition argument: at each query node, the oracles split by their answer,
and the largest fiber still produces distinct results in the corresponding subtree.

## Setting up your own query type

1. Define an inductive `Q : Type u → Type v` whose constructors are the queries, indexed by
   their response types (see `LEQuery`, `ArithQuery`).
2. Wrap each constructor with `FreeM.lift` to obtain one-step programs (`LEQuery.ask`).
3. Write algorithms in `do`-notation as values of `FreeM Q α`.
4. Prove correctness by relating `FreeM.eval` to a reference implementation, and bounds by
   equational reasoning with the `countQueries`/`cost` simp lemmas; state them with
   `Cslib.Query.UpperBound`/`Cslib.Query.LowerBound`.

items.name: Cslib.FreeM.timeMRet_liftM
items.doc: `TimeM.ret` distributes across `FreeM.liftM`.
items.statement:
theorem timeMRet_liftM {T : Type t} [AddMonoid T] (interp : {ι : Type u} → F ι → TimeM T ι)
    (p : FreeM F α) :
    (p.liftM interp).ret = Id.run (p.liftM fun i => pure (interp i).ret)

items.note:
## Interpreters

All three interpreters (`eval`, `cost`, `countQueries`) are defined as `liftM` interpretations
into target monads, routing them through the universal property of the free monad rather
than direct pattern-match on `FreeM`'s constructors:

- `eval` interprets into `Id`.
- `cost` interprets into a `TimeM` accumulator monad (a value paired with a running cost in
  an arbitrary additive monoid).
- `countQueries` is `cost` with unit weight.

The pure and lift-then-bind simp lemmas (`eval_pure`, `eval_liftBind`, `cost_pure`,
`cost_liftBind`, `countQueries_pure`, `countQueries_liftBind`) all reduce by `rfl`, giving the
same proof ergonomics as direct pattern-match definitions while honouring the universal
property as the primary abstraction.

items.name: Cslib.FreeM.eval
items.doc:
Evaluate a program by answering each query using `oracle`.
Defined as `liftM` to `Id`, the canonical interpreter into pure values.
items.statement: def eval (oracle : {ι : Type u} → F ι → ι) (p : FreeM F α) : α

items.name: Cslib.FreeM.cost
items.doc:
Weighted query cost in an additive monoid: each query has a cost given by `weight`,
accumulated along the oracle-determined path. Defined as `liftM` into `TimeM`.
items.statement:
def cost {T : Type t} [AddMonoid T] (oracle : {ι : Type u} → F ι → ι)
(weight : {ι : Type u} → F ι → T) (p : FreeM F α) : T

items.name: Cslib.FreeM.countQueries
items.doc:
Count the number of queries along the path determined by `oracle`.

This is deliberately a `def` with its own simp lemmas, rather than an abbreviation for
`cost oracle (fun _ => 1)`, so that goals display `countQueries`.
items.statement: def countQueries (oracle : {ι : Type u} → F ι → ι) (p : FreeM F α) : Nat

items.name: Cslib.FreeM.eval_pure
items.statement:
theorem eval_pure (oracle : {ι : Type u} → F ι → ι) (a : α) :
eval oracle (pure a : FreeM F α) = a

items.name: Cslib.FreeM.eval_liftBind
items.statement:
theorem eval_liftBind (oracle : {ι : Type u} → F ι → ι)
{ι : Type u} (op : F ι) (cont : ι → FreeM F α) :
eval oracle (FreeM.lift op >>= cont) = eval oracle (cont (oracle op))

items.name: Cslib.FreeM.eval_lift
items.statement:
theorem eval_lift (oracle : {ι : Type u} → F ι → ι) {ι : Type u} (op : F ι) :
eval oracle (FreeM.lift op) = oracle op

items.name: Cslib.FreeM.eval_bind
items.statement:
theorem eval_bind (oracle : {ι : Type u} → F ι → ι)
(t : FreeM F α) (f : α → FreeM F β) :
eval oracle (t >>= f) = eval oracle (f (eval oracle t))

items.name: Cslib.FreeM.eval_map
items.statement:
theorem eval_map (oracle : {ι : Type u} → F ι → ι)
(t : FreeM F α) (f : α → β) :
eval oracle (f <$> t) = f (eval oracle t)

items.name: Cslib.FreeM.isMonadHom_pure_eval
items.statement:
theorem isMonadHom_pure_eval (oracle : {ι : Type u} → F ι → ι) :
    IsMonadHom (FreeM F) Id (fun x => pure (x.eval oracle))

items.name: Cslib.FreeM.cost_pure
items.statement:
theorem cost_pure {T : Type t} [AddMonoid T] (oracle : {ι : Type u} → F ι → ι)
(weight : {ι : Type u} → F ι → T) (a : α) :
cost oracle weight (pure a : FreeM F α) = 0

items.name: Cslib.FreeM.cost_liftBind
items.statement:
theorem cost_liftBind {T : Type t} [AddMonoid T]
(oracle : {ι : Type u} → F ι → ι) (weight : {ι : Type u} → F ι → T)
{ι : Type u} (op : F ι) (cont : ι → FreeM F α) :
cost oracle weight (FreeM.lift op >>= cont) =
weight op + cost oracle weight (cont (oracle op))

items.name: Cslib.FreeM.cost_lift
items.statement:
theorem cost_lift {T : Type t} [AddMonoid T]
(oracle : {ι : Type u} → F ι → ι) (weight : {ι : Type u} → F ι → T)
{ι : Type u} (op : F ι) :
cost oracle weight (FreeM.lift op) = weight op

items.name: Cslib.FreeM.cost_bind
items.statement:
theorem cost_bind {T : Type t} [AddMonoid T] (oracle : {ι : Type u} → F ι → ι)
(weight : {ι : Type u} → F ι → T) (t : FreeM F α) (f : α → FreeM F β) :
cost oracle weight (t >>= f) =
cost oracle weight t + cost oracle weight (f (eval oracle t))

items.name: Cslib.FreeM.cost_map
items.statement:
theorem cost_map {T : Type t} [AddMonoid T]
(oracle : {ι : Type u} → F ι → ι) (weight : {ι : Type u} → F ι → T)
(t : FreeM F α) (f : α → β) :
cost oracle weight (f <$> t) = cost oracle weight t

items.name: Cslib.FreeM.countQueries_pure
items.statement:
theorem countQueries_pure (oracle : {ι : Type u} → F ι → ι) (a : α) :
countQueries oracle (pure a : FreeM F α) = 0

items.name: Cslib.FreeM.countQueries_liftBind
items.statement:
theorem countQueries_liftBind (oracle : {ι : Type u} → F ι → ι)
{ι : Type u} (op : F ι) (cont : ι → FreeM F α) :
countQueries oracle (FreeM.lift op >>= cont) =
1 + countQueries oracle (cont (oracle op))

items.name: Cslib.FreeM.countQueries_lift
items.statement:
theorem countQueries_lift (oracle : {ι : Type u} → F ι → ι)
{ι : Type u} (op : F ι) :
countQueries oracle (FreeM.lift op) = 1

items.name: Cslib.FreeM.countQueries_bind
items.statement:
theorem countQueries_bind (oracle : {ι : Type u} → F ι → ι)
(t : FreeM F α) (f : α → FreeM F β) :
countQueries oracle (t >>= f) =
countQueries oracle t + countQueries oracle (f (eval oracle t))

items.name: Cslib.FreeM.countQueries_map
items.statement:
theorem countQueries_map (oracle : {ι : Type u} → F ι → ι)
(t : FreeM F α) (f : α → β) :
countQueries oracle (f <$> t) = countQueries oracle t

items.name: Cslib.FreeM.countQueries_eq_cost_one
items.statement:
theorem countQueries_eq_cost_one (oracle : {ι : Type u} → F ι → ι) (p : FreeM F α) :
    countQueries oracle p = cost oracle (fun _ => 1) p

items.name: Cslib.FreeM.countQueries_ite
items.statement:
theorem countQueries_ite (oracle : {ι : Type u} → F ι → ι) (P : Prop) [Decidable P]
    (p q : FreeM F α) :
    (if P then p else q).countQueries oracle =
      if P then p.countQueries oracle else q.countQueries oracle

items.name: Cslib.FreeM.countQueries_dite
items.statement:
theorem countQueries_dite (oracle : {ι : Type u} → F ι → ι) (P : Prop) [Decidable P]
    (p : P → FreeM F α) (q : ¬P → FreeM F α) :
    (if h : P then p h else q h).countQueries oracle =
      if h : P then (p h).countQueries oracle else (q h).countQueries oracle

items.name: Cslib.FreeM.exists_countQueries_ge_clog
items.doc:
If `n` oracles produce `n` distinct evaluation results from a `FreeM F α` program
whose every response type has cardinality at most `r` (and hence is finite), then some
oracle makes at least `⌈log_r n⌉` queries.

This is the core combinatorial lemma for query complexity lower bounds. The proof uses
the adversarial/partition argument: at each query node, the `n` oracles split by their
answer; the largest group (size ≥ ⌈n/r⌉) still produces distinct results in the
corresponding subtree, and the induction proceeds there.
items.statement:
theorem exists_countQueries_ge_clog (r : Nat)
    (h_card : ∀ {ρ : Type u}, F ρ → #ρ ≤ r)
    (p : FreeM F α) {n : Nat}
    (oracles : Fin n → ({ρ : Type u} → F ρ → ρ))
    (hn : 0 < n)
    (h_inj : Function.Injective (fun i => p.eval (oracles i))) :
    ∃ i : Fin n, p.countQueries (oracles i) ≥ Nat.clog r n

items.name: Cslib.Query.orderedInsert
items.doc: Insert `x` into a sorted list using comparison queries.
items.statement: abbrev orderedInsert (x : α) (xs : List α) : FreeM (LEQuery α) (List α)

items.statement: abbrev insertionSort (xs : List α) : FreeM (LEQuery α) (List α)

modules.authors: Kim Morrison, Shreyas Srinivas, Eric Wieser
modules.title: Insertion Sort: Correctness and Upper Bound
modules.doc:
Proofs that `insertionSort` is a correct comparison sort and uses at most `n * (n - 1) / 2`
queries (with `n²` as a corollary). All proofs are by plain equational reasoning on
`FreeM.eval` and `FreeM.countQueries`.

items.name: Cslib.Query.eval_orderedInsert
items.doc:
Evaluating query-based insertion agrees with `List.orderedInsert` using the relation
supplied by the oracle.
items.statement:
theorem eval_orderedInsert (oracle : {ι : Type} → LEQuery α ι → ι)
(x : α) (xs : List α) :
(orderedInsert x xs).eval oracle =
xs.orderedInsert (fun x y => oracle (.le x y)) x

items.name: Cslib.Query.eval_insertionSort
items.doc:
Evaluating query-based insertion sort agrees with `List.insertionSort` using the relation
supplied by the oracle.

This is the essential correctness statement: it identifies the query program as *the*
insertion sort operation, so correctness properties (permutation, sortedness) transfer
directly from the `List.insertionSort` API rather than being restated here.
items.statement:
theorem eval_insertionSort (oracle : {ι : Type} → LEQuery α ι → ι) (xs : List α) :
(insertionSort xs).eval oracle =
xs.insertionSort (fun x y => oracle (.le x y))

items.name: Cslib.Query.orderedInsert_countQueries_le
items.statement:
theorem orderedInsert_countQueries_le (oracle : {ι : Type} → LEQuery α ι → ι)
    (x : α) (xs : List α) :
    (orderedInsert x xs).countQueries oracle ≤ xs.length

items.name: Cslib.Query.insertionSort_countQueries_le
items.doc:
Insertion sort makes at most `n * (n - 1) / 2` queries: inserting into the sorted
prefix of length `k` costs at most `k` queries. This bound is attained by the all-`false`
oracle.
items.statement:
theorem insertionSort_countQueries_le (oracle : {ι : Type} → LEQuery α ι → ι)
    (xs : List α) :
    (insertionSort xs).countQueries oracle ≤ xs.length * (xs.length - 1) / 2

items.name: Cslib.Query.insertionSort_countQueries_le_sq
items.statement:
theorem insertionSort_countQueries_le_sq (oracle : {ι : Type} → LEQuery α ι → ι)
    (xs : List α) :
    (insertionSort xs).countQueries oracle ≤ xs.length ^ 2

items.name: Cslib.Query.insertionSort_upperBound
items.statement:
theorem insertionSort_upperBound :
    UpperBound (insertionSort (α := α)) List.length (· ^ 2)

items.name: Cslib.Query.insertionSort_isSort
items.statement: theorem insertionSort_isSort : IsSort (insertionSort (α := α))

modules.title: IsSort: Specification for Comparison Sorts
modules.doc:
`IsSort sort` asserts that `sort` is a correct comparison sort when viewed as a `FreeM`
over `LEQuery α`. Correctness means: for any oracle, the result is a permutation of the
input; and for any oracle implementing a total order, the result is sorted.

items.name: Cslib.Query.IsSort
items.doc:
A `FreeM`-based function is a correct comparison sort if it always produces a permutation
of its input, and produces a sorted list when the oracle implements a total order.
items.statement:
structure IsSort (sort : List α → FreeM (LEQuery α) (List α)) : Prop where
  /-- The sort produces a permutation of its input, for any oracle. -/
  perm : ∀ (xs : List α) (oracle : {ι : Type} → LEQuery α ι → ι),
    ((sort xs).eval oracle).Perm xs
  /-- The sort produces a sorted list, when the oracle implements a total order. -/
  sorted : ∀ (xs : List α) (oracle : {ι : Type} → LEQuery α ι → ι)
    (r : α → α → Prop) [DecidableRel r] [Std.Total r] [IsTrans α r]
    (_ : ∀ a b, oracle (.le a b) = decide (r a b)),
    ((sort xs).eval oracle).Pairwise r

items.name: Cslib.Query.IsSort.eval_eq
items.doc:
`IsSort` determines the output: under an oracle implementing an antisymmetric total
transitive relation, all correct comparison sorts produce the same list.
items.statement:
theorem IsSort.eval_eq {sort₁ sort₂ : List α → FreeM (LEQuery α) (List α)}
    (h₁ : IsSort sort₁) (h₂ : IsSort sort₂)
    (r : α → α → Prop) [DecidableRel r] [Std.Total r] [IsTrans α r] [Std.Antisymm r]
    (oracle : {ι : Type} → LEQuery α ι → ι)
    (horacle : ∀ a b, oracle (.le a b) = decide (r a b)) (xs : List α) :
    (sort₁ xs).eval oracle = (sort₂ xs).eval oracle

modules.authors: Sebastian Graf, Kim Morrison, Shreyas Srinivas
modules.title: LEQuery: Comparison Queries for Sorting
modules.doc:
`LEQuery α` is the query type for comparison-based sorting algorithms.
A query `LEQuery.le a b` asks whether `a ≤ b` and returns a `Bool`.

items.name: Cslib.Query.LEQuery
items.doc: Comparison query: asks whether `a ≤ b`, returning a `Bool`.
items.statement:
inductive LEQuery (α : Type) : Type → Type where
  | le (a b : α) : LEQuery α Bool

items.name: Cslib.Query.LEQuery.ask
items.doc: Lift `LEQuery.le a b` into a `FreeM` that returns the comparison result.
items.statement: abbrev LEQuery.ask (a b : α) : FreeM (LEQuery α) Bool

items.name: Cslib.Query.LEQuery.eval_ask
items.statement:
theorem LEQuery.eval_ask (oracle : {ι : Type} → LEQuery α ι → ι) (a b : α) :
(LEQuery.ask a b).eval oracle = oracle (.le a b)

items.name: Cslib.Query.LEQuery.oracleOf
items.doc: Build an oracle for `LEQuery α` from a binary predicate `α → α → Bool`.
items.statement: def LEQuery.oracleOf (f : α → α → Bool) : {ι : Type} → LEQuery α ι → ι

items.name: Cslib.Query.LEQuery.oracleOf_le
items.statement:
theorem LEQuery.oracleOf_le (f : α → α → Bool) (a b : α) :
LEQuery.oracleOf f (.le a b) = f a b

items.name: Cslib.Query.LEQuery.cardResponse_eq_two
items.doc: Every `LEQuery α ι` has response type `ι = Bool`, of cardinality two.
items.statement: theorem LEQuery.cardResponse_eq_two : ∀ {ι : Type}, LEQuery α ι → #ι = 2

items.name: Cslib.Query.LEQuery.cardResponse_le_two
items.statement: theorem LEQuery.cardResponse_le_two {ι : Type} (op : LEQuery α ι) : #ι ≤ 2

modules.authors: Kim Morrison, Shreyas Srinivas, Eric Wieser
modules.title: Comparison Sorting Lower Bound
modules.doc:
`IsSort.lowerBound_infinite`: any correct comparison sort on an infinite type
has query complexity at least `⌈log₂(n!)⌉` for every input size `n`.

The proof constructs `n!` distinct total orders on `α` (one per permutation of `n`
embedded elements), shows they produce distinct sorted outputs, and applies
`FreeM.exists_countQueries_ge_clog` with `LEQuery.cardResponse_le_two` witnessing that
all responses come from `Bool` (cardinality 2).

items.note: ## PrefixPermOrder: constructing n! distinct total orders

items.name: Cslib.Query.IsSort.lowerBound_infinite
items.doc:
Any correct comparison sort on an infinite type has query complexity at least `⌈log₂(n!)⌉`
for every input size `n`.
items.statement:
theorem IsSort.lowerBound_infinite [Infinite α]
    {sort : List α → FreeM (LEQuery α) (List α)}
    (hs : IsSort sort) :
    LowerBound sort List.length (fun n => Nat.clog 2 (Nat.factorial n))

modules.title: Merge Sort: Combined Bounds
modules.doc:
Instantiating the general comparison-sorting lower bound at `mergeSort`, and comparing it
with the `n * ⌈log₂ n⌉` upper bound. Since `LowerBound.le_upperBound` makes the two
bounds meet, the purely arithmetic fact `⌈log₂ n!⌉ ≤ n * ⌈log₂ n⌉` falls out of the
framework with no further work.

items.name: Cslib.Query.mergeSort_lowerBound
items.doc: Merge sort has worst-case query complexity at least `⌈log₂(n!)⌉`.
items.statement:
theorem mergeSort_lowerBound [Infinite α] :
    LowerBound (mergeSort (α := α)) List.length (fun n => Nat.clog 2 (Nat.factorial n))

items.name: Cslib.Query.clog_factorial_le_mul_clog
items.doc:
Sanity check that the bounds compose: comparing merge sort's upper and lower bounds
yields this arithmetic fact with no further work.
items.statement:
theorem clog_factorial_le_mul_clog (n : ℕ) :
    Nat.clog 2 (Nat.factorial n) ≤ n * Nat.clog 2 n

modules.authors: Kim Morrison, Shreyas Srinivas, Eric Wieser, Sorrachai Yingchareonthawornchai
modules.title: Merge Sort as a Query Program
modules.doc:
Merge sort implemented as a `FreeM (LEQuery α)`, making all comparison queries explicit.
The definitions mirror `List.merge` and `List.mergeSort` exactly: the list is split into
contiguous halves and the merge prefers the left element on ties. Consequently evaluating
the query program against any oracle produces literally the same list as `List.mergeSort`
with the comparator induced by the oracle (`eval_mergeSort` in
`Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.Query.Sort.Merge.Lemmas`); in particular the sort is stable.
The recursive calls of `mergeSort` are not structural, since the two halves are not
syntactic subterms, and are justified separately using their lengths.

items.name: List.split
items.doc:
Split a list into contiguous halves; if the length is odd, the first half is one element
longer. This agrees with `List.MergeSort.Internal.splitInTwo`, so that `mergeSort` agrees
with `List.mergeSort`.
items.statement: def split (xs : List α) : List α × List α

items.name: List.split_fst_length_eq
items.statement:
theorem split_fst_length_eq (xs : List α) :
(split xs).1.length = (xs.length + 1) / 2

items.name: List.split_snd_length_eq
items.statement:
theorem split_snd_length_eq (xs : List α) :
(split xs).2.length = xs.length / 2

items.name: List.split_fst_append_split_snd
items.statement: theorem split_fst_append_split_snd (xs : List α) : (split xs).1 ++ (split xs).2 = xs

items.name: List.splitInTwo_fst
items.statement:
theorem splitInTwo_fst (xs : {l : List α // l.length = n}) :
    (List.MergeSort.Internal.splitInTwo xs).1 = xs.val.split.1

items.name: List.splitInTwo_snd
items.statement:
theorem splitInTwo_snd (xs : {l : List α // l.length = n}) :
    (List.MergeSort.Internal.splitInTwo xs).2 = xs.val.split.2

items.name: Cslib.Query.merge
items.doc: Merge two sorted lists using comparison queries.
items.statement: abbrev merge (xs ys : List α) : FreeM (LEQuery α) (List α)

items.name: Cslib.Query.mergeSort
items.doc: Sort a list using merge sort with comparison queries.
items.statement: abbrev mergeSort (xs : List α) : FreeM (LEQuery α) (List α)

modules.authors: Kim Morrison, Shreyas Srinivas, Eric Wieser, Sorrachai Yingchareonthawornchai
modules.title: Merge Sort: Correctness and Upper Bound
modules.doc:
Proofs that `mergeSort` is a correct comparison sort and uses at most `n * ⌈log₂ n⌉` queries.

`eval_mergeSort` identifies the query program with `List.mergeSort`: evaluating against any
oracle produces the same list as `List.mergeSort` with the comparator induced by the oracle.
Correctness properties (permutation, sortedness) transfer directly from the `List.mergeSort`
API. The query bound is proved by equational reasoning on `FreeM.countQueries`, which has no
`List` counterpart.

items.name: Cslib.Query.eval_merge
items.doc:
Evaluating the query-based merge agrees with `List.merge` using the relation supplied
by the oracle.
items.statement:
theorem eval_merge (oracle : {ι : Type} → LEQuery α ι → ι) (xs ys : List α) :
(merge xs ys).eval oracle = xs.merge ys (fun a b => oracle (.le a b))

items.name: Cslib.Query.eval_mergeSort
items.doc:
Evaluating query-based merge sort agrees with `List.mergeSort` using the relation
supplied by the oracle.

This is the essential correctness statement: it identifies the query program as *the*
merge sort operation, so correctness properties (permutation, sortedness, stability)
transfer directly from the `List.mergeSort` API rather than being restated here.
items.statement:
theorem eval_mergeSort (oracle : {ι : Type} → LEQuery α ι → ι) (xs : List α) :
(mergeSort xs).eval oracle = xs.mergeSort (fun a b => oracle (.le a b))

items.name: Cslib.Query.mergeSort_perm
items.statement:
theorem mergeSort_perm (oracle : {ι : Type} → LEQuery α ι → ι) (xs : List α) :
    (mergeSort xs).eval oracle ~ xs

items.name: Cslib.Query.mergeSort_sorted
items.statement:
theorem mergeSort_sorted
    (r : α → α → Prop) [DecidableRel r] [Std.Total r] [IsTrans α r]
    (oracle : {ι : Type} → LEQuery α ι → ι)
    (horacle : ∀ a b, oracle (.le a b) = decide (r a b))
    (xs : List α) :
    ((mergeSort xs).eval oracle).Pairwise r

items.name: Cslib.Query.countQueries_merge_nil_left
items.statement:
theorem countQueries_merge_nil_left (oracle : {ι : Type} → LEQuery α ι → ι) (ys : List α) :
    (merge ([] : List α) ys).countQueries oracle = 0

items.name: Cslib.Query.countQueries_merge_nil_right
items.statement:
theorem countQueries_merge_nil_right (oracle : {ι : Type} → LEQuery α ι → ι) (xs : List α) :
    (merge xs ([] : List α)).countQueries oracle = 0

items.name: Cslib.Query.countQueries_merge_cons_cons
items.statement:
theorem countQueries_merge_cons_cons (oracle : {ι : Type} → LEQuery α ι → ι)
    (x : α) (xs' : List α) (y : α) (ys' : List α) :
    (merge (x :: xs') (y :: ys')).countQueries oracle =
      1 + if oracle (.le x y)
      then (merge xs' (y :: ys')).countQueries oracle
      else (merge (x :: xs') ys').countQueries oracle

items.name: Cslib.Query.countQueries_mergeSort_nil
items.statement:
theorem countQueries_mergeSort_nil (oracle : {ι : Type} → LEQuery α ι → ι) :
    (mergeSort (α := α) []).countQueries oracle = 0

items.name: Cslib.Query.countQueries_mergeSort_singleton
items.statement:
theorem countQueries_mergeSort_singleton (oracle : {ι : Type} → LEQuery α ι → ι) (x : α) :
    (mergeSort [x]).countQueries oracle = 0

items.name: Cslib.Query.countQueries_mergeSort_cons_cons
items.statement:
theorem countQueries_mergeSort_cons_cons (oracle : {ι : Type} → LEQuery α ι → ι)
(x y : α) (zs : List α) :
(mergeSort (x :: y :: zs)).countQueries oracle =
(mergeSort (x :: y :: zs).split.1).countQueries oracle +
((mergeSort (x :: y :: zs).split.2).countQueries oracle +
(merge ((x :: y :: zs).split.1.mergeSort fun a b => oracle (.le a b))
      ((x :: y :: zs).split.2.mergeSort fun a b => oracle (.le a b))).countQueries
 oracle)

items.name: Cslib.Query.merge_countQueries_le
items.statement:
theorem merge_countQueries_le (oracle : {ι : Type} → LEQuery α ι → ι)
    (xs ys : List α) :
    (merge xs ys).countQueries oracle ≤ xs.length + ys.length

items.name: Cslib.Query.mergeSort_countQueries_le
items.statement:
theorem mergeSort_countQueries_le (oracle : {ι : Type} → LEQuery α ι → ι)
    (xs : List α) :
    (mergeSort xs).countQueries oracle ≤ xs.length * Nat.clog 2 xs.length

items.name: Cslib.Query.mergeSort_upperBound
items.statement:
theorem mergeSort_upperBound :
    UpperBound (mergeSort (α := α)) List.length (fun n => n * Nat.clog 2 n)

items.name: Cslib.Query.mergeSort_isSort
items.statement: theorem mergeSort_isSort : IsSort (mergeSort (α := α))

modules.title: TimeM: Time Complexity Monad
modules.doc:
`TimeM T α` represents a computation that produces a value of type `α` and tracks its time cost.

`T` is usually instantiated as `ℕ` to count operations, but can be instantiated as `ℝ` to count
actual wall time, or as more complex types in order to model more general costs.

## Design Principles
1. **Pure inputs, timed outputs**: Functions take plain values and return `TimeM` results
2. **Time annotations are trusted**: The `time` field is NOT verified against actual cost.
   You must manually ensure annotations match the algorithm's complexity in your cost model.
3. **Separation of concerns**: Prove correctness properties on `.ret`, prove complexity on `.time`

## Cost Model
**Document your cost model explicitly** Decide and be consistent about:
- **What costs 1 unit?** (comparison, arithmetic operation, etc.)
- **What is free?** (variable lookup, pattern matching, etc.)
- **Recursive calls:** Do you charge for the call itself?

## Notation
- **`✓`** : A tick of time, see `tick`.
- **`⟪tm⟫`** : Extract the pure value from a `TimeM` computation (notation for `tm.ret`)

## References

See [Danielsson2008] for the discussion.

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM
items.doc:
A monad for tracking time complexity of computations.
`TimeM T α` represents a computation that returns a value of type `α`
and accumulates a time cost (represented as a type `T`, typically `ℕ`).
items.statement:
structure TimeM (T : Type*) (α : Type*) where
  /-- The return value of the computation -/
  ret : α
  /-- The accumulated time cost of the computation -/
  time : T

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.pure
items.doc:
Lifts a pure value into a `TimeM` computation with zero time cost.

Prefer to use `pure` instead of `TimeM.pure`.
items.statement: protected def pure [Zero T] {α} (a : α) : TimeM T α

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.bind
items.doc:
Sequentially composes two `TimeM` computations, summing their time costs.

Prefer to use the `>>=` notation.
items.statement: protected def bind {α β} [Add T] (m : TimeM T α) (f : α → TimeM T β) : TimeM T β

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.ret_pure
items.statement: theorem ret_pure {α} [Zero T] (a : α) : (pure a : TimeM T α).ret = a

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.ret_bind
items.statement:
theorem ret_bind {α β} [Add T] (m : TimeM T α) (f : α → TimeM T β) :
(m >>= f).ret = (f m.ret).ret

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.ret_map
items.statement: theorem ret_map {α β} (f : α → β) (x : TimeM T α) : (f <$> x).ret = f x.ret

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.ret_mapConst
items.statement:
theorem ret_mapConst {α β} (a : α) (x : TimeM T β) :
(Functor.mapConst a x).ret = a

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.ret_seqRight
items.statement:
theorem ret_seqRight {α} (x : TimeM T α) (y : Unit → TimeM T β) [Add T] :
(SeqRight.seqRight x y).ret = (y ()).ret

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.ret_seqLeft
items.statement:
theorem ret_seqLeft {α} [Add T] (x : TimeM T α) (y : Unit → TimeM T β) :
(SeqLeft.seqLeft x y).ret = x.ret

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.ret_seq
items.statement:
theorem ret_seq {α β} [Add T] (f : TimeM T (α → β)) (x : Unit → TimeM T α) :
(Seq.seq f x).ret = f.ret (x ()).ret

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.isMonadHom_pure_ret
items.statement: theorem isMonadHom_pure_ret [AddZero T] : Cslib.IsMonadHom (TimeM T) Id (fun x => pure x.ret)

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.time_bind
items.statement:
theorem time_bind {α β} [Add T] (m : TimeM T α) (f : α → TimeM T β) :
(m >>= f).time = m.time + (f m.ret).time

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.time_pure
items.statement: theorem time_pure {α} [Zero T] (a : α) : (pure a : TimeM T α).time = 0

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.time_map
items.statement: theorem time_map {α β} (f : α → β) (x : TimeM T α) : (f <$> x).time = x.time

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.time_seqRight
items.statement:
theorem time_seqRight {α} [Add T] (x : TimeM T α) (y : Unit → TimeM T β) :
(SeqRight.seqRight x y).time = x.time + (y ()).time

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.time_seqLeft
items.statement:
theorem time_seqLeft {α} [Add T] (x : TimeM T α) (y : Unit → TimeM T β) :
(SeqLeft.seqLeft x y).time = x.time + (y ()).time

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.time_seq
items.statement:
theorem time_seq {α β} [Add T] (f : TimeM T (α → β)) (x : Unit → TimeM T α) :
(Seq.seq f x).time = f.time + (x ()).time

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.tick
items.doc: Creates a `TimeM` computation with a time cost.
items.statement: def tick (c : T) : TimeM T PUnit

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.ret_tick
items.statement: theorem ret_tick (c : T) : (tick c).ret = ()

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.TimeM.time_tick
items.statement: theorem time_tick (c : T) : (tick c).time = c

modules.title: Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange in Stateful Processes (testbed)
modules.doc:
This module formalises the Diffie-Hellman key exchange protocol in `StatefulProcesses`.

It is also intended as a simple testbed to measure improvement on how CSLib deals with embedded DSLs
like Stateful Processes and reasoning on operational semantics.

Current aspects that stand out and could be more ergonomic are:
1. The integration of Lean terms within expressions for computation at processes requires
  significant plumbing. Ideally, it should be seamless.
2. The protocol has two obvious symbolic traces, yet proving `net_completeTraces` is cumbersome.
  Perhaps an API for unique transitions could be partially helpful:
```
def _root_.Cslib.LTS.TrUnique (lts : LTS State Label) (s : State) (μ : Label) (s' : State) :=
  lts.Tr s μ s' ∧ ∀ μ' s'', lts.Tr s μ' s'' → μ' = μ ∧ s'' = s'
```
  The terms for `Alice` and `Bob` after one and two steps of their executions are provided as
  reference for this endeavour.
3. As a consequence of (2), proving `net_fun_correct` is cumbersome.

## Implementation notes

The current implementation requires proofs that `p` is prime and that `g` is a primitive root modulo
`p`, but does not use these facts. They are reserved for future work on security results.

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.StatefulProcesses.DiffieHellman.Params
items.doc: Parameters of the DH protocol.
items.statement:
structure Params (Pid Var : Type*) where
  /-- Alice. -/
  alice : Pid
  /-- Bob. -/
  bob : Pid
  /-- Alice and Bob have different names. -/
  alice_neq_bob : alice ≠ bob
  /-- Alice's private key (secret). -/
  a : ℕ
  /-- Bob's private key (secret). -/
  b : ℕ
  /-- Bob's variable to store Alice's message. -/
  x : Var
  /-- Alice's variable to store Bob's message. -/
  y : Var
  /-- The variable used to store the shared key. -/
  s : Var
  /-- The prime modulus `p`. -/
  p : ℕ
  /-- `p` is prime. -/
  p_prime : Nat.Prime p
  /-- The generator `g`. -/
  g : ZMod p
  /-- `g` is a primitive root modulo `p`. -/
  g_primitive_root_p : IsPrimitiveRoot g (p - 1)
  /-- SelLabel type for instantiating stateful processes. -/
  SelLabel : Type*
  /-- ProcName type for instantiating stateful processes. -/
  ProcName : Type*

items.name: Cslib.Algorithms.StatefulProcesses.DiffieHellman.computePublicMessage_computeSharedSecret_eq

theorem computePublicMessage_computeSharedSecret_eq (p : ℕ) (g : ZMod p) (a b : ℕ) :

items.name: Cslib.Automata.Acceptor
items.doc: An `Acceptor` is a machine that recognises strings (lists of symbols in an alphabet).
items.statement:
class Acceptor (A : Type u) (Symbol : outParam (Type v)) where
  /-- Predicate that establishes whether a string `xs` is accepted. -/

items.name: Cslib.Automata.Acceptor.mem_language
items.doc: A string is in the language of an acceptor iff the acceptor accepts it.

modules.title: Deterministic Automata
modules.doc:
A Deterministic Automaton (`DA`) is an automaton defined by a transition function equipped with an
initial state.

Automata with different accepting conditions are then defined as extensions of `DA`.
These include, for example, a generalised version of DFA as found in the literature (without
finiteness assumptions), deterministic Buchi automata, and deterministic Muller automata.

## References

* [J. E. Hopcroft, R. Motwani, J. D. Ullman,
  *Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation*][Hopcroft2006]

items.name: Cslib.Automata.DA
items.doc: A deterministic automaton extends a `FLTS` with a unique initial state.
items.statement:
structure DA (State Symbol : Type*) extends FLTS State Symbol where
  /-- The initial state of the automaton. -/
  start : State

items.name: Cslib.Automata.DA.run'
items.doc: Helper function for defining `run` below.
items.statement: def run' (da : DA State Symbol) (xs : ωSequence Symbol) : ℕ → State

items.name: Cslib.Automata.DA.run
items.doc: Infinite run.
items.statement: def run (da : DA State Symbol) (xs : ωSequence Symbol) : ωSequence State

items.name: Cslib.Automata.DA.run_zero
items.statement:
theorem run_zero {da : DA State Symbol} {xs : ωSequence Symbol} :
    da.run xs 0 = da.start

items.name: Cslib.Automata.DA.run_succ
items.statement:
theorem run_succ {da : DA State Symbol} {xs : ωSequence Symbol} {n : ℕ} :
    da.run xs (n + 1) = da.tr (da.run xs n) (xs n)

items.name: Cslib.Automata.DA.mtr_extract_eq_run
items.statement:
theorem mtr_extract_eq_run {da : DA State Symbol} {xs : ωSequence Symbol} {n : ℕ} :
    da.mtr da.start (xs.extract 0 n) = da.run xs n

items.name: Cslib.Automata.DA.FinAcc
items.doc: A deterministic automaton that accepts finite strings (lists of symbols).
items.statement:
structure FinAcc (State Symbol : Type*) extends DA State Symbol where
  /-- The set of accepting states. -/
  accept : Set State

items.name: Cslib.Automata.DA.Buchi
items.doc: Deterministic Buchi automaton.
items.statement:
structure Buchi (State Symbol : Type*) extends DA State Symbol where
  /-- The set of accepting states. -/
  accept : Set State

items.name: Cslib.Automata.DA.Muller
items.doc: Deterministic Muller automaton.
items.statement:
structure Muller (State Symbol : Type*) extends DA State Symbol where
  /-- The set of sets of accepting states. -/
  accept : Set (Set State)

items.name: Cslib.Automata.DA.buchi_eq_finAcc_omegaLim
items.doc:
The ω-language accepted by a deterministic Buchi automaton is the ω-limit
of the language accepted by the same automaton.
items.statement:
theorem buchi_eq_finAcc_omegaLim {da : DA State Symbol} {acc : Set State} :
    language (Buchi.mk da acc) = (language (FinAcc.mk da acc))↗ω

modules.title: Deterministic automaton corresponding to a right congruence.

items.name: Language.RightCongruence.toDA
items.doc:
Every right congruence gives rise to a DA whose states are the equivalence classes of
the right congruence, whose start state is the empty word, and whose transition functiuon
is concatenation on the right of the input symbol. Note that the transition function is
well-defined only because `c` is a right congruence.
items.statement: def RightCongruence.toDA [c : RightCongruence Symbol] : Automata.DA (Quotient c.eq) Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Automata.DA.congr_mtr_eq
items.doc:
After consuming a finite word `xs`, `c.toDA` reaches the state `⟦ xs ⟧` which is
the equivalence class of `xs`.
items.statement:
theorem congr_mtr_eq {xs : List Symbol} :
    c.toDA.mtr c.toDA.start xs = ⟦ xs ⟧

items.name: Cslib.Automata.DA.congr_mtr_append
items.doc:
After consuming a finite word `ys` from the state `⟦ xs ⟧`, `c.toDA` reaches
the state `⟦ xs ++ ys ⟧`.
items.statement:
theorem congr_mtr_append {xs ys : List Symbol} :
    c.toDA.mtr ⟦ xs ⟧ ys = ⟦ xs ++ ys ⟧

items.name: Cslib.Automata.DA.FinAcc.congr_language_eq
items.doc:
The language of `c.toDA` with a single accepting state `s` is exactly
the equivalence class corresponding to `s`.
items.statement: theorem congr_language_eq {a : Quotient c.eq} : language (FinAcc.mk c.toDA {a}) = eqvCls a

items.name: Cslib.Automata.DA.prod
items.doc: The product of two deterministic automata.
items.statement: def prod (da1 : DA State1 Symbol) (da2 : DA State2 Symbol) : DA (State1 × State2) Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Automata.DA.prod_mtr_eq
items.doc:
A state is reachable by the product automaton iff its components are reachable by
the respective automaton components.
items.statement:
theorem prod_mtr_eq (da1 : DA State1 Symbol) (da2 : DA State2 Symbol)
    (s : State1 × State2) (xs : List Symbol) :
    (da1.prod da2).mtr s xs = (da1.mtr s.fst xs, da2.mtr s.snd xs)

modules.doc: This is the general version of the standard translation of DFAs into NFAs.

items.doc: `DA` is a special case of `NA`.
items.statement: def toNA (a : DA State Symbol) : NA State Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Automata.DA.toNA_run
items.statement:
theorem toNA_run {a : DA State Symbol} {xs : ωSequence Symbol} {ss : ωSequence State} :
    a.toNA.Run xs ss ↔ a.run xs = ss
