items.doc: `DA.FinAcc` is a special case of `NA.FinAcc`.
items.statement: def toNAFinAcc (a : DA.FinAcc State Symbol) : NA.FinAcc State Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Automata.DA.FinAcc.toNAFinAcc_language_eq
items.doc: The `NA.FinAcc` constructed from a `DA.FinAcc` has the same language.
items.statement:
theorem toNAFinAcc_language_eq {a : DA.FinAcc State Symbol} :
    language a.toNAFinAcc = language a

items.name: Cslib.Automata.DA.Buchi.toNABuchi
items.doc: `DA.Buchi` is a special case of `NA.Buchi`.
items.statement: def toNABuchi (a : DA.Buchi State Symbol) : NA.Buchi State Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Automata.DA.Buchi.toNABuchi_language_eq
items.doc: The `NA.Buchi` constructed from a `DA.Buchi` has the same ω-language.
items.statement:
theorem toNABuchi_language_eq {a : DA.Buchi State Symbol} :
    language a.toNABuchi = language a

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA
items.doc:
A nondeterministic finite automaton with ε-transitions (`εNA`) is an `NA` with an `Option`
symbol type. The special symbol ε is represented by the `Option.none` case.

Internally, ε (`Option.none`) is treated as the `τ` label of the underlying transition system,
allowing for reusing the definitions and results on saturated transitions of `LTS` to deal with
ε-closure.
items.statement: structure εNA (State Symbol : Type*) extends NA State (Option Symbol)

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.εClosure
items.doc:
The `ε`-closure of a set of states `S` is the set of states reachable by any state in `S`
by performing only `ε`-transitions. We use `LTS.τClosure` since `ε` (`Option.none`) is an instance
of `HasTau.τ`.
items.statement: abbrev εNA.εClosure (a : εNA State Symbol) (S : Set State)

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.filter_ne_τ_eq_map_some
items.statement:
theorem filter_ne_τ_eq_map_some {μs : List (Option Symbol)} :
    μs.filter (· ≠ HasTau.τ) = μs.reduceOption.map some

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc
items.doc: The finite-word acceptance condition of an `εNA` is a set of accepting states.
items.statement:
structure FinAcc (State Symbol : Type*) extends εNA State Symbol where
  /-- The set of accepting states. -/
  accept : Set State

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.mem_language_iff
items.doc:
A word is accepted if and only if a plain run from an initial to an accepting state reads it
once its `ε`s are dropped.
items.statement:
theorem mem_language_iff {a : FinAcc State Symbol} {xs : List Symbol} :
    xs ∈ language a ↔ ∃ s ∈ a.start, ∃ t ∈ a.accept,
      ∃ μs : List (Option Symbol), μs.reduceOption = xs ∧ a.MTr s μs t

modules.title: The ε-NA of a regular expression
modules.doc:
Thompson's construction [Thompson1968]: every regular expression is sent to an `εNA` with finitely
many states that accepts exactly its language, by assembling the automata of
`Cslib.Computability.Automata.EpsilonNA.ThompsonConstruction`.

## Main definitions

* `RegularExpression.State r`: the states of the automaton of `r`.
* `RegularExpression.toEpsilonNA r`: the automaton of `r`.

## Main statements

* `RegularExpression.language_toEpsilonNA`: the automaton of `r` accepts exactly `r.matches'`.

## References

* [K. Thompson, *Regular expression search algorithm*][Thompson1968]

items.name: RegularExpression.State
items.doc: The states of the automaton of a regular expression.
items.statement: def State : RegularExpression α → Type

items.name: RegularExpression.instFiniteState
items.doc: The automaton of a regular expression has finitely many states.
items.statement: instance instFiniteState : (r : RegularExpression α) → Finite r.State

items.name: RegularExpression.toEpsilonNA
items.doc: Thompson's construction: the `εNA` of a regular expression.
items.statement: def toEpsilonNA : (r : RegularExpression α) → FinAcc r.State α

items.name: RegularExpression.language_toEpsilonNA
items.doc: The automaton of a regular expression accepts exactly its language.
items.statement:
theorem language_toEpsilonNA (r : RegularExpression α) :
    language r.toEpsilonNA = r.matches'

modules.title: Thompson's construction
modules.doc:
Thompson's construction turns a regular expression into an `εNA` with a single initial state and
at most one accepting state [Thompson1968]. This file defines the automata it is assembled from,
with their languages.

## Main definitions

* `εNA.FinAcc.zero`, `εNA.FinAcc.epsilon`, `εNA.FinAcc.char x`: automata for the empty language,
  the empty word and the word `[x]`.
* `εNA.FinAcc.sum a b`: the states and transitions of `a` and `b` side by side, through
  `LTS.unionSum`.
* `εNA.FinAcc.union a b`: `sum a b` with a single initial and a single accepting state, through
  `toSingleStartAccept`.
* `εNA.FinAcc.concat a b`: `ε`-transitions from the accepting states of `a` to the initial states
  of `b`.
* `εNA.FinAcc.star a`: a fresh hub state, initial and accepting, with `ε`-transitions to the
  initial states of `a` and from its accepting states.

## Main statements

* `εNA.FinAcc.language_zero`, `εNA.FinAcc.language_epsilon`, `εNA.FinAcc.language_char`,
  `εNA.FinAcc.language_sum`, `εNA.FinAcc.language_union`, `εNA.FinAcc.language_concat` and
  `εNA.FinAcc.language_star`.

## References

* [K. Thompson, *Regular expression search algorithm*][Thompson1968]

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.zero
items.doc: An automaton with a single state, initial but not accepting, and no transitions.
items.statement: def zero : FinAcc Unit Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.epsilon
items.doc: An automaton with a single state, initial and accepting, and no transitions.
items.statement: def epsilon : FinAcc Unit Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.char
items.doc:
An automaton with two states, `false` initial and `true` accepting, joined by an
`x`-transition.
items.statement: def char (x : Symbol) : FinAcc Bool Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.language_zero
items.statement: theorem language_zero : language (zero : FinAcc Unit Symbol) = 0

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.language_epsilon
items.statement: theorem language_epsilon : language (epsilon : FinAcc Unit Symbol) = 1

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.language_char
items.statement: theorem language_char (x : Symbol) : language (char x) = {[x]}

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.sum
items.doc:
The disjoint sum of `a` and `b`: their states and transitions side by side (`LTS.unionSum`),
with the initial and the accepting states of both.
items.statement: def sum (a : FinAcc S₁ Symbol) (b : FinAcc S₂ Symbol) : FinAcc (S₁ ⊕ S₂) Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.language_sum
items.statement:
theorem language_sum (a : FinAcc S₁ Symbol) (b : FinAcc S₂ Symbol) :
    language (sum a b) = language a + language b

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.union
items.doc:
The union of `a` and `b`: their disjoint sum, with a single initial state and a single
accepting state added by `toSingleStartAccept`.
items.statement: def union (a : FinAcc S₁ Symbol) (b : FinAcc S₂ Symbol) : FinAcc (Bool ⊕ (S₁ ⊕ S₂)) Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.language_union
items.statement:
theorem language_union (a : FinAcc S₁ Symbol) (b : FinAcc S₂ Symbol) :
    language (union a b) = language a + language b

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.ConcatTr
items.doc: The transitions of `concat a b`, whose states are those of `a` followed by those of `b`.
items.statement:
inductive ConcatTr (a : FinAcc S₁ Symbol) (b : FinAcc S₂ Symbol) :
    S₁ ⊕ S₂ → Option Symbol → S₁ ⊕ S₂ → Prop
  | left {s μ s'} : a.Tr s μ s' → ConcatTr a b (.inl s) μ (.inl s')
  | right {s μ s'} : b.Tr s μ s' → ConcatTr a b (.inr s) μ (.inr s')
  | bridge {s s'} : s ∈ a.accept → s' ∈ b.start → ConcatTr a b (.inl s) none (.inr s')

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.concat
items.doc:
The concatenation of `a` and `b`: `ε`-transitions lead from the accepting states of `a` to the
initial states of `b`.
items.statement: def concat (a : FinAcc S₁ Symbol) (b : FinAcc S₂ Symbol) : FinAcc (S₁ ⊕ S₂) Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.concat_mTr_inr
items.doc: A run of `concat a b` between two states of `b` is a run of `b`.
items.statement:
theorem concat_mTr_inr {s t : S₂} {μs : List (Option Symbol)}
    (h : (concat a b).MTr (.inr s) μs (.inr t)) : b.MTr s μs t

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.concat_mTr_inl
items.doc:
A run of `concat a b` from a state of `a` to a state of `b` is a run of `a` to an accepting
state, an `ε`-transition to an initial state of `b`, and a run of `b`.
items.statement:
theorem concat_mTr_inl {s : S₁} {t : S₂} {μs : List (Option Symbol)}
    (h : (concat a b).MTr (.inl s) μs (.inr t)) :
    ∃ s₁ ∈ a.accept, ∃ s₂ ∈ b.start, ∃ μs₁ μs₂, a.MTr s μs₁ s₁ ∧ b.MTr s₂ μs₂ t ∧
      μs = μs₁ ++ none :: μs₂

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.language_concat
items.statement:
theorem language_concat (a : FinAcc S₁ Symbol) (b : FinAcc S₂ Symbol) :
    language (concat a b) = language a * language b

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.StarTr
items.doc: The transitions of `star a`, whose states are a fresh hub `inl ()` and the states of `a`.
items.statement:
inductive StarTr (a : FinAcc S₁ Symbol) : Unit ⊕ S₁ → Option Symbol → Unit ⊕ S₁ → Prop
  | inner {s μ s'} : a.Tr s μ s' → StarTr a (.inr s) μ (.inr s')
  | enter {s} : s ∈ a.start → StarTr a (.inl ()) none (.inr s)
  | exit {s} : s ∈ a.accept → StarTr a (.inr s) none (.inl ())

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.star
items.doc:
The Kleene star of `a`: a fresh hub state, initial and accepting, with `ε`-transitions to the
initial states of `a` and from its accepting states.
items.statement: def star (a : FinAcc S₁ Symbol) : FinAcc (Unit ⊕ S₁) Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.star_mTr_inr
items.doc:
A run of `star a` from a state of `a` to the hub is a run of `a` to an accepting state, an
`ε`-transition to the hub, and a run from the hub back to the hub.
items.statement:
theorem star_mTr_inr {s : S₁} {μs : List (Option Symbol)}
    (h : (star a).MTr (.inr s) μs (.inl ())) :
    ∃ t ∈ a.accept, ∃ μs₁ μs₂, a.MTr s μs₁ t ∧ (star a).MTr (.inl ()) μs₂ (.inl ()) ∧
      μs = μs₁ ++ none :: μs₂

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.reduceOption_mem_kstar_of_star_mTr
items.doc: A run of `star a` from the hub back to the hub reads a word of `(language a)∗`.
items.statement:
theorem reduceOption_mem_kstar_of_star_mTr {μs : List (Option Symbol)}
    (h : (star a).MTr (.inl ()) μs (.inl ())) : μs.reduceOption ∈ (language a)∗

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.exists_star_mTr_of_mem_kstar
items.doc: Every word of `(language a)∗` is read by a run of `star a` from the hub back to the hub.
items.statement:
theorem exists_star_mTr_of_mem_kstar {xs : List Symbol} (hxs : xs ∈ (language a)∗) :
    ∃ μs : List (Option Symbol), μs.reduceOption = xs ∧ (star a).MTr (.inl ()) μs (.inl ())

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.language_star
items.statement: theorem language_star (a : FinAcc S₁ Symbol) : language (star a) = (language a)∗

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.toNAFinAcc
items.doc: Any `εNA.FinAcc` can be converted into an `NA.FinAcc` that does not use ε-transitions.
items.statement: def toNAFinAcc (a : εNA.FinAcc State Symbol) : NA.FinAcc State Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.toNAFinAcc_language_eq
items.doc: Correctness of `toNAFinAcc`.
items.statement:
theorem toNAFinAcc_language_eq {a : εNA.FinAcc State Symbol} :
    language a.toNAFinAcc = language a

modules.title: Translation of εNA into εNA with a single start and a single accept state
modules.doc:
Defines the transformation `toSingleStartAccept` for `εNA.FinAcc`, which adds a start state with
ε-transitions to the original start states and no incoming transitions, and an accept state with
ε-transitions from the original accept states and no outgoing transitions. The transformation
preserves the language of the automaton.

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.toSingleStartAccept
items.doc:
Any `εNA.FinAcc` can be converted into an `εNA.FinAcc` with a single start state and a single
accept state. The original states are wrapped in `inr`, and the fresh state `inl b` is accepting
exactly when `b`: the start state `inl false` has ε-transitions to the original start states, and
the original accept states have ε-transitions to the accept state `inl true`.
items.statement: def toSingleStartAccept (a : εNA.FinAcc State Symbol) : εNA.FinAcc (Bool ⊕ State) Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.toSingleStartAccept_start
items.statement: theorem toSingleStartAccept_start : a.toSingleStartAccept.start = {.inl false}

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.toSingleStartAccept_accept
items.statement: theorem toSingleStartAccept_accept : a.toSingleStartAccept.accept = {.inl true}

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.toSingleStartAccept_tr_inr_inr
items.statement:
theorem toSingleStartAccept_tr_inr_inr {s s' : State} {μ : Option Symbol} :
    a.toSingleStartAccept.Tr (.inr s) μ (.inr s') ↔ a.Tr s μ s'

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.toSingleStartAccept_tr_start
items.statement:
theorem toSingleStartAccept_tr_start {s : State} (hs : s ∈ a.start) :
    a.toSingleStartAccept.Tr (.inl false) none (.inr s)

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.toSingleStartAccept_tr_accept
items.statement:
theorem toSingleStartAccept_tr_accept {s : State} (hs : s ∈ a.accept) :
    a.toSingleStartAccept.Tr (.inr s) none (.inl true)

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.toSingleStartAccept_tr_inl_false
items.doc: The transitions from the start state are ε-transitions to the original start states.

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.toSingleStartAccept_not_tr_inl_false
items.doc: No transition leads to the start state.
items.statement:
theorem toSingleStartAccept_not_tr_inl_false {x : Bool ⊕ State} {μ : Option Symbol} :
    ¬a.toSingleStartAccept.Tr x μ (.inl false)

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.toSingleStartAccept_not_tr_inl_true
items.doc: No transition leaves the accept state.
items.statement:
theorem toSingleStartAccept_not_tr_inl_true {μ : Option Symbol} {y : Bool ⊕ State} :
    ¬a.toSingleStartAccept.Tr (.inl true) μ y

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.toSingleStartAccept_mTr_inr_inl_true
items.doc:
A run from an original state to the accept state is a run of the original automaton to an
original accept state, followed by the ε-transition to the accept state.

items.name: Cslib.Automata.εNA.FinAcc.toSingleStartAccept_language_eq
items.doc: `toSingleStartAccept` preserves the language of the input automaton.
items.statement: theorem toSingleStartAccept_language_eq : language a.toSingleStartAccept = language a

modules.authors: Fabrizio Montesi, Ching-Tsun Chou, Chris Henson
modules.title: Nondeterministic Automaton
modules.doc:
A Nondeterministic Automaton (NA) is a transition relation equipped with a set of initial states.

Automata with different accepting conditions are then defined as extensions of `NA`.
These include, for example, a generalised version of NFA as found in the literature (without
finiteness assumptions), nondeterministic Buchi automata, and nondeterministic Muller automata.

This definition extends `LTS` and thus stores the transition system as a relation `Tr` of the form
`State → Symbol → State → Prop`. Note that you can also instantiate `Tr` by passing an argument of
type `State → Symbol → Set State`; it gets automatically expanded to the former shape.

## References

* [J. E. Hopcroft, R. Motwani, J. D. Ullman,
  *Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation*][Hopcroft2006]

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA
items.doc: A nondeterministic automaton extends a `LTS` with a set of initial states.
items.statement:
structure NA (State Symbol : Type*) extends LTS State Symbol where
  /-- The set of initial states of the automaton. -/
  start : Set State

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.Run
items.doc: Infinite run.
items.statement:
structure Run (na : NA State Symbol) (xs : ωSequence Symbol) (ss : ωSequence State) where
  start : ss 0 ∈ na.start
  trans : na.OmegaExecution ss xs

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.FinAcc
items.doc: A nondeterministic automaton that accepts finite strings (lists of symbols).
items.statement:
structure FinAcc (State Symbol : Type*) extends NA State Symbol where
  /-- The set of accepting states. -/
  accept : Set State

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.Buchi
items.doc: Nondeterministic Buchi automaton.
items.statement:
structure Buchi (State Symbol : Type*) extends NA State Symbol where
  /-- The set of accepting states. -/
  accept : Set State

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.Muller
items.doc: Nondeterministic Muller automaton.
items.statement:
structure Muller (State Symbol : Type*) extends NA State Symbol where
  /-- The set of sets of accepting states. -/
  accept : Set (Set State)

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.Buchi.reindex
items.doc: Lifts an equivalence on states to an equivalence on NBAs.
items.statement: def reindex (f : State ≃ State') : Buchi State Symbol ≃ Buchi State' Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.Buchi.reindex_run_iff
Cslib.Automata.NA.Buchi.reindex_run_iff'
Cslib.Automata.NA.Buchi.reindex_language_eq
items.statement:
theorem reindex_language_eq {f : State ≃ State'} {nba : Buchi State Symbol} :
    language (nba.reindex f) = language nba

modules.title: Intersection of nondeterministic Buchi automata.
modules.doc:
The intersection automaton consists of the product of the two automata to be intersected
plus a history state which is a pointer to one of the two automata. It waits for the
accepting condition of the automaton being pointed to by the history state. Once it sees that,
it toggles the history state to wait for the accepting condition of the other automaton.
The intersection automaton accepts iff the toggling happens infinitely many times.

The two automata to be intersected are indexed by the type `Bool`.  We choose `Bool`
simply because toggling can be easily modeled by the boolean operation `not`.

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.Buchi.histStart
items.doc: The initial history state.
items.statement: def histStart (_ : Π i, State i) : Bool

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.Buchi.interAcc
items.doc: The two accepting conditions of the intersection automaton.
items.statement: def interAcc (j : Bool) (acc : (i : Bool) → Set (State i)) : Set ((Π i, State i) × Bool)

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.Buchi.histTrans
items.doc: The transition function of the history state.
items.statement:
noncomputable def histTrans (acc : (i : Bool) → Set (State i))
    (s : (Π i, State i) × Bool) (_ : Symbol) (_ : Π i, State i) : Bool

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.Buchi.interNA
items.doc: The intersection automaton.
items.statement:
noncomputable def interNA (na : (i : Bool) → NA (State i) Symbol)
    (acc : (i : Bool) → Set (State i)) : NA ((Π i, State i) × Bool) Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.Buchi.interAccept
items.doc: The overall accepting condition of the intersection automaton.
items.statement: def interAccept (acc : (i : Bool) → Set (State i)) : Set ((Π i, State i) × Bool)

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.Buchi.inter_freq_acc_freq_acc
items.doc:
If the intersection automaton sees one accepting condition infinitely many times,
then it sees the other accepting condition infinitely many times as well.

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.Buchi.inter_freq_comp_acc_freq_acc
items.doc:
If the intersection automaton sees the accepting conditions of both component automata
infinitely many times, then its own accepting condition also happens infinitely many times.
items.statement:
lemma inter_freq_comp_acc_freq_acc {xs : ωSequence Symbol} {ss : ωSequence ((Π i, State i) × Bool)}
    (h_run : (interNA na acc).Run xs ss)
    (h_inf_f : ∃ᶠ k in atTop, ss k ∈ {s | s.fst false ∈ acc false})
    (h_inf_t : ∃ᶠ k in atTop, ss k ∈ {s | s.fst true ∈ acc true}) :
    ∃ᶠ k in atTop, ss k ∈ interAccept acc

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.Buchi.inter_language_eq
items.doc:
The language accepted by the intersection automaton is the intersection of
the languages accepted by the two component automata.
items.statement:
theorem inter_language_eq :
    language (Buchi.mk (interNA na acc) (interAccept acc)) =
    ⨅ i, language (Buchi.mk (na i) (acc i))

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.concat
items.doc:
`concat na1 na2` starts by running `na1` and then nondeterministically switches to `na2`
by identifying an accepting state of `na1` with an initial state of `na2`. If `na1` accepts the
empty word, it may also start running `na2` from the beginning. Once it starts running `na2`,
it cannot go back to `na1`.
items.statement: def concat (na1 : FinAcc State1 Symbol) (na2 : NA State2 Symbol) : NA (State1 ⊕ State2) Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.concat_start_right
items.statement:
lemma concat_start_right {xs : ωSequence Symbol} {ss : ωSequence (State1 ⊕ State2)}
    (hc : (concat na1 na2).Run xs ss) (hr : (ss 0).isRight) : [] ∈ language na1

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.concat_run_left
Cslib.Automata.NA.concat_run_left_right
Cslib.Automata.NA.concat_run_right
Cslib.Automata.NA.concat_run_proj
items.doc:
A run of `concat na1 na2` containing at least one `na2` state is the concatenation of
an accepting finite run of `na1` followed by a run of `na2`.
items.statement:
theorem concat_run_proj {xs : ωSequence Symbol} {ss : ωSequence (State1 ⊕ State2)} {k : ℕ}
    (hc : (concat na1 na2).Run xs ss) (hr : (ss k).isRight) :
    ∃ n, n ≤ k ∧ xs.take n ∈ language na1 ∧
    ∃ ss2, na2.Run (xs.drop n) ss2 ∧ ss.drop n = ss2.map inr

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.concat_run_exists
items.doc:
Given an accepting finite run of `na1` and a run of `na2`, there exists a run of
`concat na1 na2` that is the concatenation of the two runs.

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.Buchi.concat_language_eq
items.doc:
The Buchi automaton formed from `concat na1 na2` accepts the ω-language that is
the concatenation of the language of `na1` and the ω-language of `na2`.
items.statement:
theorem concat_language_eq {acc2 : Set State2} :
    language (Buchi.mk (concat na1 na2) (inr '' acc2)) =
    language na1 * language (Buchi.mk na2 acc2)

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.FinAcc.finConcat
items.doc: `finConcat na1 na2` is the concatenation of the "totalized" versions of `na1` and `na2`.
items.statement:
def finConcat (na1 : FinAcc State1 Symbol) (na2 : FinAcc State2 Symbol)
  : NA (Option State1 ⊕ Option State2) Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.FinAcc.finConcat_language_eq
items.doc: `finConcat na1 na2` accepts the concatenation of the languages of `na1` and `na2`.
items.statement:
theorem finConcat_language_eq [Inhabited Symbol] :
    language (FinAcc.mk (finConcat na1 na2) (inr '' (some '' na2.accept))) =
    language na1 * language na2

modules.title: Nondeterministic finite ε-transducers
modules.doc: Transducers based on `NA` with an invisible symbol in their input and output alphabets.

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.εTransducer
items.doc:
A nondeterministic ε-transducer of finite strings where the input and output alphabets include
an invisible symbol, modelled as `HasTau.τ` (typically called `ε`).
items.statement:
structure εTransducer (State InSymbol OutSymbol : Type*)
    extends NA State (InSymbol × OutSymbol) where
  /-- The set of accepting states. -/
  accept : Set State

items.name: List.dropTaus
items.doc: Removes all `τ`s from a list.
items.statement: def _root_.List.dropTaus [HasTau α] [DecidableEqTau α] (l : List α) : List α

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.εTransducer.MTransl
items.doc:
An `εTransducer` translates `xs` into `ys` from state `s` to state `s'` if there is a
multistep transition from `s` to `s'` whose visible projection is `(xs, ys)`.
`MTransl` is short for Multistep Translation relation.
items.statement:
def MTransl [DecidableEqTau InSymbol] [DecidableEqTau OutSymbol]
    (a : εTransducer State InSymbol OutSymbol) (s : State)
    (xs : List InSymbol) (ys : List OutSymbol) (s' : State) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.εTransducer.MTransl.comp
items.doc: Composition of multistep translations.
items.statement:
theorem MTransl.comp [DecidableEqTau InSymbol] [DecidableEqTau OutSymbol]
    {a : εTransducer State InSymbol OutSymbol}
    {s₁ s₂ s₃ : State} {xs xs' : List InSymbol} {ys ys' : List OutSymbol} :
    a.MTransl s₁ xs ys s₂ → a.MTransl s₂ xs' ys' s₃ →
    a.MTransl s₁ (xs ++ xs') (ys ++ ys') s₃

modules.title: Adding a history states to a nondeterministic automaton.
modules.doc:
The evolution of the history state can depend on both the original state and the past history
state. But the evolution of the original state is not constrained by the history state.

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.addHist
items.doc:
The construction of adding a history state.  Note that `start'` can depend on the initial
value of the original state and `tr'` can depend on the new value of the original state.
So there is no loss of generality in their being functions, rather than relations.
items.statement:
def addHist (na : NA State Symbol) (start' : State → Hist)
    (tr' : State × Hist → Symbol → State → Hist) : NA (State × Hist) Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.hist_run_proj
items.doc: Every run of the history automaton projects onto a run of the original automaton.
items.statement:
theorem hist_run_proj {xs : ωSequence Symbol} {ss : ωSequence (State × Hist)}
    (h_run : (na.addHist start' tr').Run xs ss) : na.Run xs (ss.map fst)

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.makeHist
items.doc: Given a run of the original automaton, `makeHist` builds a run of the history state.
items.statement:
def makeHist (start' : State → Hist) (tr' : State × Hist → Symbol → State → Hist)
    (xs : ωSequence Symbol) (ss : ωSequence State) : ℕ → Hist

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.hist_run_exists
items.doc:
For every run `ss` of the original automaton, there exists a run `ss'` of the history automaton
which projects back onto `ss`.
items.statement:
theorem hist_run_exists {xs : ωSequence Symbol} {ss : ωSequence State}
    (h_run : na.Run xs ss) : ∃ ss', (na.addHist start' tr').Run xs ss' ∧ ss'.map fst = ss

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.FinAcc.loop
items.doc:
`na.loop` mimics `na`, but can nondeterministically decide to "loop back" by identifying
an accepting state of `na` with a starting state of `na`.  This identification is achieved
via a new dummy state `()`, which is the sole starting state and the sole accepting state
of `na.loop`.
items.statement: def FinAcc.loop (na : FinAcc State Symbol) : NA (Unit ⊕ State) Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.loop_run_left_left
items.statement:
lemma loop_run_left_left {xs : ωSequence Symbol} {ss : ωSequence (Unit ⊕ State)}
    (h : na.loop.Run xs ss) (h1 : (ss 1).isLeft) : [xs 0] ∈ language na

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.loop_run_left_right
Cslib.Automata.NA.loop_run_left_right_left
Cslib.Automata.NA.loop_run_from_left
Cslib.Automata.NA.loop_run_one_iter
items.doc:
A run of `na.loop` containing at least one non-initial `()` state is the concatenation
of a nonempty finite run of `na` followed by a run of `na.loop`.

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.loop_fin_run_exists
items.doc: For any finite word in `language na`, there is a corresponding finite run of `na.loop`.
items.statement:
theorem loop_fin_run_exists {xl : List Symbol} (h : xl ∈ language na) :
    ∃ sl : List (Unit ⊕ State), ∃ _ : sl.length = xl.length + 1,
    sl[0] = inl () ∧ sl[xl.length] = inl () ∧
    ∀ k, (_ : k < xl.length) → na.loop.Tr sl[k] xl[k] sl[k + 1]

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.loop_fin_run_mtr
items.doc:
For any finite word in `language na`, there is a corresponding multistep transition
of `na.loop`.
items.statement:
theorem loop_fin_run_mtr {xl : List Symbol} (h : xl ∈ language na) :
    na.loop.MTr (inl ()) xl (inl ())

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.loop_run_exists
items.doc:
For any infinite sequence `xls` of nonempty finite words from `language na`,
there is an infinite run of `na.loop` corresponding to `xls.flatten` in which
the state `()` marks the boundaries between the finite words in `xls`.

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.Buchi.loop_language_eq
items.doc: The Buchi ω-language accepted by `na.loop` is the ω-power of the language accepted by `na`.
items.statement:
theorem loop_language_eq [Inhabited Symbol] :
    language (Buchi.mk na.loop {inl ()}) = (language na)^ω

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.FinAcc.finLoop
items.doc: `finLoop na` is the loop construction applied to the "totalized" version of `na`.
items.statement: def finLoop (na : FinAcc State Symbol) : NA (Unit ⊕ Option State) Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.FinAcc.loop_language_eq
items.doc:
`finLoop na` accepts the Kleene star of the language of `na`, assuming that
the latter is nonempty.
items.statement:
theorem loop_language_eq [Inhabited Symbol] (h : ¬ language na = 0) :
    language (FinAcc.mk na.finLoop {inl ()}) = (language na)∗

modules.title: Languages determined by pairs of states

items.name: Cslib.LTS.pairLang
items.doc:
`LTS.pairLang s t` is the language of finite words that can take the LTS
from state `s` to state `t`.
items.statement: def LTS.pairLang (lts : LTS State Symbol) (s t : State) : Language Symbol

items.name: Cslib.LTS.mem_pairLang
items.statement:
theorem LTS.mem_pairLang {lts : LTS State Symbol} {s t : State} {xs : List Symbol} :
    xs ∈ lts.pairLang s t ↔ lts.MTr s xs t

items.name: Cslib.LTS.pairLang_regular
items.doc: `LTS.pairLang s t` is a regular language if there are only finitely many states.
items.statement:
theorem LTS.pairLang_regular [Finite State] {lts : LTS State Symbol} {s t : State} :
    (lts.pairLang s t).IsRegular

items.name: Cslib.LTS.pairViaLang
items.doc:
`LTS.pairViaLang via s t` is the language of finite words that can take the LTS

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.Buchi.language_eq_fin_iSup_hmul_omegaPow
items.doc:
The ω-language accepted by a finite-state Büchi automaton is the finite union of ω-languages
of the form `L * M^ω`, where all `L`s and `M`s are regular languages.
items.statement:
theorem language_eq_fin_iSup_hmul_omegaPow
    [Inhabited Symbol] [Finite State] (na : Buchi State Symbol) :
    language na = ⨆ s ∈ na.start, ⨆ t ∈ na.accept, (na.pairLang s t) * (na.pairLang t t)^ω

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.FinAcc.preimage
items.doc:
Given a language homomorphism `f` from `Symbol'` to `Symbol` and an NA `na` on `Symbol`,
`na.preimage f` is an NA on `Symbol` with the same state space, start states, and
accept states, but with a different transition relation: the step that `na.preimage f` takes
on input `x` is the composition of the steps taken by `na` on inputs `f [x]`.
items.statement: def preimage (na : FinAcc State Symbol) : FinAcc State Symbol'

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.FinAcc.accepts_preimage

modules.title: Reversal of nondeterministic automata
modules.doc:
This file defines `Cslib.Automata.NA.FinAcc.reverse`, which reverses every transition of a
nondeterministic automaton and swaps its start and accept states. Its underlying transition system
is `Cslib.LTS.reverse`, so the transition results are inherited from
`Cslib/Foundations/Semantics/LTS/Reverse.lean`.

The main result is `FinAcc.reverse_language_eq`: the language accepted by `na.reverse` is the
`Language.reverse` of the language accepted by `na`. It follows from `FinAcc.accepts_reverse`,
the statement that `na.reverse` accepts `xs` iff `na` accepts `xs.reverse`.

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.FinAcc.reverse
items.doc:
`na.reverse` reverses every transition of `na` and swaps its start and accept states,
so that it accepts exactly the reversals of the words accepted by `na`.
items.statement: def reverse (na : FinAcc State Symbol) : FinAcc State Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.FinAcc.reverse_reverse
items.doc: Reversing an automaton twice gives back the original automaton.
items.statement: theorem reverse_reverse (na : FinAcc State Symbol) : na.reverse.reverse = na

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.FinAcc.reverse_involutive
items.doc: Reversal of an automaton is an involution.
items.statement: theorem reverse_involutive : Function.Involutive (reverse (State := State) (Symbol := Symbol))

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.FinAcc.reverse_start
items.doc: The start states of `na.reverse` are the accept states of `na`.
items.statement: theorem reverse_start (na : FinAcc State Symbol) : na.reverse.start = na.accept

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.FinAcc.reverse_accept
items.doc: The accept states of `na.reverse` are the start states of `na`.
items.statement: theorem reverse_accept (na : FinAcc State Symbol) : na.reverse.accept = na.start

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.FinAcc.reverse_mTr
items.doc:
The multistep transitions of `na.reverse` are exactly the reversed multistep transitions
of `na`.
items.statement:
theorem reverse_mTr (na : FinAcc State Symbol) {xs : List Symbol} {s s' : State} :
    na.reverse.MTr s' xs s ↔ na.MTr s xs.reverse s'

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.FinAcc.accepts_reverse
items.doc: `na.reverse` accepts a word iff `na` accepts its reversal.
items.statement:
theorem accepts_reverse {na : FinAcc State Symbol} {xs : List Symbol} :
    Accepts na.reverse xs ↔ Accepts na xs.reverse

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.FinAcc.reverse_language_eq
items.doc: `na.reverse` accepts exactly the reversals of the words accepted by `na`.
items.statement:
theorem reverse_language_eq (na : FinAcc State Symbol) :
    language na.reverse = (language na).reverse

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.Buchi.iSum_language_eq
items.doc:
The ω-language accepted by the Buchi sum automata is the union of the ω-languages accepted
by its component automata.
items.statement:
theorem iSum_language_eq {na : (i : I) → NA (State i) Symbol} {acc : (i : I) → Set (State i)} :

    ⨆ i, language (Buchi.mk (na i) (acc i))

modules.title: Nondeterministic Two-Way Automaton
modules.doc:
A Nondeterministic Two-Way Automaton (`TwoWayNA`) reads a finite input word on a tape and may move
its input head in either direction. A transition reads the symbol under the head and, besides
changing the state, moves the head one cell to the left, keeps it in place, or moves it one cell to
the right.

The input head cannot leave the input word to the left (in the sense that execution gets stuck in
this case) and once it leaves the word to the right, it stops. A run is accepting if and only if it
ends in an accepting state with the head just past the end of the input.

## Main definitions

* `TwoWayNA`, the automaton itself
* `TwoWayNACfg`, a configuration of a `TwoWayNA`: Its input plus a state and the head position.
* `TwoWayNA.toCfgNA`, the finite acceptor on configurations whose runs on a fixed input are
  the runs of the two-way automaton on that input. It also provides the `Acceptor` instance.

## Implementation notes

The definition of `TwoWayNA` is kept close to [Vardi][Vardi1989]'s, because the main point is to
prove that it accepts the same languages as `NA.FinAcc` via his proof. This means we do not allow
the head to move off the input to the left (in the sense that if the transition relation has an
entry that would cause that, there is no successor configuration, the computation is stuck), but
also do not provide an end marker. Once the head moves off to the right, the machine instantly
stops, so it also cannot move back into the word.

## References

* [Moshe Y. Vardi, *A Note on the Reduction of Two-Way Automata to One-Way Automata*][Vardi1989]

items.name: Cslib.Automata.TwoWayNA
items.doc:
A nondeterministic two-way automaton: a transition relation that reads an input symbol and
moves the input head, together with a set of initial and a set of accepting states.
items.statement:
structure TwoWayNA (State Symbol : Type*) where
  /-- The transition relation. `Tr q x m q'` means that, while reading the symbol `x`, the
  automaton attempts to transition from state `q` to state `q'` and move its head according to
  `m`. -/
  Tr (q : State) (x : Symbol) (m : SignType) (q' : State) : Prop
  /-- The set of initial states of the automaton. -/
  start : Set State
  /-- The set of accepting states of the automaton. -/
  accept : Set State

items.name: Cslib.Automata.TwoWayNACfg
items.doc: The configuration of a two-way nondeterministic automaton.
items.statement:
structure TwoWayNACfg (State Symbol : Type*) where
  /-- The original input to the automaton. -/
  input : List Symbol
  /-- The state of the automaton. -/
  state : State
  /-- The input head position of the automaton: it can be on any symbol of the input or on the
  position one step to the right of the input. -/
  pos : Fin (input.length + 1)

items.name: Cslib.Automata.TwoWayNACfg.IsInitialForInput
items.doc: This defines the set of initial configurations on a specific input.
items.statement:
def TwoWayNACfg.IsInitialForInput (a : TwoWayNA State Symbol) (c : TwoWayNACfg State Symbol)
    (input : List Symbol) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.Automata.TwoWayNACfg.IsAccepting
items.doc: If a configuration is a accepting.
items.statement: def TwoWayNACfg.IsAccepting (a : TwoWayNA State Symbol) (c : TwoWayNACfg State Symbol) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.Automata.TwoWayNA.toCfgNA
items.doc:
Returns a nondeterministic finite acceptor on the configurations as states, accepting exactly
the runs of the two-way automaton on `input` that end in an accepting configuration.

items.name: Cslib.Automata.TwoWayNA.toCfgNA_input_eq
items.doc: Any reachable state of `a.toCfgNA input` contains the original input.
items.statement:
lemma TwoWayNA.toCfgNA_input_eq {State Symbol : Type*} (a : TwoWayNA State Symbol)
    (input : List Symbol) :
    (a.toCfgNA input).TrInv (fun c => c.input = input)

items.name: Cslib.Automata.TwoWayNACfg.eta
items.doc: A configuration running on `input` is the one determined by its state and head position.

items.name: Cslib.Automata.TwoWayNA.getElem_of_tr
items.doc: A step reads the symbol at the head position, which therefore lies inside the input.

modules.title: A finite acceptor for the complement of the language of a two-way automaton
modules.doc:
For every nondeterministic two-way automaton (`TwoWayNA`) `a`, this file constructs a
nondeterministic finite acceptor (`NA.FinAcc`) that accepts exactly the words rejected by `a`
(`TwoWayNA.complToNA`, `TwoWayNA.language_complToNA`). We follow Vardi's proof, which --
unlike Shepherdson's crossing-sequence argument -- characterises non-acceptance in a way that can
be checked by a single left-to-right sweep over the input.

This result is the main ingredient in proving equivalence of two-way and one-way automata, which
can be found in `Cslib.Computability.Languages.RegularLanguages`.

## Vardi's condition of non-acceptance

Fix a `TwoWayNA` `a` and an input word `input` of length `n`. A *rejection certificate* is a family
of subsets `cert i ⊆ State`, one for every head position `i ∈ {0, …, n}`, subject to three
conditions:

1. `cert` contains every initial state at position `0` (`IsRejectionCert.start_mem`);
2. `cert` is an invariant of the transitions of `a`: if the state `c.state` is in `cert c.pos` and
  `a` can step from the configuration `c` to the configuration `c'`, then `c'.state` is in
  `cert c'.pos` (`TwoWayNA.IsStepClosed`, `IsRejectionCert.step_closed`);
3. no state in `cert n`, i.e. at the position just past the end of the input, is accepting
   (`IsRejectionCert.accept_notMem`).

Intuitively, `cert i` over-approximates the set of states in which `a` can be while its head sits at
position `i`: conditions 1 and 2 make `cert` an inductive invariant of the reachable configurations,
and condition 3 says that this invariant rules out acceptance -- being preserved by every step, it
holds at the end of every run (`LTS.mtrInv_of_trInv`). Conversely, the reachable states
(`TwoWayNA.reachable`) themselves form the least such family, so a certificate exists exactly when
`a` rejects (`TwoWayNA.not_accepts_iff_exists_isRejectionCert`).

## The finite acceptor for the complement

The point of the reformulation is locality: `TwoWayNA.isStepClosed_iff_localOK` turns condition 2
into a condition `TwoWayNA.LocalOK` relating only `cert (i - 1)`, `cert i` and `cert (i + 1)` with
the symbol at position `i`. A finite acceptor can therefore guess the certificate while scanning the
input, keeping only the last two subsets in its state. This is `TwoWayNA.complToNA`, and
`TwoWayNA.accepts_complToNA_iff` shows that it accepts exactly the words rejected by `a`.

## Implementation notes

A rejection certificate is an `ωSequence`, i.e. indexed by `ℕ` rather than by
`Fin (input.length + 1)`, the type of `TwoWayNACfg.pos`: positions past the end of the input are
simply left unconstrained, which avoids casts when the certificate is compared along a run, whose
configurations carry their own input. The subset for the missing position to the left of the input
is supplied by prepending `Set.univ` with `ωSequence.cons`.

`TwoWayNA.exists_accepting_mTr_iff` is proved by induction on the input word, prepending a subset
to the certificate at each step with `ωSequence.cons` and dropping one with `ωSequence.tail`.

## References

* [M. Y. Vardi, *A note on the reduction of two-way automata to one-way automata*][Vardi1989]

items.name: Cslib.Automata.TwoWayNA.IsStepClosed
items.doc:
Every step of `a` on `input` out of a state that `cert` attaches to the head position lands in a
state that `cert` attaches to the new head position. The conjunct on the input restricts the
invariant to the configurations that run on `input`.
items.statement:
def IsStepClosed (a : TwoWayNA State Symbol) (input : List Symbol)
    (cert : ωSequence (Set State)) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.Automata.TwoWayNA.IsRejectionCert
items.doc:
A family of subsets of the state set, one for every position of the input head on `input`,
which contains all initial states, is closed under the transitions of `a`, and contains no
accepting state at the position just past the end of the input.
items.statement:
structure IsRejectionCert (a : TwoWayNA State Symbol) (input : List Symbol)
    (cert : ωSequence (Set State)) : Prop where
  /-- Every initial state occurs at the initial head position. -/
  start_mem : ∀ s ∈ a.start, s ∈ cert 0
  /-- The family is an invariant of the transitions of `a`. -/
  step_closed : a.IsStepClosed input cert
  /-- No accepting state occurs past the end of the input. -/
  accept_notMem : ∀ s ∈ cert input.length, s ∉ a.accept

items.name: Cslib.Automata.TwoWayNA.IsRejectionCert.not_accepts
items.doc: If a rejection certificate for `input` exists, then `a` does not accept `input`.
items.statement:
theorem IsRejectionCert.not_accepts (hT : a.IsRejectionCert input cert) :
    ¬ Accepts a input

items.name: Cslib.Automata.TwoWayNA.reachable
items.doc:
The set of states that `a` can be in while its head sits at position `i` of `input`, having
started in an initial configuration.
items.statement: def reachable (a : TwoWayNA State Symbol) (input : List Symbol) : ωSequence (Set State)

items.name: Cslib.Automata.TwoWayNA.isRejectionCert_reachable
items.doc: If `a` does not accept `input`, then its reachable states form a rejection certificate.
items.statement:
theorem isRejectionCert_reachable (h : ¬ Accepts a input) :
    a.IsRejectionCert input (a.reachable input)

items.name: Cslib.Automata.TwoWayNA.not_accepts_iff_exists_isRejectionCert
items.doc: A two-way automaton rejects an input exactly when a rejection certificate for it exists.
items.statement:
theorem not_accepts_iff_exists_isRejectionCert (a : TwoWayNA State Symbol)
    (input : List Symbol) :
    ¬ Accepts a input ↔ ∃ T, a.IsRejectionCert input T

items.name: Cslib.Automata.TwoWayNA.LocalOK
items.doc:
Every move of `a` out of a state in `cur` while reading `x` lands in `left`, in `cur` or in
`right`, according to whether it moves the head to the left, keeps it in place, or moves it to the
right.
items.statement: def LocalOK (a : TwoWayNA State Symbol) (x : Symbol) (left cur right : Set State) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.Automata.TwoWayNA.isStepClosed_iff_localOK
items.doc:
Closure of `cert` under the transitions of `a` is the same as local consistency of `cert` at
every position carrying an input symbol.
items.statement:
theorem isStepClosed_iff_localOK :
    a.IsStepClosed input cert ↔
      ∀ i : Fin input.length,
        a.LocalOK input[i] ((Set.univ ::ω cert) i) (cert i) (cert (i + 1))

items.note: ## The finite acceptor for the complement

items.name: Cslib.Automata.TwoWayNA.complToNA
items.doc:
The nondeterministic finite acceptor that guesses a rejection certificate `cert` for `a` while
scanning the input, keeping the pair `(cert (i - 1), cert i)` in its state after reading `i`
symbols.
Reading the symbol at position `i` guesses `cert (i + 1)` and checks local consistency at `i`.
items.statement: def complToNA (a : TwoWayNA State Symbol) : NA.FinAcc (Set State × Set State) Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Automata.TwoWayNA.exists_accepting_mTr_iff
items.doc:
An accepting multistep transition of `a.complToNA` out of `(left, cur)` over `xs` is the same
thing as a certificate starting with `left` and `cur` that is locally consistent at every position
of `xs` and has no accepting state at the position just past `xs`.
items.statement:
theorem exists_accepting_mTr_iff (a : TwoWayNA State Symbol) (xs : List Symbol)
    (left cur : Set State) :
    (∃ f ∈ a.complToNA.accept, a.complToNA.MTr (left, cur) xs f) ↔
      ∃ cert : ωSequence (Set State), cert 0 = left ∧ cert 1 = cur ∧
        (∀ i, ∀ hi : i < xs.length, a.LocalOK xs[i] (cert i) (cert (i + 1)) (cert (i + 2))) ∧
          ∀ s ∈ cert (xs.length + 1), s ∉ a.accept

items.name: Cslib.Automata.TwoWayNA.accepts_complToNA_iff
items.doc: `a.complToNA` accepts exactly the words that `a` rejects.
items.statement:
theorem accepts_complToNA_iff (a : TwoWayNA State Symbol) (input : List Symbol) :
    Accepts a.complToNA input ↔ ¬ Accepts a input

items.name: Cslib.Automata.TwoWayNA.language_complToNA
items.doc: `a.complToNA` recognises the complement of the language of `a`.
items.statement: theorem language_complToNA (a : TwoWayNA State Symbol) : language a.complToNA = (language a)ᶜ

modules.title: Finite acceptors as two-way automata
modules.doc:
A nondeterministic finite acceptor (`NA.FinAcc`) is the special case of a nondeterministic two-way
automaton (`TwoWayNA`) that moves its head one symbol to the right in every step,
`NA.FinAcc.toTwoWayNA`.

The head of `a.toTwoWayNA` is thus at position `i` exactly when `a` has read the first `i`
symbols of the input, so the runs of the two-way automaton are in lockstep with the multistep
transitions of `a` (`TwoWayNA.mTr_take_of_mTr_toCfgNA`, `TwoWayNA.mTr_toCfgNA_of_mTr`) and the two
accept the same words (`TwoWayNA.accepts_toTwoWayNA_iff`, `TwoWayNA.language_toTwoWayNA`).

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.FinAcc.toTwoWayNA
items.doc:
The two-way automaton that performs the transitions of the nondeterministic finite acceptor
`n`, always moving its head one symbol to the right.
items.statement: def NA.FinAcc.toTwoWayNA (n : NA.FinAcc State Symbol) : TwoWayNA State Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Automata.TwoWayNA.mTr_take_of_mTr_toCfgNA
items.doc:
A run of `a.toTwoWayNA` that starts in an initial configuration reads a multistep transition
of `a` over the prefix of `input` that its head has scanned.

items.name: Cslib.Automata.TwoWayNA.mTr_toCfgNA_of_mTr
items.doc:
A multistep transition of `a` over a prefix of `input` is read by the run of `a.toTwoWayNA`
that takes its head from the beginning of the input to the end of that prefix, moving one symbol
to the right in every step.
items.statement:
theorem mTr_toCfgNA_of_mTr {s s' : State} {pre : List Symbol} (hpre : pre <+: input)
    (hmtr : a.MTr s pre s') :
    (a.toTwoWayNA.toCfgNA input).MTr ⟨input, s, 0⟩ (pre.map (·, SignType.pos))
      ⟨input, s', ⟨pre.length, by grind⟩⟩

items.name: Cslib.Automata.TwoWayNA.accepts_toTwoWayNA_iff
items.doc: A nondeterministic finite acceptor and its two-way rendering accept the same words.
items.statement:
theorem accepts_toTwoWayNA_iff (a : NA.FinAcc State Symbol) (input : List Symbol) :
    Accepts a.toTwoWayNA input ↔ Accepts a input

items.name: Cslib.Automata.TwoWayNA.language_toTwoWayNA
items.doc: A nondeterministic finite acceptor and its two-way rendering recognise the same language.
items.statement: theorem language_toTwoWayNA (a : NA.FinAcc State Symbol) : language a.toTwoWayNA = language a

modules.title: Circuits
modules.doc:
A circuit is a straight-line `Program` together with a choice of output wires.
Any input or internal-gate wire may be designated as an output, and designating
an output is free: projections and duplicated outputs cost no gates. The size
of a circuit is its gate count and its depth is the maximum depth of a
designated output wire.

For the standard Boolean circuit model, see [Arora and Barak, Section 6.1][AroraBarak09].
Here a topological ordering is part of the representation, and the Boolean gate
basis is generalized to an arbitrary `Signature` and `Interpretation`. Our size
counts only operation gates; Arora and Barak count all nodes, including inputs.
An output wire may also supply a later gate.

A circuit computes a function with as many values as it has outputs when its designated
outputs agree with the function on every input; a single-valued function `f`, written `single f`,
is computed by a circuit with one output. Evaluation commutes with homomorphisms of interpretations.

## References

* [S. Arora and B. Barak, *Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach*,
  Section 6.1][AroraBarak09]

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit
items.doc: A straight-line program with designated output wires.
items.statement:
structure Circuit (σ : Signature) (inputCount outputCount : Nat) where
  /-- The number of gates in the program; inputs and designated outputs cost nothing. -/
  {size : Nat}
  /-- The internal gates of the circuit. -/
  program : Program σ inputCount size
  /-- The input or internal-gate wire carrying each output. -/
  outputs : Fin outputCount → Wire inputCount size

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.ext
items.statement:
protected theorem Circuit.ext {c₁ c₂ : Circuit σ inputCount outputCount} (hsize : c₁.size = c₂.size)
    (hp : c₁.program = hsize ▸ c₂.program) (ho : c₁.outputs = hsize ▸ c₂.outputs) : c₁ = c₂

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.wiring
items.doc:
The zero-gate circuit whose outputs are the inputs chosen by `select`. Projections,
duplications, and permutations of the inputs cost no gates.
items.statement:
def Circuit.wiring (σ : Signature) (select : Fin outputCount → Fin inputCount) :
    Circuit σ inputCount outputCount

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.id
items.doc: The zero-gate identity circuit, whose outputs are its inputs.
items.statement: protected abbrev Circuit.id (σ : Signature) (inputCount : Nat) : Circuit σ inputCount inputCount

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.size_wiring
items.statement:
theorem Circuit.size_wiring (select : Fin outputCount → Fin inputCount) :
(wiring σ select).size = 0

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.program_wiring
items.statement:
theorem Circuit.program_wiring (select : Fin outputCount → Fin inputCount) :
(wiring σ select).program = .empty

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.outputs_wiring
items.statement:
theorem Circuit.outputs_wiring (select : Fin outputCount → Fin inputCount) :
(wiring σ select).outputs = .input ∘ select

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.mapInputs
items.doc: Map the inputs of a circuit through a function.
items.statement:
def Circuit.mapInputs {inputCount' : ℕ} (f : Fin inputCount → Fin inputCount')
    (c : Circuit σ inputCount outputCount) : Circuit σ inputCount' outputCount

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.mapInputs_id
items.statement:
theorem Circuit.mapInputs_id :
(Circuit.mapInputs id :
Circuit σ inputCount outputCount → Circuit σ inputCount outputCount) = id

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.mapInputs_mapInputs
Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.comapOutputs
items.doc: Map the outputs of a circuit through a function.
items.statement:
def Circuit.comapOutputs {outputCount' : ℕ} (f : Fin outputCount' → Fin outputCount)
    (c : Circuit σ inputCount outputCount) : Circuit σ inputCount outputCount'

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.comapOutputs_id
items.statement:
theorem Circuit.comapOutputs_id :
(Circuit.comapOutputs id :
Circuit σ inputCount outputCount → Circuit σ inputCount outputCount) = id

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.comapOutputs_comapOutputs
items.statement:
theorem Circuit.comapOutputs_comapOutputs {outputCount' outputCount'' : ℕ}
    (g : Fin outputCount'' → Fin outputCount') (f : Fin outputCount' → Fin outputCount)
    (c : Circuit σ inputCount outputCount) :
    (c.comapOutputs f).comapOutputs g = c.comapOutputs (f ∘ g)

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.FanInAtMost
items.doc: Every gate in a circuit has at most `r` arguments.
items.statement: def Circuit.FanInAtMost (c : Circuit σ inputCount outputCount) (r : Nat) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.instDecidableFanInAtMost
items.doc: Bounded fan-in is decidable for every concrete circuit.
items.statement:
instance Circuit.instDecidableFanInAtMost
    (c : Circuit σ inputCount outputCount)
    (r : Nat) : Decidable (c.FanInAtMost r)

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.fanInAtMost_wiring
items.statement:
theorem Circuit.fanInAtMost_wiring (select : Fin outputCount → Fin inputCount)
(r : Nat) : (Circuit.wiring σ select).FanInAtMost r

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.outputDepths
items.doc: The depth of every designated output wire in a circuit.
items.statement: def Circuit.outputDepths (c : Circuit σ inputCount outputCount) : Fin outputCount → Nat

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.depth
items.doc: The maximum depth of a designated output wire in a circuit.
items.statement: def Circuit.depth (c : Circuit σ inputCount outputCount) : Nat

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.outputDepths_wiring
items.statement:
theorem Circuit.outputDepths_wiring (select : Fin outputCount → Fin inputCount) :
(Circuit.wiring σ select).outputDepths = fun _ => 0

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.depth_wiring
items.statement:
theorem Circuit.depth_wiring (select : Fin outputCount → Fin inputCount) :
(Circuit.wiring σ select).depth = 0

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.eval
items.doc: Read the designated output wires after evaluating the program.
items.statement:
def Circuit.eval
    (c : Circuit σ inputCount outputCount)
    (i : Interpretation σ U)
    (x : Fin inputCount → U) : Fin outputCount → U

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.inputSupport
items.doc: The original inputs that can reach a designated output.
items.statement:
def Circuit.inputSupport
    (c : Circuit σ inputCount outputCount) : Finset (Fin inputCount)

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.mem_inputSupport
items.statement:
theorem Circuit.mem_inputSupport
{c : Circuit σ inputCount outputCount}
{input : Fin inputCount} :
input ∈ c.inputSupport ↔
∃ output, input ∈ c.program.wireSupport (c.outputs output)

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.dependsOn_eval
items.doc: Circuit evaluation depends only on the inputs that can reach an output.
items.statement:
theorem Circuit.dependsOn_eval
    (c : Circuit σ inputCount outputCount)
    (interpretation : Interpretation σ U) :
    DependsOn (c.eval interpretation) (c.inputSupport : Set (Fin inputCount))

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.eval_wiring
items.doc: Output `j` of a wiring circuit is input `select j`.
items.statement:
theorem Circuit.eval_wiring (select : Fin outputCount → Fin inputCount)
(interpretation : Interpretation σ U) (input : Fin inputCount → U) :
(Circuit.wiring σ select).eval interpretation input = input ∘ select

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.eval_mapInputs
items.doc: Evaluating a circuit with relabeled inputs precomposes its input valuation.
items.statement:
theorem Circuit.eval_mapInputs {inputCount' : ℕ}
(c : Circuit σ inputCount outputCount) (f : Fin inputCount → Fin inputCount')
(i : Interpretation σ U) (inputs : Fin inputCount' → U) :
(c.mapInputs f).eval i inputs = c.eval i (inputs ∘ f)

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.eval_comapOutputs
items.doc: Selecting output wires selects the corresponding values after evaluation.
items.statement:
theorem Circuit.eval_comapOutputs {outputCount' : ℕ}
(c : Circuit σ inputCount outputCount) (f : Fin outputCount' → Fin outputCount)
(i : Interpretation σ U) (inputs : Fin inputCount → U) :
(c.comapOutputs f).eval i inputs = c.eval i inputs ∘ f

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.Computes
items.doc: A circuit computes `f` when its outputs agree with `f` on every input.

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.single
items.doc:
A single-valued function as a function with one output, which is what a circuit with one
output computes.
items.statement: def single (f : (Fin inputCount → U) → U) : (Fin inputCount → U) → Fin 1 → U

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.single_apply
items.statement:
theorem single_apply (f : (Fin inputCount → U) → U) (x : Fin inputCount → U)
(i : Fin 1) : single f x i = f x

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.ComputesOn
items.doc:
A circuit computes `f` on the support `S` when its outputs agree with `f` on every input in
`S`; what `f` does outside `S` does not matter.

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.computesOn_univ_iff
items.doc: Computing on every input is computing.
items.statement:
theorem Circuit.computesOn_univ_iff (c : Circuit σ inputCount outputCount)
(interpretation : Interpretation σ U) (f : (Fin inputCount → U) → Fin outputCount → U) :
c.ComputesOn interpretation Set.univ f ↔ c.Computes interpretation f

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.Computes.computesOn
items.doc: A circuit that computes `f` computes it on every support.

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.wiring_computes
items.doc: A wiring circuit computes the selection of its inputs.
items.statement:
theorem Circuit.wiring_computes (select : Fin outputCount → Fin inputCount)
    (interpretation : Interpretation σ U) :
    (Circuit.wiring σ select).Computes interpretation fun x => x ∘ select

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.map_eval
items.doc: Evaluating a circuit commutes with a homomorphism.
items.statement:
theorem Circuit.map_eval
    {i₁ : Interpretation σ U₁}
    {i₂ : Interpretation σ U₂}
    (c : Circuit σ inputCount outputCount)
    (h : Homomorphism i₁ i₂)
    (x : Fin inputCount → U₁) :
    h.map ∘ c.eval i₁ x = c.eval i₂ (h.map ∘ x)

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.computation
items.doc: All internal-gate values followed by the designated output values.
items.statement:
def Circuit.computation
    (c : Circuit σ inputCount outputCount)
    (i : Interpretation σ U)
    (x : Fin inputCount → U) : Fin (c.size + outputCount) → U

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.trace
items.doc: The input and internal-gate values followed by the designated outputs.
items.statement:
def Circuit.trace
    (c : Circuit σ inputCount outputCount)
    (i : Interpretation σ U)
    (x : Fin inputCount → U) : Fin (inputCount + c.size + outputCount) → U

modules.title: Boolean circuits
modules.doc:
The De Morgan basis consists of binary AND and OR, unary NOT, and Boolean constants.
Every gate has fan-in at most two, so these are the usual bounded fan-in Boolean circuits
(`Program.fanInAtMost_two`). Circuit size counts every gate, including constants;
designated output wires are free.

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Boolean.Op
items.doc: Operations of the De Morgan basis, including constants.
items.statement:
inductive Op where
  /-- A Boolean constant. -/
  | const (value : Bool)
  /-- Negation. -/
  | not
  /-- Binary conjunction. -/
  | and
  /-- Binary disjunction. -/
  | or
  deriving DecidableEq, Fintype

/-- The De Morgan basis has five operation symbols, counting its two constants. -/
@[simp] theorem Op.card : Fintype.card Op = 5 := rfl

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Boolean.Op.card
items.doc: The De Morgan basis has five operation symbols, counting its two constants.
items.statement: theorem Op.card : Fintype.card Op = 5

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Boolean.signature
items.doc: The De Morgan signature.
items.statement: abbrev signature : Signature

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Boolean.interpretation
items.doc: The usual Boolean interpretation.
items.statement: def interpretation : Interpretation signature Bool

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Program.fanInAtMost_two
items.doc: Every De Morgan program has fan-in at most two.
items.statement:
theorem Program.fanInAtMost_two {n g : ℕ} (p : Program Boolean.signature n g) :
    p.FanInAtMost 2

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Circuit.fanInAtMost_two
items.doc: Every De Morgan circuit has fan-in at most two.
items.statement:
theorem Circuit.fanInAtMost_two {n o : ℕ} (c : Circuit Boolean.signature n o) :
    c.FanInAtMost 2

modules.title: Completeness of the De Morgan basis
modules.doc:
Every Boolean function has a De Morgan circuit, by the Lupanov construction with no data
bits, so the basis is complete and `complexity interpretation f` is the circuit complexity of
`f` over it, for any number of outputs. This agrees with the standard measure of
[Jukna, Chapter 1][Jukna2012] up to the counting of constants and negations; see
`Cslib.Computability.Circuit.Boolean.Basic`.

## References

* [Stasys Jukna, *Boolean Function Complexity: Advances and Frontiers*][Jukna2012]

modules.title: Counting De Morgan circuits
modules.doc:
This file specializes the generic circuit counting bound to the five De Morgan operations,
all of arity at most two. The resulting factorial correction is used in Shannon's lower bound.

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Boolean.computableFunctions
items.doc: Boolean functions on `n` inputs computable with at most `s` De Morgan gates.
items.statement: noncomputable abbrev computableFunctions (n s : ℕ) : Finset (BooleanFunction n)

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Boolean.mem_computableFunctions
items.statement:
theorem mem_computableFunctions {f : BooleanFunction n} :
    f ∈ computableFunctions n s ↔
      ∃ c : Circuit signature n 1, c.Computes interpretation (single f) ∧ c.size ≤ s

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Boolean.card_computableFunctions_mul_factorial_le
items.doc: The De Morgan counting bound, accounting for gate relabelings.
items.statement:
theorem card_computableFunctions_mul_factorial_le (n s : ℕ) :
    (computableFunctions n s).card * s.factorial ≤
      (s + 1) * (5 * (n + s + 1) ^ 2) ^ s * (n + s)

modules.title: Lupanov's asymptotically optimal upper bound
modules.doc:
Every Boolean function on `n` inputs has a De Morgan circuit with at most
`(1 + ε) * 2 ^ n / n` gates for all sufficiently large `n`, given any `ε > 0`.
The threshold is uniform in the function; size counts constants and negations.
This matches Shannon's counting lower bound up to the factor `1 + ε`, which is why the
bound is called asymptotically optimal.

This file only does the asymptotics. The circuit comes from the block construction in
`LupanovConstruction.lean`, which gives, for any split of the inputs into `k` address bits
and `d` data bits and any positive block size `s`, a circuit with at most `bound k d s` gates.

## Choosing the parameters

Write `l = log₂ n`. We take `k = 3 l` address bits, `d = n - 3 l` data bits, and blocks of
`s = n - 5 l` rows. Then:

* the leading term of `bound` is `(2 ^ k / s + 1) · 2 ^ d ≈ 2 ^ n / s`, and since
  `s = n - 5 l` is `n (1 - o(1))`, this is `(1 + o(1)) 2 ^ n / n` (`mainTerm_le`);
* the minterms cost about `(2 ^ k + 2 ^ d) · 2 n = O(n ^ 4) + O(2 ^ n / n ^ 2)`, using
  `2 ^ k ≤ n ^ 3`;
* the `left` parts cost about `(2 ^ k / s) · 2 ^ s · 2 s ≈ 2 ^ (k + s) = 2 ^ (n - 2 l)`,
  which is `O(2 ^ n / n ^ 2)`.

`bound_le` packages the two error terms as `3 n ^ 4 + 16 n · 2 ^ d`;
`Nat.eventually_mul_pow_le_pow` and `error_le` show that the polynomial and the exponential
term are each `o(2 ^ n / n)`. Then `eventually_bound_le` combines everything into
`P · n · bound ≤ (P + 1) · 2 ^ n` for all large `n`, for any natural number `P`.
Taking `P > 1 / ε` in `exists_circuit` gives the theorem; `complexity_le` states it as a
bound on circuit complexity.

## References

* [O. B. Lupanov, *On a Method of Circuit Synthesis*][Lupanov1958],
  Theorem 4 and Section 6, pp. 131-135: the upper bound for general weighted bases,
  specialized here to the De Morgan basis.
* [Stasys Jukna, *Boolean Function Complexity: Advances and Frontiers*][Jukna2012],
  Theorem 1.15: a modern exposition.

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Boolean.Lupanov.exists_circuit
items.doc:
Lupanov's upper bound: every Boolean function on `n` inputs has a De Morgan circuit
with at most `(1 + ε) 2ⁿ/n` gates, uniformly for sufficiently large `n`.

Pick a natural number `P > 1 / ε`, so that `(P + 1) / P < 1 + ε`; then the threshold `m`
comes from `eventually_bound_le P`.
items.statement:
theorem exists_circuit (ε : ℝ) (hε : 0 < ε) :
    ∃ m : ℕ, ∀ n ≥ m, ∀ f : BooleanFunction n,
      ∃ c : Circuit signature n 1,
        c.Computes interpretation (single f) ∧ (c.size : ℝ) ≤ (1 + ε) * 2 ^ n / n

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Boolean.Lupanov.complexity_le
items.doc:
Lupanov's upper bound for circuit complexity: every Boolean function on `n` inputs has
complexity at most `(1 + ε) 2ⁿ/n`, uniformly for sufficiently large `n`.
items.statement:
theorem complexity_le (ε : ℝ) (hε : 0 < ε) :
    ∃ m : ℕ, ∀ n ≥ m, ∀ f : BooleanFunction n,
      (complexity interpretation (single f) : ℝ) ≤ (1 + ε) * 2 ^ n / n

modules.title: Lupanov's block construction
modules.doc:
This file is the finite, parametrised core of Lupanov's upper bound. Its purpose is to give a
gate budget `bound k d s` that is valid for every Boolean function on `k + d` inputs and every
positive block size `s`, and to prove (`synthesis`) that the budget suffices. The asymptotic file
`Lupanov.lean` then chooses `k`, `d`, and `s` as functions of `n` and shows that the budget is
`(1 + ε) 2 ^ n / n`. No asymptotics happen here.

## Why not the disjunctive normal form?

Writing `f` as the disjunction of its true minterms uses up to `2 ^ n` minterms of `n`
literals each, so roughly `n 2 ^ n` gates. The waste is that nothing is shared between
minterms. Lupanov's construction shares almost everything.

## The picture

Split the `n = k + d` inputs into `k` *address* bits and `d` *data* bits, and view the truth
table of `f` as a `2 ^ k × 2 ^ d` matrix: row `a` is an address assignment, column `b` is a
data assignment, and the entry is `f (a ++ b)`. Cut the rows into blocks of `s` consecutive
rows. Inside one block every column is a bit string of length `s`, its *pattern* in that
block; there are only `2 ^ s` possible patterns, however many columns there are.

For each block `B` and pattern `v` define two functions:

* `left B v`, of the address bits only: true at `a` when row `a` lies in `B` and `v` has a
  `1` at the position of `a` within `B`;
* `right f B v`, of the data bits only: true at `b` when column `b` has pattern `v` in `B`.

Both are functions of the full input that ignore the other half of it. Then
`left B v a ∧ right f B v b` holds exactly when `a` lies in `B`, `v` is the pattern of
column `b` inside `B`, and the entry `f (a ++ b)` is `true`. So `f` is the disjunction over
all pairs `(B, v)` of `left B v ∧ right f B v` (`table_eq`).

## Counting gates

All `2 ^ k` address minterms and `2 ^ d` data minterms are built once and shared. Each
`left B v` is a disjunction of at most `s` address minterms, so it costs `O(s)` gates, and
there are `(2 ^ k / s + 1) · 2 ^ s` of them. Each `right f B v` is a disjunction of data
minterms, one per column with pattern `v`; the columns of a block are partitioned by their
patterns (`support_card_sum`), so all the `right f B v` of one block together cost about
`2 ^ d` gates. Summing over blocks, the dominant contribution is

  `(2 ^ k / s) · 2 ^ d = 2 ^ n / s`.

For the parameters chosen in `Lupanov.lean` the remaining terms are of lower order, and
`s ≈ n` makes this `2 ^ n / n`. The exact expression is `bound`.

## References

* [O. B. Lupanov, *On a Method of Circuit Synthesis*][Lupanov1958],
  Section 1, equation (1.1), pp. 120-122: the original `(k, s)` representation.
* [Stasys Jukna, *Boolean Function Complexity: Advances and Frontiers*][Jukna2012],
  Theorem 1.15: a modern exposition.
* [C. E. Shannon, *The Synthesis of Two-Terminal Switching Circuits*][Shannon1949],
  Section 3(d), pp. 73-77: the earlier universal-network method for relay contacts.

items.note:
### The block decomposition

Rows `block * s, …, block * s + s - 1` form block number `block`. The final block may be
partial, and when `s ∣ 2 ^ k` there is an empty extra block; rows past `2 ^ k` are read as
`false` throughout.

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Boolean.Lupanov.bound
items.doc:
Gate budget for `k` address bits, `d` data bits, and blocks of `s` rows, as spent by
`synthesis`. In order: the shared minterms; then for each of the `2 ^ k / s + 1` blocks
(a partial final block, or an empty extra block when `s ∣ 2 ^ k`), `2 s + 4` gates per
pattern, namely `2 s + 1` for its `left` part, the constant starting its `right` part, the
conjunction of the two, and the OR into the running disjunction, plus `2 ^ d` gates in total
for the ORs inside the `right` parts of the block, one per column; and one constant for the
empty outer disjunction. The leading term is `(2 ^ k / s) · 2 ^ d ≈ 2 ^ n / s`.
items.statement: def bound (k d s : ℕ) : ℕ

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Boolean.Lupanov.synthesis
items.doc:
Every Boolean function on `k + d` inputs can be built from the input projections within
`bound k d s` gates: build all minterms, then the disjunction over block-pattern pairs of
`left ∧ right`, which equals `f` by `table_eq`.
items.statement:
theorem synthesis (f : BooleanFunction (k + d)) (hs : 0 < s) :
    Synthesis interpretation (inputs (k + d)) {f} (bound k d s)

modules.title: Shannon's lower bound for De Morgan circuits
modules.doc:
This is the De Morgan specialization of `Cslib.Circuits.Shannon.exists_hard_function`,
stated for circuits and for circuit complexity. Together with Lupanov's construction, it
gives the asymptotically sharp gate count `2ⁿ/n`.

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Boolean.Shannon.exists_hard_function
items.doc:
For all sufficiently large `n`, some Boolean function on `n` inputs requires
more than `2ⁿ/n` De Morgan gates, counting constants and negations.
items.statement:
theorem exists_hard_function :
    ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ n ≥ N, ∃ f : BooleanFunction n,
      ∀ c : Circuit signature n 1,
        c.Computes interpretation (single f) → 2 ^ n / (n : ℝ) < (c.size : ℝ)

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Boolean.Shannon.lt_complexity
items.doc:
Shannon's lower bound for circuit complexity: for all sufficiently large `n`, some Boolean
function on `n` inputs has complexity more than `2ⁿ/n`.
items.statement:
theorem lt_complexity :
    ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ n ≥ N, ∃ f : BooleanFunction n,
      2 ^ n / (n : ℝ) < (complexity interpretation (single f) : ℝ)

modules.title: Boolean synthesis
modules.doc:
The generic synthesis rules specialize to the De Morgan basis: constants, negation, conjunction,
and disjunction. Finite conjunctions and disjunctions use the generic fold bound, and
`synthesis_minterm` combines literals to test a specified tuple of input bits.

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Synthesis.const
items.doc: Constants cost one gate.
items.statement: theorem const (value : Bool) : Synthesis interpretation s {fun _ => value} 1

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Synthesis.not
items.doc: Apply negation to a synthesized function.
items.statement:
theorem not (h : Synthesis interpretation s {f} a) :
    Synthesis interpretation s {fun x => !f x} (a + 1)

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Synthesis.and
items.doc: Binary conjunction costs one gate beyond its arguments.
items.statement:
theorem and (hf : Synthesis interpretation s {f} a) (hg : Synthesis interpretation s {g} b) :
    Synthesis interpretation s {fun x => f x && g x} (a + b + 1)

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Synthesis.or
items.doc: Binary disjunction costs one gate beyond its arguments.
items.statement:
theorem or (hf : Synthesis interpretation s {f} a) (hg : Synthesis interpretation s {g} b) :
    Synthesis interpretation s {fun x => f x || g x} (a + b + 1)

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Synthesis.exists_mem
items.doc: Disjoin a finite family of functions. The extra gate supplies the empty disjunction.
items.statement:
theorem exists_mem (indices : Finset ι) (f : ι → BooleanFunction n) (cost : ι → ℕ)
    (h : ∀ i ∈ indices, Synthesis interpretation s {f i} (cost i)) :
    Synthesis interpretation s {fun x => decide (∃ i ∈ indices, f i x = true)}
      ((∑ i ∈ indices, (cost i + 1)) + 1)

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Synthesis.forall_mem
items.doc: Conjoin a finite family of functions. The extra gate supplies the empty conjunction.
items.statement:
theorem forall_mem (indices : Finset ι) (f : ι → BooleanFunction n) (cost : ι → ℕ)
    (h : ∀ i ∈ indices, Synthesis interpretation s {f i} (cost i)) :
    Synthesis interpretation s {fun x => decide (∀ i ∈ indices, f i x = true)}
      ((∑ i ∈ indices, (cost i + 1)) + 1)

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Boolean.synthesis_minterm
items.doc: A conjunction testing a specified tuple of input bits.

modules.title: Circuit complexity
modules.doc:
The complexity of a function `f` on a support `S`, written `C^S(f)`, is the least number of gates
in a circuit whose outputs agree with `f` on every input in `S`. The function may have several
values, one for each output of the circuit, and nothing is asked of the circuit outside `S`, so
`C^S(f)` depends only on the restriction of `f` to `S`. The complexity `C(f)` of `f` is its
complexity on all inputs, and the complexity of `f` relative to a function `g`, in
`Cslib.Computability.Circuit.RelativeComplexity`, is a complexity on the graph of `g`.

Over an arbitrary signature and interpretation some functions have no circuit at all. We represent
`C^S(f)` by `ecomplexityOn I S f` and `C(f)` by `ecomplexity I f`, taking values in `ℕ∞` with
`⊤` when no circuit exists. The prefix `e` stands for "extended". Over a complete basis, one over
which every function has a circuit, `complexityOn I S f` and `complexity I f` give the corresponding
natural-number values.

Support complexity obeys a small calculus from which the rules for complexity and relative
complexity follow. It grows with the support and ignores the function outside the support.
Wiring, which only selects, permutes, or duplicates inputs, costs nothing. The composite `g ∘ f`
costs at most the complexity of `f` on `S` plus that of `g` on the image of `S`, and computing two
functions side by side costs at most the sum of their complexities.

See [Jukna, Chapter 1][Jukna2012] for the Boolean case.

## References

* [Stasys Jukna, *Boolean Function Complexity: Advances and Frontiers*][Jukna2012]

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Interpretation.IsComplete
items.doc:
Following [Jukna, Section 1.1][Jukna2012], a basis is complete when every single-valued
function, on every number of inputs, is computed by some circuit over it. Circuits here have no
constant inputs, so this includes the constants, which is why NAND alone is not complete in this
sense. Functions with several values then have circuits too, built by running circuits for their
values side by side.
items.statement:
class Interpretation.IsComplete (I : Interpretation σ U) : Prop where
  /-- Every single-valued function has a circuit. -/
  exists_computes_single :
    ∀ {n : ℕ} (f : (Fin n → U) → U), ∃ c : Circuit σ n 1, c.Computes I (single f)

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.Interpretation.IsComplete.exists_computes
items.doc: Over a complete basis every function, with any number of values, has a circuit.
items.statement:
theorem Interpretation.IsComplete.exists_computes {I : Interpretation σ U} [I.IsComplete] :
    ∀ {n m : ℕ} (f : (Fin n → U) → Fin m → U), ∃ c : Circuit σ n m, c.Computes I f
  | _, 0, _ => ⟨Circuit.wiring σ Fin.elim0, fun _ => funext fun i => i.elim0⟩
  | _, m + 1, f => by
    obtain ⟨c, hc⟩

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.ecomplexityOn
items.doc:
The complexity `C^S(f)` of `f` on the support `S`: the least size of a circuit computing `f`
on `S` under `I`, or `⊤` if there is none.
items.statement:
noncomputable def ecomplexityOn (I : Interpretation σ U) (S : Set (Fin n → U))
    (f : (Fin n → U) → Fin m → U) : ℕ∞

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.ecomplexity
items.doc: The complexity `C(f)` of `f`: its complexity on all inputs.
items.statement: noncomputable def ecomplexity (I : Interpretation σ U) (f : (Fin n → U) → Fin m → U) : ℕ∞

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.ecomplexityOn_le_of_computesOn
items.statement:
theorem ecomplexityOn_le_of_computesOn (c : Circuit σ n m) (hc : c.ComputesOn I S f) :
    ecomplexityOn I S f ≤ c.size

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.ecomplexityOn_ne_top_iff
items.statement:
theorem ecomplexityOn_ne_top_iff :
    ecomplexityOn I S f ≠ ⊤ ↔ ∃ c : Circuit σ n m, c.ComputesOn I S f

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.exists_computesOn_size_eq_ecomplexityOn
items.doc:
When some circuit computes `f` on `S`, the least size is attained by some
(potentially different) circuit.
items.statement:
theorem exists_computesOn_size_eq_ecomplexityOn (h : ∃ c : Circuit σ n m, c.ComputesOn I S f) :
    ∃ c : Circuit σ n m, c.ComputesOn I S f ∧ (c.size : ℕ∞) = ecomplexityOn I S f

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.ecomplexityOn_le_iff
items.statement:
theorem ecomplexityOn_le_iff :
    ecomplexityOn I S f ≤ k ↔ ∃ c : Circuit σ n m, c.ComputesOn I S f ∧ c.size ≤ k

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.le_ecomplexityOn_iff
items.doc:
Lower bounds on support complexity are exactly lower bounds on the size of every circuit
computing the function on the support, including when no such circuit exists.
items.statement:
theorem le_ecomplexityOn_iff {k : ℕ∞} :
    k ≤ ecomplexityOn I S f ↔
      ∀ c : Circuit σ n m, c.ComputesOn I S f → k ≤ c.size

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.ecomplexityOn_mono
items.doc: A larger support is harder to compute on.
items.statement: theorem ecomplexityOn_mono (h : S ⊆ T) : ecomplexityOn I S f ≤ ecomplexityOn I T f

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.ecomplexityOn_congr
items.doc: Complexity on a support depends only on the values of the function on the support.
items.statement: theorem ecomplexityOn_congr (h : Set.EqOn f f' S) : ecomplexityOn I S f = ecomplexityOn I S f'

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.ecomplexityOn_le_ecomplexity
items.statement: theorem ecomplexityOn_le_ecomplexity : ecomplexityOn I S f ≤ ecomplexity I f

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.ecomplexityOn_wiring
items.doc: Selecting, permuting, or duplicating inputs costs nothing.
items.statement:
theorem ecomplexityOn_wiring (select : Fin m → Fin n) :
ecomplexityOn I S (fun x => x ∘ select) = 0

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.ecomplexityOn_comp_le
items.doc:
The composition rule: computing `g ∘ f` on `S` costs at most computing `f` on `S` and then
`g` on the values `f` takes there.
items.statement:
theorem ecomplexityOn_comp_le (f : (Fin n → U) → Fin m → U) (g : (Fin m → U) → Fin p → U) :
    ecomplexityOn I S (g ∘ f) ≤ ecomplexityOn I S f + ecomplexityOn I (f '' S) g

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.ecomplexityOn_append_le
items.doc:
The pairing rule: computing `f` and `g` side by side on `S` costs at most the sum of their
complexities on `S`.
items.statement:
theorem ecomplexityOn_append_le (f : (Fin n → U) → Fin m → U) (g : (Fin n → U) → Fin p → U) :
    ecomplexityOn I S (fun x => Fin.append (f x) (g x)) ≤
      ecomplexityOn I S f + ecomplexityOn I S g

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.ecomplexityOn_comp_wiring_le
items.doc:
Reading the inputs through a wiring costs nothing beyond computing `f` on the rewired
support.
items.statement:
theorem ecomplexityOn_comp_wiring_le {S : Set (Fin p → U)} (select : Fin n → Fin p)
    (f : (Fin n → U) → Fin m → U) :
    ecomplexityOn I S (fun x => f (x ∘ select)) ≤ ecomplexityOn I ((· ∘ select) '' S) f

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.ecomplexityOn_wiring_comp_le
items.doc: Selecting, permuting, or duplicating the values of `f` costs nothing.
items.statement:
theorem ecomplexityOn_wiring_comp_le (select : Fin p → Fin m) (f : (Fin n → U) → Fin m → U) :
    ecomplexityOn I S (fun x => f x ∘ select) ≤ ecomplexityOn I S f

items.name: Cslib.Circuits.ecomplexityOn_le_ecomplexityOn_append_left
