modules.title: Kleene's Algorithm
modules.doc:
Kleene's algorithm constructs a regular expression by induction on a bound that restricts
which interior states an execution may pass through.
It is used to prove a direction of `Cslib.Language.IsRegular.iff_regex`, that
every language accepted by a DFA comprised of finite states is the language of a regular expression.
We implement Kleene's algorithm for the more general case of an NFA instead of DFA,
since `Execution` is developed for `LTS` but not `FLTS`.
The main theorem is `NA.FinAcc.nfa_eq_regex`.

## Main definitions
- `LTS.bddLang start last bound`: The language of finite words that are accepted by an execution
of an LTS with state type `Fin n`, where the start state is `start`, the last state is `last`,
and all states of the execution except for the first and last are less than `bound`.
- `LTS.regex s t r`: The regular expression for the executions of an LTS with state type `Fin n`
from state `s` to state `t`, whose interior states are all under the bound `r`.

## Main results
- `NA.FinAcc.nfa_eq_regex`: Any NFA has a matching regular expression.
- `LTS.bddLang_eq_nfa`: `LTS.bddLang` is equal to the language of an NFA
when `bound` is greater than or equal to the total number of states.
- `LTS.bddLang_eq_regex`: `LTS.regex s t r` matches the language `LTS.bddLang s t r`.

## References

* [J. E. Hopcroft, R. Motwani, J. D. Ullman,
  *Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation*][Hopcroft2006]

items.name: List.AllButFirstLast
items.doc: All but the first and last elements of the list `as` satisfy the predicate `p`.
items.statement: def AllButFirstLast (p : α → Bool) (as : List α) : Prop

items.name: List.allButFirstLast_iff_getElem
items.statement:
theorem allButFirstLast_iff_getElem (p : α → Bool) (as : List α) :
    as.AllButFirstLast p ↔ ∀ i (_ : 0 < i ∧ i < as.length - 1), p as[i]

items.name: List.allButFirstLast_imp
items.statement:
theorem allButFirstLast_imp {p q : α → Bool} {as : List α} (h : ∀ x, p x → q x)
    (hp : as.AllButFirstLast p) : as.AllButFirstLast q

items.name: List.allButFirstLast_append
items.statement:
theorem allButFirstLast_append {p : α → Bool} {as bs : List α} (hlen : 0 < as.length)
    (ha_last : p as[as.length - 1]) (ha : as.AllButFirstLast p) (hb : bs.AllButFirstLast p) :
    (as ++ bs.tail).AllButFirstLast p

items.name: List.findIdxButFirstLast?
items.doc:
The index of the first element in a list `as` that satisfies a predicate `p`,
excluding the first and last element.
items.statement: def findIdxButFirstLast? (p : α → Bool) (as : List α) : Option ℕ

items.name: List.findIdxButFirstLast?_isSome
items.statement:
theorem findIdxButFirstLast?_isSome (p : α → Bool) (as : List α) :
    (as.findIdxButFirstLast? p).isSome ↔ (∃ x ∈ as.tail.dropLast, p x)

items.name: List.findIdxButFirstLast?_eq
items.statement:
theorem findIdxButFirstLast?_eq {p : α → Bool} {as : List α} {i : ℕ} :
    as.findIdxButFirstLast? p = some i ↔
    ∃ _ : 0 < i ∧ i < as.length - 1, p as[i] ∧
      ∀ j (_ : 0 < j ∧ j < i), p as[j] = false

items.name: List.findIdxButFirstLastRev?
items.doc:
The index of the last element in a list `as` that satisfies a predicate `p`,
excluding the first and last element.
items.statement: def findIdxButFirstLastRev? (p : α → Bool) (as : List α) : Option ℕ

items.name: List.findIdxButFirstLastRev?_eq
items.statement:
theorem findIdxButFirstLastRev?_eq {p : α → Bool} {as : List α} {i : ℕ} :
    as.findIdxButFirstLastRev? p = some i ↔
    ∃ _ : 0 < i ∧ i < as.length - 1, p as[i] ∧
      ∀ j (_ : i < j ∧ j < as.length - 1), p as[j] = false

items.name: Cslib.LTS.BddExec
items.doc:
An execution of an LTS with state type `Fin n`,
where all states of the execution except for the first and last are less than `bound`.
items.statement:
def BddExec (lts : LTS (Fin n) Symbol) (start : Fin n) (xs : List Symbol) (last : Fin n)
    (ss : List (Fin n)) (bound : ℕ) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.LTS.bddLang
items.doc: The language of finite words that are accepted by a `BddExec`.
items.statement: def bddLang (lts : LTS (Fin n) Symbol) (start last : Fin n) (bound : ℕ) : Language Symbol

items.name: Cslib.LTS.bddLang_bound_zero
items.statement:
theorem bddLang_bound_zero (lts : LTS (Fin n) Symbol) (s t : Fin n) {xs : List Symbol}
   (hxs : ¬xs = []) : xs ∈ lts.bddLang s t 0 ↔ ∃ a, lts.Tr s a t ∧ xs = [a]

items.name: Cslib.LTS.bddLang_eq_nfa
items.statement:
theorem bddLang_eq_nfa (lts : LTS (Fin n) Symbol) (s t : Fin n) {r : ℕ} (_ : n ≤ r) :
    lts.bddLang s t r = language (NA.FinAcc.mk ⟨lts, {s}⟩ {t})

items.name: Cslib.LTS.splitFirstTake
items.doc:
With an execution of the string `xs` through states `ss`,
`splitFirstTake xs ss r` returns a prefix of `xs`
which ends at the FIRST occurrence (excluding the first and last state) of state `r` in `ss`.
When no such occurrence of `r` exists, `splitFirstTake` returns the empty string; however,
the current file does not use the `splitFirstTake` in such situation.
The actual definition does not require an execution, just the string `xs` and the states `ss`.
items.statement: def splitFirstTake (xs : List Symbol) (ss : List (Fin n)) (r : Fin n) : List Symbol

items.name: Cslib.LTS.splitFirstDrop
items.doc:
With an execution of the string `xs` through states `ss`,
`splitFirstDrop xs ss r` returns a suffix of `xs`
which starts at the FIRST occurrence (excluding the first and last state) of state `r` in `ss`.
When no such occurrence of `r` exists, `splitFirstDrop` returns the full string; however,
the current file does not use the `splitFirstDrop` in such situation.
The actual definition does not require an execution, just the string `xs` and the states `ss`.
items.statement: def splitFirstDrop (xs : List Symbol) (ss : List (Fin n)) (r : Fin n) : List Symbol

items.name: Cslib.LTS.splitFirst_mem
items.statement:
theorem splitFirst_mem {lts : LTS (Fin n) Symbol} {s t r : Fin n} {xs : List Symbol}
    {ss : List (Fin n)} (hex : lts.Execution s xs t ss) (hbdd : ss.AllButFirstLast (· ≤ r))
    (hbdd' : ¬ss.AllButFirstLast (· < r)) :
    splitFirstTake xs ss r ∈ lts.bddLang s r r ∧
    splitFirstDrop xs ss r ∈ lts.bddLang r t (r + 1)

items.name: Cslib.LTS.bddLang_splitFirst
items.doc:
Part of the recursion step of Kleene's algorithm.
A run from `s` to `t` whose interior states are `≤ r` either has all interior states `< r`,
or it splits at its first visit to `r` into
an execution from `s` to `r` with all interior states `< r`, followed by
an execution from `r` to `t` with all interior states `≤ r`.
items.statement:
theorem bddLang_splitFirst (lts : LTS (Fin n) Symbol) (s t r : Fin n) :
    lts.bddLang s t (r + 1) = lts.bddLang s t r + lts.bddLang s r r * lts.bddLang r t (r + 1)

items.name: Cslib.LTS.splitLastTake
items.doc:
With an execution of the string `xs` through states `ss`,
`splitLastTake xs ss r` returns a prefix of `xs`
which ends at the LAST occurrence (excluding the first and last state) of state `r` in `ss`.
When no such occurrence of `r` exists, `splitLastTake` returns the empty string.
The actual definition does not require an execution, just the string `xs` and the states `ss`.
items.statement: def splitLastTake (xs : List Symbol) (ss : List (Fin n)) (r : Fin n) : List Symbol

items.name: Cslib.LTS.splitLastDrop
items.doc:
With an execution of the string `xs` through states `ss`,
`splitLastDrop xs ss r` returns a prefix of `xs`
which ends at the LAST occurrence (excluding the first and last state) of state `r` in `ss`.
When no such occurrence of `r` exists, `splitLastDrop` returns the full string.
The actual definition does not require an execution, just the string `xs` and the states `ss`.
items.statement: def splitLastDrop (xs : List Symbol) (ss : List (Fin n)) (r : Fin n) : List Symbol

items.name: Cslib.LTS.splitLast_mem
items.statement:
theorem splitLast_mem {lts : LTS (Fin n) Symbol} {t r : Fin n} {xs : List Symbol}
    {ss : List (Fin n)} (hex : lts.Execution r xs t ss) (hbdd : ss.AllButFirstLast (· ≤ r)) :
    splitLastTake xs ss r ∈ lts.bddLang r r (r + 1) ∧
    splitLastDrop xs ss r ∈ lts.bddLang r t r

items.name: Cslib.LTS.splitLastDrop_mem_nonempty
Cslib.LTS.bddLang_splitLast
items.doc:
Part of the recursion step of Kleene's algorithm.
An execution from `r` to `t` whose interior states are `≤ r` splits at its last visit to `r` into
an execution from `r` to `r` with all interior states `≤ r`, followed by
an execution from `r` to `t` with all interior states `< r`.
items.statement:
theorem bddLang_splitLast (lts : LTS (Fin n) Symbol) (t r : Fin n) :
    lts.bddLang r t (r + 1) = lts.bddLang r r (r + 1) * lts.bddLang r t r

items.name: Cslib.LTS.bddLang_kstar
items.doc:
Part of the recursion step of Kleene's algorithm.
An execution from `r` to `r` whose interior states are `≤ r` is
a concatenation of executions from `r` to `r` whose interior states are all `≤ r`.
items.statement:
theorem bddLang_kstar (lts : LTS (Fin n) Symbol) (r : Fin n) :
    lts.bddLang r r (r + 1) = (lts.bddLang r r r)∗

items.name: Cslib.LTS.regex
items.doc:
`regex s t r` is the regular expression for the path from state `s` to `t`
passing through states `< r`.
When `r = 0`, `s = t`, the regex is empty string `ε` union all characters from state `s` to `s`.
When `r = 0`, `s ≠ t`, the regex is all characters from state `s` to `t`.
For `r + 1`, the regex is the union of `regex s t r` and
`(regex s r r) (regex r r r)∗ (regex r t r)`.
items.statement: noncomputable def regex (lts : LTS (Fin n) Symbol) (s t : Fin n) : ℕ → RegularExpression Symbol

items.name: Cslib.LTS.bddLang_eq_regex
items.doc: `LTS.regex s t r` matches the language `LTS.bddLang s t r`.
items.statement:
theorem bddLang_eq_regex {r : ℕ} {lts : LTS (Fin n) Symbol} {s t : Fin n} :
    lts.bddLang s t r = (regex lts s t r).matches'

items.name: Cslib.LTS.fin_nfa_single_start_accept_eq_regex
items.doc:
An NFA with state type `Fin n` and with exactly one start state `s` and
exactly one accept state `t` has a matching regular expression given by `LTS.regex s t n`.
items.statement:
theorem fin_nfa_single_start_accept_eq_regex (lts : LTS (Fin n) Symbol) (s t : Fin n) :
    language (NA.FinAcc.mk ⟨lts, {s}⟩ {t}) = (lts.regex s t n).matches'

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.FinAcc.nfa_single_start_accept_reindex
items.statement:
theorem nfa_single_start_accept_reindex (nfa : NA.FinAcc State Symbol) (e : State ≃ State')
    {s t : State} (hstart : nfa.start = {s}) (haccept : nfa.accept = {t}) :
    language nfa = language (NA.FinAcc.mk ⟨(nfa.toLTS.reindex e), {e s}⟩ {e t})

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.FinAcc.nfa_single_start_accept_eq_regex
items.doc:
An NFA with exactly one start state and exactly one accept state
has a matching regular expression.
items.statement:
theorem nfa_single_start_accept_eq_regex [Finite Symbol] [Finite State]
    (nfa : NA.FinAcc State Symbol) (s t : State)
    (hstart : nfa.start = {s}) (haccept : nfa.accept = {t}) :
    ∃ r : RegularExpression Symbol, language nfa = r.matches'

items.name: Cslib.Automata.NA.FinAcc.nfa_eq_regex
items.doc: Any NFA has a matching regular expression.
items.statement:
theorem nfa_eq_regex [Finite Symbol] [Finite State] (nfa : NA.FinAcc State Symbol) :
    ∃ r : RegularExpression Symbol, language nfa = r.matches'

modules.title: Language (additional definitions and theorems)
modules.doc:
This file contains additional definitions and theorems about `Language`
as defined and developed in `Mathlib.Computability.Language`.

items.name: List.eq_nil_ofIsEmpty
items.doc: `[]` is the only list over an empty type.
items.statement: theorem eq_nil_ofIsEmpty [IsEmpty α] (xl : List α) : xl = []

items.name: Language.eq_zero_or_one_ofIsEmpty
items.doc: `0` and `1` are the only possible languages over an empty type.
items.statement: theorem eq_zero_or_one_ofIsEmpty [IsEmpty α] (l : Language α) : l = 0 ∨ l = 1

items.name: Language.mem_biInf
items.statement:
theorem mem_biInf {I : Type*} (s : Set I) (l : I → Language α) (x : List α) :
    (x ∈ ⨅ i ∈ s, l i) ↔ ∀ i ∈ s, x ∈ l i

items.name: Language.mem_biSup
items.doc: A grind regression found moving to nightly-2026-03-31 (changes from lean#13166)
items.statement:
theorem mem_biSup {I : Type*} (s : Set I) (l : I → Language α) (x : List α) :
    (x ∈ ⨆ i ∈ s, l i) ↔ ∃ i ∈ s, x ∈ l i

items.name: Language.le_one_iff_eq
items.statement: theorem le_one_iff_eq : l ≤ 1 ↔ l = 0 ∨ l = 1

items.name: Language.mem_singleton
items.statement: theorem mem_singleton (x y : List α) : x ∈ ({y} : Language α) ↔ x = y

items.name: Language.mem_sub_one
items.statement: theorem mem_sub_one (x : List α) : x ∈ (l - 1) ↔ x ∈ l ∧ x ≠ []

items.name: Language.reverse_sub
items.statement: theorem reverse_sub (l m : Language α) : (l - m).reverse = l.reverse - m.reverse

items.name: Language.sub_one_mul
items.doc: A grind regression found moving to nightly-2026-03-31 (changes from lean#13166)
items.statement: theorem sub_one_mul : (l - 1) * l = l * l - 1

items.name: Language.mul_sub_one
items.statement: theorem mul_sub_one : l * (l - 1) = l * l - 1

items.name: Language.kstar_sub_one
items.doc: A grind regression found moving to nightly-2026-03-31 (changes from lean#13166)
items.statement: theorem kstar_sub_one : l∗ - 1 = (l - 1) * l∗

items.name: Language.sub_one_kstar
items.statement: theorem sub_one_kstar : (l - 1)∗ = l∗

items.name: Language.kstar_iff_mul_add
items.statement: theorem kstar_iff_mul_add : m = l∗ ↔ m = (l - 1) * m + 1

items.name: Language.self_eq_add_mul_iff
items.doc: The reverse version of Arden's lemma `Language.self_eq_mul_add_iff`.
items.statement:
theorem self_eq_add_mul_iff {l m n : Language α} (hm : [] ∉ m) :
    l = l * m + n ↔ l = n * m∗

items.name: Language.Hom
items.doc:
A language homomorphism from `α` to `β` is a map from `List α` to `List β` which
preserves the empty word `[]` and concatenation `(· ++ ·)`.
items.statement:
structure Hom (α β : Type*) where
  /-- The map of a language homomorphism. -/
  toFun : List α → List β
  map_nil' : toFun [] = []
  map_append' (as as' : List α) : toFun (as ++ as') = toFun as ++ toFun as'

items.name: Language.Hom.ext_iff'
items.statement:
theorem ext_iff' (f f' : Hom α β) :
    f = f' ↔ ∀ as, f as = f' as

items.name: Language.Hom.map_nil
items.statement: theorem map_nil (f : Hom α β) : f [] = []

items.name: Language.Hom.map_append
items.statement: theorem map_append (f : Hom α β) (as as' : List α) : f (as ++ as') = (f as) ++ (f as')

items.name: Language.Hom.map_cons
items.statement:
theorem map_cons (f : Hom α β) (a : α) (as : List α) :
    f (a :: as) = f [a] ++ f as

items.name: Language.Hom.liftAux
items.doc:
This auxiliary function should not be used outside this file.
Instead, use the equivalence `lift` below.
items.statement: def liftAux (f : α → List β) : Hom α β

items.name: Language.Hom.liftAux_eq_flatMap
items.statement: theorem liftAux_eq_flatMap (f : α → List β) : liftAux f = List.flatMap f

items.name: Language.Hom.listAux_left_inv
items.statement:
theorem listAux_left_inv (f : α → List β) :
    (fun f a ↦ f [a]) (liftAux f) = f

items.name: Language.Hom.listAux_right_inv
items.statement:
theorem listAux_right_inv (f : Hom α β) :
    liftAux (fun a ↦ f [a]) = f

items.name: Language.Hom.lift
items.doc:
An equivalence from `f : α → List β` to `Hom α β`, whose forward direction can be
used to define language homomorphisms conveniently.
items.statement: def lift : (α → List β) ≃ (Hom α β)

items.name: Language.Hom.lift_eq_flatMap
items.doc: `lift.toFun` is in fact `List.flatMap`.
items.statement: theorem lift_eq_flatMap (f : α → List β) : lift f = List.flatMap f

items.name: Language.Hom.reduceOption
items.doc: Dropping the `none`s from a list of options is a language homomorphism.
items.statement: def reduceOption : Hom (Option α) α

items.name: Language.Hom.reduceOption_apply
items.statement: theorem reduceOption_apply (as : List (Option α)) : reduceOption as = as.reduceOption

items.name: Language.image
items.doc: The image of a language under a function `f`, which need not be a language homomorphism.
items.statement: def image (f : List α → List β) (l : Language α) : Language β

items.name: Language.preimage
items.doc: The preimage of a language under a function `f`, which need not be a language homomorphism.
items.statement: def preimage (f : List α → List β) (l : Language β) : Language α

items.name: Language.mem_image
items.statement:
theorem mem_image (f : List α → List β) (l : Language α) (bs : List β) :
    bs ∈ l.image f ↔ ∃ as, as ∈ l ∧ f as = bs

items.name: Language.mem_preimage
items.statement:
theorem mem_preimage (f : List α → List β) (l : Language β) (as : List α) :
    as ∈ l.preimage f ↔ f as ∈ l

items.name: Language.image_singleton
items.statement:
theorem image_singleton (f : List α → List β) (as : List α) :
    ({as} : Language α).image f = {f as}

items.name: Language.image_zero
items.statement: theorem image_zero (f : List α → List β) : (0 : Language α).image f = 0

items.name: Language.image_add
items.statement:
theorem image_add (f : List α → List β) (l1 l2 : Language α) :
    (l1 + l2).image f = l1.image f + l2.image f

items.name: Language.image_iSup
items.statement:
theorem image_iSup (f : List α → List β) {I : Type*} (l : I → Language α) :
    (⨆ i : I, l i).image f = ⨆ i : I, (l i).image f

items.note:
The following distributive laws for the `image` operation requires the function `f`
to be a language homomorphism.

items.name: Language.image_one
items.statement: theorem image_one (f : Hom α β) : (1 : Language α).image f = 1

items.name: Language.image_mul
items.statement:
theorem image_mul (f : Hom α β) (l1 l2 : Language α) :
    (l1 * l2).image f = l1.image f * l2.image f

items.name: Language.image_pow
items.statement:
theorem image_pow (f : Hom α β) (l : Language α) (n : ℕ) :
    (l^n).image f = (l.image f)^n

items.name: Language.image_kstar
items.statement:
theorem image_kstar (f : Hom α β) (l : Language α) :
    (l∗).image f = (l.image f)∗

modules.title: Myhill-Nerode Theorem
modules.doc:
Let `l` be a language on an alphabet `α`. The Nerode congruence (referred to as `c_l`
in comments below) of a language `l` is a right congruence on strings where two strings are
related iff all their right extensions are either both in the language or both not in it.

The Myhill-Nerode theorem has three parts [WikipediaMyhillNerode2026]:

(1) `l` is regular iff `c_l` has a finite number `N` of equivalence classes.

(2) `N` is the number of states of the minimal DFA accepting `l`.

(3) The minimal DFA is unique up to unique isomorphism. That is, for any
    minimal DFA accepting `l`, there exists exactly an isomorphism from it to the
    canonical DFA whose states are the equivalence classes of `c_l`, whose
    state transitions are of the form `⟦ x ⟧ → ⟦ x ++ [a] ⟧` (where `a : α`
    and `x : List α`), whose initial state is `⟦ [] ⟧`, and whose accepting states
    are `{ ⟦ x ⟧ | x ∈ l }`.

## References

* [J. E. Hopcroft, R. Motwani, J. D. Ullman,
  *Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation*][Hopcroft2006]
* [T. Malkin, *COMS W3261: Computer Science Theory, Handout 3: The Myhill-Nerode Theorem
   and Implications*][Malkin2024]
* [Wikipedia contributors, Myhill–Nerode theorem][WikipediaMyhillNerode2026]

items.name: Language.NerodeCongruence
items.doc:
The Nerode congruence (henceforth called `c_l`) of a language `l` is a right congruence on
strings where two strings are related iff all their right extensions are either both in the language
or both not in it.
items.statement: def NerodeCongruence (l : Language α) : RightCongruence α

items.name: Language.NerodeQuotient
items.doc: The quotient type of a Nerode congruence.
items.statement: abbrev NerodeQuotient (l : Language α)

items.name: Language.NerodeCongruenceDA
items.doc:
The Nerode congruence of a language `l` gives rise to a DFA where each state corresponds to an
equivalence class of the language under the Nerode congruence. Note that this is simply the DFA
given rise to by the underlying right congruence with only the accept states specified here as
`{⟦ x ⟧ | x ∈ l}`.
items.statement: def NerodeCongruenceDA (l : Language α) : DA.FinAcc (l.NerodeQuotient) α

items.name: Language.nerodeCongruenceDA_language_eq
items.doc: The DFA constructed from the Nerode congruence `c_l` on `l` accepts `l`.
items.statement:
theorem nerodeCongruenceDA_language_eq (l : Language α) :
    language (l.NerodeCongruenceDA) = l

items.name: Language.da_nerodeCongruence_iff
items.doc:
The statement (two strings are related by the Nerode congruence `c_l` on `l` iff all their right
extensions are either both in the language or both not in it) is equivalent to stating that (all
their right extensions are either both accepted or rejected by the DFA given rise to by `c_l`.)
items.statement:
theorem da_nerodeCongruence_iff {State : Type*} (M : DA.FinAcc State α) (x y : List α) :
    ((language M).NerodeCongruence).r x y ↔
    ∀ z, M.mtr (M.mtr M.start x) z ∈ M.accept ↔ M.mtr (M.mtr M.start y) z ∈ M.accept

items.name: Language.IsRegular.finite_nerodeQuotient
items.doc: If `l` is regular then the Nerode congruence on `l` has finitely many equivalence classes.
items.statement:
theorem IsRegular.finite_nerodeQuotient (h : l.IsRegular) :
    Finite (l.NerodeQuotient)

items.name: Language.IsRegular.iff_finite_nerodeQuotient
items.doc: `l` is regular iff the Nerode congruence on `l` has finitely many equivalence classes.
items.statement:
theorem IsRegular.iff_finite_nerodeQuotient {l : Language α} :
    l.IsRegular ↔ Finite (l.NerodeQuotient)

items.name: Language.dfa_num_state_ge
items.doc:
Given a set of strings all distinguishable by `l` (i.e., not related to each other by the Nerode
congruence on `l`), the number of states in the DFA accepting `l` is at least the number of strings
in the set.
items.statement:
theorem dfa_num_state_ge
    {l : Language α} {ws : Set (List α)} [Finite ws]
    (hws : ws.Pairwise (¬ (l.NerodeCongruence).r · ·))
    {State : Type*} [Finite State] {M : DA.FinAcc State α} (hm : language M = l) :
    Nat.card ws ≤ Nat.card State

items.name: Language.dfa_num_state_min
items.doc:
All DFAs accepting `l` must have at least as many states as the number of equivalence classes
of the Nerode congruence on `l`.
items.statement:
theorem dfa_num_state_min {State : Type} {M : DA.FinAcc State α} [Finite State] :
    Nat.card (language M).NerodeQuotient ≤ Nat.card State

items.name: Cslib.Automata.DA.FinAcc.IsMinimalAutomaton
items.doc:
The minimal DFA accepting `l` has the same number of states as the number of equivalence classes
of the Nerode congruence on `l`.
items.statement: def IsMinimalAutomaton {State : Type*} (M : FinAcc State α) (l : Language α)

items.name: Cslib.Automata.DA.FinAcc.StateCongruence
items.doc:
Given a DFA `M`, two strings are related iff they reach the same state under when run through
`M`. The Nerode congruence is the state congruence with respect to the minimal DFA accepting `l`.
items.statement: def StateCongruence (M : FinAcc State α) : RightCongruence α

items.name: Cslib.Automata.DA.FinAcc.stateCongruence_le_nerodeCongruence
items.doc: The Nerode congruence is the most coarse state congruence given a language.
items.statement:
theorem stateCongruence_le_nerodeCongruence {x y : List α}
    (h : (StateCongruence M).r x y) : ((language M).NerodeCongruence).r x y

items.name: Cslib.Automata.DA.FinAcc.unique_minimal
items.doc: The minimal DFA `M` accepting the language `l` is unique up to unique isomorphism.
items.statement:
theorem unique_minimal [Finite State]
    (l : Language α) (hr : l.IsRegular) (hm : M.IsMinimalAutomaton l) :
    ∃! φ : State ≃ l.NerodeQuotient, ∀ x, φ (M.mtr M.start x) = ⟦ x ⟧

modules.title: ωLanguage
modules.doc:
This file contains the definition and operations on formal ω-languages, which
are sets of infinite sequences over an alphabet `α` (namely, objects of type
`ωSequence α`).

## Main definitions and notations

In general we will use `p` and `q` to denote ω-languages and `l` and `m` to
denote languages (namely, sets of finite sequences of type `List α`).

* Set operations (union, intersection, complementation), constants (empty and
  universe sets), and the subset relation are denoted using lattice-theoretic
  notations (`p ∪ q`, `p ∩ q`, `pᶜ`, `⊥`, `⊤`, and `≤`) and terminologies in
  definition and theorem names ("inf", "sup", "compl", "bot", "top", "le").
* `p.closure`: the topological closure of `p`, where `ωLanguage α` inherits the
  product topology of `TopologicalSpace (ωSequence α)`
* `l * p`: ω-language of `x ++ω y` where `x ∈ l` and `y ∈ p`; referred to as
  "hmul" in definition and theorem names.
* `l^ω`: ω-language of infinite sequences each of which is the concatenation of
  infinitely many (nonemoty) members of `l`; referred to as "omegaPow" in
  definition and theorem names.
  + Note: Since `l^ω` is defined using `ωSequence.flatten`, any theorem about it
    needs the additional assumption `[Inhabited α]`.
* `l↗ω`: ω-language of infinite sequences each of which has infinitely many
  distinct prefixes in `l`; referred to as "omegaLim" in definition and theorem names.
* `p.map f`: transform an ω-language `p` over `α` into an ω-language over `β`
  by mapping through `f : α → β`; referred to as "map" in definition and theorem names.

## Main theorems

* Many algebraic properties of the above operations.
* `omegaPow_seq_prop`: an alternative characterization of `l^ω`.
* `omegaPow_coind`: a "coinductive" rule for proving `p` is a subset of `l^ω`.
* `hmul_omegaPow_eq_omegaPow`: `l * l^ω = l^ω`.
* `kstar_omegaPow_eq_omegaPow`: `(l∗)^ω = l^ω`.
* `kstar_hmul_omegaPow_eq_omegaPow`: `l∗ * l^ω = l^ω`.

…

items.name: Language.toSet
items.doc: The set of lists in a language.
items.statement: def Language.toSet (l : Language α) : Set (List α)

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage
items.doc: An ω-language is a set of ω-sequences over an alphabet.
items.statement:
structure ωLanguage (α : Type u) where
  /-- Construct an ω-language from a set of ω-sequences. -/
  ofSet ::
  /-- The set of ω-sequences in an ω-language. -/
  toSet : Set (ωSequence α)
deriving Inhabited

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.ofSet_toSet
items.statement: lemma ofSet_toSet (l : ωLanguage α) : ofSet l.toSet = l

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.toSet_ofSet
items.statement: lemma toSet_ofSet (s : Set (ωSequence α)) : (ofSet s).toSet = s

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.equiv
items.doc: The equivalence between `ωLanguage α` and `Set (ωSequence α)`.
items.statement: def equiv : ωLanguage α ≃ Set (ωSequence α)

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.eq_bot_ofIsEmpty
items.doc: `⊥` is the only possible ω-language over an empty type.
items.statement: theorem eq_bot_ofIsEmpty [IsEmpty α] (p : ωLanguage α) : p = ⊥

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.le_def
items.statement: lemma le_def (p q : ωLanguage α) : p ≤ q ↔ p.toSet ⊆ q.toSet

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.top_def
items.statement: lemma top_def : (⊤ : ωLanguage α) = ⟨univ⟩

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.bot_def
items.statement: lemma bot_def : (⊥ : ωLanguage α) = ⟨∅⟩

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.sup_def
items.statement: lemma sup_def (p q : ωLanguage α) : p ⊔ q = ⟨p.toSet ∪ q.toSet⟩

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.inf_def
items.statement: lemma inf_def (p q : ωLanguage α) : p ⊓ q = ⟨p.toSet ∩ q.toSet⟩

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.compl_def
items.statement: lemma compl_def (p : ωLanguage α) : pᶜ = ⟨p.toSetᶜ⟩

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.sSup_def
items.statement: lemma sSup_def (s : Set (ωLanguage α)) : sSup s = ⟨⋃ p ∈ s, p.toSet⟩

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.sInf_def
items.statement: lemma sInf_def (s : Set (ωLanguage α)) : sInf s = ⟨⋂ p ∈ s, p.toSet⟩

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.iSup_def
items.statement: lemma iSup_def {ι : Sort v} {p : ι → ωLanguage α} : ⨆ i, p i = ⟨⋃ i, (p i).toSet⟩

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.iInf_def
items.statement: lemma iInf_def {ι : Sort v} {p : ι → ωLanguage α} : ⨅ i, p i = ⟨⋂ i, (p i).toSet⟩

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.closure
items.doc: The topological closure of an ω-language.
items.statement: def closure (p : ωLanguage α) : ωLanguage α

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.hmul_def
items.statement: theorem hmul_def (l : Language α) (p : ωLanguage α) : l * p = image2 (· ++ω ·) l.toSet p.toSet

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.omegaPow
items.doc:
Concatenation of infinitely many copies of a languages, resulting in an ω-language.
A.k.a. ω-power.
items.statement: def omegaPow [Inhabited α] (l : Language α) : ωLanguage α

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.OmegaPow
items.doc: Notation class for `omegaPow`.
items.statement:
class OmegaPow (α : Type*) (β : outParam (Type*)) where
  /-- The `omegaPow` operation. -/
  omegaPow : α → β

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.omegaPow_def
items.statement:
theorem omegaPow_def [Inhabited α] (l : Language α) :
    l^ω = { s | ∃ xs : ωSequence (List α), xs.flatten = s ∧ ∀ k, xs k ∈ l - 1 }

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.omegaLim
items.doc:
The ω-limit of a language `l` is the ω-language of infinite sequences each of which
contains infinitely many distinct prefixes in `l`.
items.statement: def omegaLim (l : Language α) : ωLanguage α

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.OmegaLim
items.doc: Notation class for `omegaLim`.
items.statement:
class OmegaLim (α : Type*) (β : outParam (Type*)) where
  /-- The `omegaLim` operation. -/
  omegaLim : α → β

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.instOmegaLim
items.statement: instance instOmegaLim : OmegaLim (Language α) (ωLanguage α)

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.omegaLim_def
items.statement:
theorem omegaLim_def (l : Language α) :
    l↗ω = { s : ωSequence α | ∃ᶠ m in atTop, s.extract 0 m ∈ l }

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.map
items.doc:
transform an ω-language `p` over `α` into an ω-language over `β`
by mapping through `f : α → β`.
items.statement: def map (f : α → β) : ωLanguage α → ωLanguage β

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.map_def
items.statement:
theorem map_def (f : α → β) (p : ωLanguage α) :
    p.map f = image (ωSequence.map f) p.toSet

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.mem_def
items.statement: theorem mem_def (p : ωLanguage α) (s : ωSequence α) : s ∈ p ↔ s ∈ p.toSet

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.mem_ext
items.statement: theorem mem_ext (h : ∀ (s : ωSequence α), s ∈ p ↔ s ∈ q) : p = q

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.mem_top
items.statement: theorem mem_top (s : ωSequence α) : s ∈ (⊤ : ωLanguage α)

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.notMem_bot
items.statement: theorem notMem_bot (s : ωSequence α) : s ∉ (⊥ : ωLanguage α)

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.mem_sup
items.statement: theorem mem_sup (p q : ωLanguage α) (s : ωSequence α) : s ∈ p ⊔ q ↔ s ∈ p ∨ s ∈ q

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.mem_inf
items.statement: theorem mem_inf (p q : ωLanguage α) (s : ωSequence α) : s ∈ p ⊓ q ↔ s ∈ p ∧ s ∈ q

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.mem_compl
items.statement: theorem mem_compl (p : ωLanguage α) (s : ωSequence α) : s ∈ pᶜ ↔ ¬ s ∈ p

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.mem_sSup
items.statement:
theorem mem_sSup (ps : Set (ωLanguage α)) {s : ωSequence α} :
    s ∈ sSup ps ↔ ∃ p ∈ ps, s ∈ p

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.mem_sInf
items.statement:
theorem mem_sInf (ps : Set (ωLanguage α)) {s : ωSequence α} :
    s ∈ sInf ps ↔ ∀ p ∈ ps, s ∈ p

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.mem_iSup
items.statement:
theorem mem_iSup {ι : Sort v} {p : ι → ωLanguage α} {s : ωSequence α} :
    (s ∈ ⨆ i, p i) ↔ ∃ i, s ∈ p i

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.mem_iInf
items.statement:
theorem mem_iInf {ι : Sort v} {p : ι → ωLanguage α} {s : ωSequence α} :
    (s ∈ ⨅ i, p i) ↔ ∀ i, s ∈ p i

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.mem_hmul
items.statement: theorem mem_hmul : s ∈ l * p ↔ ∃ x ∈ l, ∃ t ∈ p, x ++ω t = s

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.append_mem_hmul
items.statement: theorem append_mem_hmul : x ∈ l → s ∈ p → x ++ω s ∈ l * p

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.mem_omegaPow
items.statement:
theorem mem_omegaPow [Inhabited α] :
    s ∈ l^ω ↔ ∃ xs : ωSequence (List α), xs.flatten = s ∧ ∀ k, xs k ∈ l - 1

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.flatten_mem_omegaPow
items.statement:
theorem flatten_mem_omegaPow [Inhabited α] {xs : ωSequence (List α)}
    (h_xs : ∀ k, xs k ∈ l - 1) : xs.flatten ∈ l^ω

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.mem_omegaLim
items.statement:
theorem mem_omegaLim :
    s ∈ l↗ω ↔ ∃ᶠ m in atTop, s.extract 0 m ∈ l

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.mul_hmul
items.statement: theorem mul_hmul : (l * m) * p = l * (m * p)

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.zero_hmul
items.statement: theorem zero_hmul : (0 : Language α) * p = ⊥

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.hmul_bot
items.statement: theorem hmul_bot : l * (⊥ : ωLanguage α) = ⊥

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.one_hmul
items.statement: theorem one_hmul : (1 : Language α) * p = p

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.hmul_sup
items.statement: theorem hmul_sup : l * (p ⊔ q) = l * p ⊔ l * q

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.add_hmul
items.statement: theorem add_hmul : (l + m) * p = l * p ⊔ m * p

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.iSup_hmul
items.statement:
theorem iSup_hmul {ι : Sort v} (l : ι → Language α) (p : ωLanguage α) :
    (⨆ i, l i) * p = ⨆ i, l i * p

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.hmul_iSup
items.statement:
theorem hmul_iSup {ι : Sort v} (p : ι → ωLanguage α) (l : Language α) :
    (l * ⨆ i, p i) = ⨆ i, l * p i

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.le_hmul_congr
items.statement:
theorem le_hmul_congr {l1 l2 : Language α} {p1 p2 : ωLanguage α} (hl : l1 ≤ l2) (hp : p1 ≤ p2) :
    l1 * p1 ≤ l2 * p2

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.le_omegaPow_congr
items.statement: theorem le_omegaPow_congr [Inhabited α] {l1 l2 : Language α} (h : l1 ≤ l2) : l1^ω ≤ l2^ω

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.omegaPow_of_sub_one
items.statement: theorem omegaPow_of_sub_one [Inhabited α] : (l - 1)^ω = l^ω

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.zero_omegaPow
items.statement: theorem zero_omegaPow [Inhabited α] : (0 : Language α)^ω = ⊥

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.one_omegaPow
items.statement: theorem one_omegaPow [Inhabited α] : (1 : Language α)^ω = ⊥

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.omegaPow_of_le_one
items.statement: theorem omegaPow_of_le_one [Inhabited α] (h : l ≤ 1) : l^ω = ⊥

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.omegaPow_eq_empty
items.doc: A grind regression found moving to nightly-2026-03-31 (from lean#13166? seems different)
items.statement: theorem omegaPow_eq_empty [Inhabited α] (h : l^ω = ⊥) : l ≤ 1

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.hmul_seq_prop
items.doc: An alternative characterization of `l * p`.
items.statement: theorem hmul_seq_prop : l * p = { s : ωSequence α | ∃ k, s.take k ∈ l ∧ s.drop k ∈ p }

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.omegaPow_seq_prop
items.doc: An alternative characterization of `l^ω`.

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.omegaPow_coind'
items.statement: theorem omegaPow_coind' [Inhabited α] (h_nn : [] ∉ l) (h_le : p ≤ l * p) : p ≤ l^ω

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.omegaPow_coind
items.doc: A "coinductive" rule for proving `p` is a subset of `l^ω`.
items.statement: theorem omegaPow_coind [Inhabited α] (h_le : p ≤ (l - 1) * p) : p ≤ l^ω

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.omegaPow_le_hmul_omegaPow'
items.doc: A grind regression found moving to nightly-2026-03-31 (changes from lean#13166)
items.statement:
theorem omegaPow_le_hmul_omegaPow' [Inhabited α] (l : Language α) :
    l^ω ≤ (l - 1) * l^ω

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.omegaPow_le_hmul_omegaPow
items.statement: theorem omegaPow_le_hmul_omegaPow [Inhabited α] (l : Language α) : l^ω ≤ l * l^ω

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.hmul_omegaPow_le_omegaPow
items.statement: theorem hmul_omegaPow_le_omegaPow [Inhabited α] (l : Language α) : l * l^ω ≤ l^ω

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.hmul_omegaPow_eq_omegaPow
items.statement: theorem hmul_omegaPow_eq_omegaPow [Inhabited α] (l : Language α) : l * l^ω = l^ω

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.omegaPow_le_kstar_omegaPow
items.statement: theorem omegaPow_le_kstar_omegaPow [Inhabited α] (l : Language α) : l^ω ≤ (l∗)^ω

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.kstar_omegaPow_le_omegaPow
items.statement: theorem kstar_omegaPow_le_omegaPow [Inhabited α] (l : Language α) : (l∗)^ω ≤ l^ω

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.kstar_omegaPow_eq_omegaPow
items.statement: theorem kstar_omegaPow_eq_omegaPow [Inhabited α] (l : Language α) : (l∗)^ω = l^ω

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.kstar_hmul_omegaPow_eq_omegaPow
items.statement: theorem kstar_hmul_omegaPow_eq_omegaPow [Inhabited α] (l : Language α) : l∗ * l^ω = l^ω

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.omegaLim_zero
items.statement: theorem omegaLim_zero : (0 : Language α)↗ω = ⊥

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.map_id
items.statement: theorem map_id (p : ωLanguage α) : map id p = p

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.map_map
items.statement: theorem map_map (g : β → γ) (f : α → β) (p : ωLanguage α) : map g (map f p) = map (g ∘ f) p

modules.title: ω-Regular languages
modules.doc: This file defines ω-regular languages and proves some properties of them.

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.IsRegular
items.doc:
An ω-language is ω-regular iff it is accepted by a
finite-state nondeterministic Buchi automaton.
items.statement: def IsRegular (p : ωLanguage Symbol)

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.isRegular_iff
items.doc:
The state space of the accepting finite-state nondeterministic Buchi automaton
can in fact be universe-polymorphic.
items.statement:
theorem isRegular_iff {p : ωLanguage Symbol} :
    p.IsRegular ↔ ∃ (σ : Type v) (_ : Finite σ) (na : NA.Buchi σ Symbol), language na = p

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.IsRegular.of_da_buchi
items.doc: The ω-language accepted by a finite-state deterministic Buchi automaton is ω-regular.
items.statement:
theorem IsRegular.of_da_buchi {State : Type} [Finite State] (da : DA.Buchi State Symbol) :
    (language da).IsRegular

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.IsRegular.not_da_buchi
items.doc:
There is an ω-regular language that is not accepted by any deterministic Buchi automaton,
where the automaton is not even required to be finite-state.
items.statement:
theorem IsRegular.not_da_buchi :
  ∃ (Symbol : Type) (p : ωLanguage Symbol), p.IsRegular ∧
    ¬ ∃ (State : Type) (da : DA.Buchi State Symbol), language da = p

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.IsRegular.regular_omegaLim
items.doc: The ω-limit of a regular language is ω-regular.
items.statement:
theorem IsRegular.regular_omegaLim {l : Language Symbol}
    (h : l.IsRegular) : (l↗ω).IsRegular

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.IsRegular.bot
items.doc: The empty language is ω-regular.
items.statement: theorem IsRegular.bot : (⊥ : ωLanguage Symbol).IsRegular

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.IsRegular.top
items.doc: The language of all ω-sequences is ω-regular.
items.statement: theorem IsRegular.top : (⊤ : ωLanguage Symbol).IsRegular

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.IsRegular.sup
items.doc: The union of two ω-regular languages is ω-regular.
items.statement:
theorem IsRegular.sup {p1 p2 : ωLanguage Symbol}
    (h1 : p1.IsRegular) (h2 : p2.IsRegular) : (p1 ⊔ p2).IsRegular

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.IsRegular.inf
items.doc: The intersection of two ω-regular languages is ω-regular.
items.statement:
theorem IsRegular.inf {p1 p2 : ωLanguage Symbol}
    (h1 : p1.IsRegular) (h2 : p2.IsRegular) : (p1 ⊓ p2).IsRegular

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.IsRegular.iSup
items.doc: The union of any finite number of ω-regular languages is ω-regular.
items.statement:
theorem IsRegular.iSup {I : Type*} [Finite I] {s : Set I} {p : I → ωLanguage Symbol}
    (h : ∀ i ∈ s, (p i).IsRegular) : (⨆ i ∈ s, p i).IsRegular

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.IsRegular.iInf
items.doc: The intersection of any finite number of ω-regular languages is ω-regular.
items.statement:
theorem IsRegular.iInf {I : Type*} [Finite I] {s : Set I} {p : I → ωLanguage Symbol}
    (h : ∀ i ∈ s, (p i).IsRegular) : (⨅ i ∈ s, p i).IsRegular

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.IsRegular.hmul
items.doc: The concatenation of a regular language and an ω-regular language is ω-regular.
items.statement:
theorem IsRegular.hmul {l : Language Symbol} {p : ωLanguage Symbol}
    (h1 : l.IsRegular) (h2 : p.IsRegular) : (l * p).IsRegular

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.IsRegular.omegaPow
items.doc: The ω-power of a regular language is an ω-regular language.
items.statement:
theorem IsRegular.omegaPow [Inhabited Symbol] {l : Language Symbol}
    (h : l.IsRegular) : (l^ω).IsRegular

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.IsRegular.eq_fin_iSup_hmul_omegaPow
items.doc:
An ω-language is regular iff it is the finite union of ω-languages of the form `L * M^ω`,
where all `L`s and `M`s are regular languages.
items.statement:
theorem IsRegular.eq_fin_iSup_hmul_omegaPow [Inhabited Symbol] (p : ωLanguage Symbol) :
    p.IsRegular ↔ ∃ n : ℕ, ∃ l m : Fin n → Language Symbol,
      (∀ i, (l i).IsRegular ∧ (m i).IsRegular) ∧ p = ⨆ i, (l i) * (m i)^ω

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.IsRegular.fin_cover_saturates
items.doc:
If an ω-language has a finite saturating cover made of ω-regular languages,
then it is an ω-regular language.
items.statement:
theorem IsRegular.fin_cover_saturates {I : Type*} [Finite I]
    {p : I → ωLanguage Symbol} {q : ωLanguage Symbol}
    (hs : Saturates (fun i ↦ (p i).toSet) q.toSet)
    (hc : ⨆ i, p i = ⊤) (hr : ∀ i, (p i).IsRegular) : q.IsRegular

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.IsRegular.fin_cover_saturates_compl
items.doc:
If an ω-language has a finite saturating cover made of ω-regular languages,
then its complement is an ω-regular language.
items.statement:
theorem IsRegular.fin_cover_saturates_compl {I : Type*} [Finite I]
    {p : I → ωLanguage Symbol} {q : ωLanguage Symbol}
    (hs : Saturates (fun i ↦ (p i).toSet) q.toSet)
    (hc : ⨆ i, p i = ⊤) (hr : ∀ i, (p i).IsRegular) : (qᶜ).IsRegular

modules.title: Regular Expressions (additional definitions and theorems)

This file contains additional definitions and theorems about `RegularExpression`

items.name: RegularExpression.mem_sum_matches'

theorem mem_sum_matches' (rs : List (RegularExpression α)) (x : List α) :
    x ∈ rs.sum.matches' ↔ ∃ r ∈ rs, x ∈ r.matches'

items.name: RegularExpression.iSup_matches'
Cslib.Language.IsRegular.iff_dfa
items.doc:
A characterization of `Language.IsRegular` in terms of `DA`. This is the only theorem in Cslib
in which Mathlib's definition of `Language.IsRegular` is used.

theorem IsRegular.iff_dfa {l : Language Symbol} :

items.name: Cslib.Language.IsRegular.iff_nfa

items.name: Cslib.Language.IsRegular.iff_epsilon_nfa

items.name: Cslib.Language.IsRegular.compl
items.doc: The complementation of a regular language is regular.
items.statement: theorem IsRegular.compl {l : Language Symbol} (h : l.IsRegular) : (lᶜ).IsRegular

items.name: Cslib.Language.IsRegular.iff_twoWayNA
items.doc:
A language is regular if and only if it is accepted by some two-way nondeterministic
automaton with finitely many states.

theorem IsRegular.iff_twoWayNA {l : Language Symbol} :
    l.IsRegular ↔ ∃ State : Type, ∃ _ : Finite State,

items.name: Cslib.Language.IsRegular.zero
items.doc: The empty language is regular.
items.statement: theorem IsRegular.zero : (0 : Language Symbol).IsRegular

items.name: Cslib.Language.IsRegular.one
items.doc: The language containing only the empty word is regular.

items.name: Cslib.Language.IsRegular.top

items.statement: theorem IsRegular.top : (⊤ : Language Symbol).IsRegular

items.name: Cslib.Language.IsRegular.inf

items.name: Cslib.Language.IsRegular.add

items.name: Cslib.Language.IsRegular.kstar

theorem IsRegular.kstar {l : Language Symbol}
    (h : l.IsRegular) : (l∗).IsRegular

items.name: Cslib.Language.IsRegular.reverse

items.statement: theorem IsRegular.reverse {l : Language Symbol} (h : l.IsRegular) : l.reverse.IsRegular

items.doc: A language is regular iff its reversal is regular.

items.name: Cslib.Language.IsRegular.preimage
items.doc: The preimage of a regular languge under a language homomorphism is regular.

theorem IsRegular.preimage (f : Hom Symbol' Symbol) {l : Language Symbol} (h : l.IsRegular) :

items.name: Cslib.Language.IsRegular.char
items.doc: The language containing only the one character string `a` is regular.
items.statement: theorem IsRegular.char (a : Symbol) : ({[a]} : Language Symbol).IsRegular

modules.title: Safety and Liveness properties of ω-sequences
modules.doc:
This file formalizes the main results of [AlpernSchneider1985].  Namely, given
an appropriate topology on ω-sequences:
* Safety properties can be identified with closed sets.
* Liveness properties can be identified with dense sets.
* Every property is the intersection of a safety property and a liveness property.

## References
* [Alpern, Bowen; Schneider, Fred B. (1985). "Defining liveness".
Information Processing Letters. 21 (4): 181–185.][AlpernSchneider1985]

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.IsSafety
items.doc: Safety properties are identified with closed sets.
items.statement: abbrev IsSafety (p : ωLanguage α) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.isSafety_iff
items.doc:
An alternative characterization of `IsSafety` that justifies its definition:
if an ω-sequence violates a safety property, then it has a finite prefix all of whose
infinite extensions also violate the property.
items.statement:
theorem isSafety_iff (p : ωLanguage α) :
    p.IsSafety ↔ ∀ xs, xs ∉ p → ∃ n, ∀ ys, (xs.take n) ++ω ys ∉ p

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.IsLiveness
items.doc: Liveness properties are identified with dense sets.
items.statement: abbrev IsLiveness (p : ωLanguage α) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.isLiveness_iff
items.doc:
An alternative characterization of `IsLiveness` that justifies its definition:
any finite sequence can be extended to an infinite sequence satisfying a liveness property.
items.statement:
theorem isLiveness_iff (p : ωLanguage α) :
    p.IsLiveness ↔ ∀ (xs : ωSequence α) (n : ℕ), ∃ ys, (xs.take n) ++ω ys ∈ p

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.isSafety_closure
items.doc: `p.closure` is always a safety property for any ω-language `p`.
items.statement:
theorem isSafety_closure (p : ωLanguage α) :
    p.closure.IsSafety

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.isLiveness_sup_compl_closure
items.doc: `p ⊔ p.closureᶜ` is always a liveness property for any ω-language `p`.
items.statement:
theorem isLiveness_sup_compl_closure (p : ωLanguage α) :
    (p ⊔ p.closureᶜ).IsLiveness

items.name: Cslib.ωLanguage.exists_safetyLivenessDecomposition
items.doc:
Every property `p` is the intersection of a safety property (namely, `p.closure`) and
a liveness property (namely, `p ⊔ p.closureᶜ`).
items.statement:
theorem exists_safetyLivenessDecomposition (p : ωLanguage α) :
    ∃ q r : ωLanguage α, q.IsSafety ∧ r.IsLiveness ∧ p = q ⊓ r

modules.title: Slices of languages
modules.doc:
A language is the union of its slices, one for each word length. The slice at length `n` is a
Boolean-valued function of the `n` letters of a word, so it can be handled by models of
computation with a fixed number of inputs, such as circuits. Conversely, one such function for
each length assembles into a language, and slicing that language recovers the functions.

Membership in an arbitrary language is not decidable, so a slice is defined classically. This is
what lets notions defined for Boolean-valued functions, such as circuit complexity, apply to every
language rather than only to decidable ones.

items.name: Language.slice
items.doc: The words of length `n` in `L`, as a Boolean-valued function of their letters.
items.statement: noncomputable def slice (L : Language α) (n : ℕ) : (Fin n → α) → Bool

items.name: Language.slice_eq_true_iff
items.statement:
theorem slice_eq_true_iff {L : Language α} {n : ℕ} {x : Fin n → α} :
L.slice n x = true ↔ List.ofFn x ∈ L

items.name: Language.ofSlices
items.doc: The language whose slice at each length `n` is `f n`.
items.statement: def ofSlices (f : ∀ n, (Fin n → α) → Bool) : Language α

items.name: Language.mem_ofSlices
items.statement:
theorem mem_ofSlices {f : ∀ n, (Fin n → α) → Bool} {w : List α} :
    w ∈ ofSlices f ↔ f w.length (w[·])

items.name: Language.ofFn_mem_ofSlices
items.statement:
theorem ofFn_mem_ofSlices {f : ∀ n, (Fin n → α) → Bool} {n : ℕ} {x : Fin n → α} :
.ofFn x ∈ ofSlices f ↔ f n x

items.name: Language.slice_ofSlices
items.statement:
theorem slice_ofSlices (f : ∀ n, (Fin n → α) → Bool) (n : ℕ) :
(ofSlices f).slice n = f n

modules.title: Syntactic monoid
modules.doc:
This file has two main results:
(1) We define the syntactic monoid of a language `l` and show that `l` is regular
if and only if its syntactic monoid is finite.
(2) Using (1), we show that a language is regular if and only if it is the preimage of a subset
of a finite monoid `M` under a monoid homomorphism from the free monoid on its alphabet to `M`

## References

[Holcombe1982] Holcombe, W.M.L. (1982). Algebraic automata theory. Section 5.3

items.name: Language.Congruence.toCon
items.doc:
Converting a (two-sided) congruence `c` on finite words to a congruence relation
on the (multiplicative) free monoid.
items.statement: def Congruence.toCon [c : Congruence α] : Con (FreeMonoid α)

items.name: Language.SyntacticMonoid
items.doc:
The syntactic monoid of a language `l` is the quotient of the free monoid
by the Myhill congruence of `l`.
items.statement: abbrev SyntacticMonoid (l : Language α)

items.name: Language.homSyntacticMonoid
items.doc:
The natural homomorphism from `FreeMonoid α` to `l.SyntacticMonoid` induced
by the Myhill congruence of `l`.
items.statement: abbrev homSyntacticMonoid (l : Language α)

items.name: Language.syntacticMonoidEquivMyhillQuotient
items.doc:
The syntactic monoid of a language `l` and its Myhill quotient are the quotients of
`FreeMonoid α` and of `List α` by the same relation, hence in bijection.
items.statement:
def syntacticMonoidEquivMyhillQuotient (l : Language α) :
    l.SyntacticMonoid ≃ l.MyhillQuotient

items.name: Language.IsRegular.iff_finite_syntacticMonoid
items.doc: A language `l` is regular if and only if its syntactic monoid is finite.
items.statement:
theorem IsRegular.iff_finite_syntacticMonoid (l : Language α) :
    l.IsRegular ↔ Finite (l.SyntacticMonoid)

items.name: Language.homSyntacticMonoid_iff_myhillCongruence
items.doc: The congruence induced by `homSyntacticMonoid` is exactly the Myhill congruence.
items.statement:
theorem homSyntacticMonoid_iff_myhillCongruence {l : Language α} {x y : List α} :
    l.homSyntacticMonoid (ofList x) = l.homSyntacticMonoid (ofList y) ↔
    l.MyhillCongruence.eq x y

items.name: Language.IsRegular.exists_finite_monoid
items.doc:
Any regular language is the preimage of a subset of a finite monoid `M`
under a monoid homomorphism from the free monoid on its alphabet to `M`.
items.statement:
theorem IsRegular.exists_finite_monoid {l : Language α} (h : l.IsRegular) :
    ∃ M : Type, ∃ _ : Monoid M, ∃ _ : Finite M, ∃ f : FreeMonoid α →* M, ∃ s : Set M,
    (f ∘ ofList) ⁻¹' s = l

items.name: Language.inducedCongr
items.doc:
Given a monoid homomorphism `f` from `FreeMonoid α` to another monoid `M`,
`inducedCongr f` is the language congruence induced by `f`.
items.statement: def inducedCongr : RightCongruence α

items.name: Language.inducedCongr_ofList
items.statement:
theorem inducedCongr_ofList (x : List α) :
    (f ∘ ofList) ⁻¹' {(f ∘ ofList) x} = (inducedCongr f).eqvCls ⟦ x ⟧

items.name: Language.IsRegular.of_finite_monoid_singleton
items.doc:
The preimage of a singleton in a finite monoid `M` under a monoid homomorphism
from the free monoid to `M` is regular.
items.statement:
theorem IsRegular.of_finite_monoid_singleton [Finite M]
    (m : M) : IsRegular ((f ∘ ofList) ⁻¹' {m})

items.name: Language.IsRegular.of_finite_monoid
items.doc:
The preimage of a subset of a finite monoid `M` under a monoid homomorphism
from the free monoid to `M` is regular.
items.statement:
theorem IsRegular.of_finite_monoid [Finite M]
    (s : Set M) : IsRegular ((f ∘ ofList) ⁻¹' s)

items.name: Language.IsRegular.iff_finite_monoid
items.doc:
A language is regular if and only if it is the preimage of a subset of a finite monoid `M`
under a monoid homomorphism from the free monoid on its alphabet to `M`.
items.statement:
theorem IsRegular.iff_finite_monoid {l : Language α} :
    l.IsRegular ↔
    ∃ M : Type, ∃ _ : Monoid M, ∃ _ : Finite M, ∃ f : FreeMonoid α →* M, ∃ s : Set M,
    (f ∘ ofList) ⁻¹' s = l

modules.title: Complexity of Almost Constant Functions
modules.doc:
A function `f : α → β` that is constant except for a finite number of arguments is computable in
constant time and zero space: the machine reads the encoded input while remembering the prefix it
has seen so far. After a finite number of steps it either reaches the end of the input or a point
where the prefix cannot be extended to the encoding of one of the finitely many exceptions. In both
cases, it emits the corresponding output one symbol at a time.

This result also holds for functions whose domain is already finite.

## Main Results

* `encodedComputableInTimeAndSpace_of_finite`: Every function on a finite type is computable in
    constant time and zero space, relative to any encoding.
* `encodedComputableInTimeAndSpace_of_exists_finite_ne`: Every function that is constant except
    for a finite number of arguments is computable in constant time and zero space, relative to any
    encoding.
* `encodedComputableInTimeAndSpace_of_const`: Every constant function is computable in constant
    time and zero space, relative to any encoding.
* `encodedComputableInTimeAndSpace_almostConstTime` and
    `encodedComputableInTimeAndSpace_finiteFunTime`: The same with explicit time bounds.

items.note:
## The machine computing a function that is constant outside a finite set

The machine `almostConstTM encIn encOut f S out` computes `f`, provided that the encoded output
of `f` is the fixed Boolean string `out` outside of the finite set `S`.

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.encPrefixes
items.doc:
The prefixes of the encodings of the elements of a finite set `S`, together with the empty list.

The empty list has to be added explicitly for the case where `S` is empty: `almostConstTM` uses
the elements of this set as its states while reading the input, so the set has to contain the
starting state `[]` even if there is nothing to distinguish.
items.statement: def encPrefixes (encIn : α ↪ List Bool) (S : Finset α) : Finset (List Bool)

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.mem_encPrefixes
items.statement:
lemma mem_encPrefixes {p : List Bool} {a : α} (ha : a ∈ S) (h : p <+: encIn a) :
    p ∈ encPrefixes encIn S

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.prefix_mem_encPrefixes
items.doc: The set of prefixes is closed under taking prefixes.
items.statement:
lemma prefix_mem_encPrefixes {p q : List Bool} (h : p ∈ encPrefixes encIn S) (hq : q <+: p) :
    q ∈ encPrefixes encIn S

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.outSuffixes
items.doc: The suffixes of the default output and of the encoded values of `f` on `S`.
items.statement:
def outSuffixes (encOut : β ↪ List Bool) (f : α → β) (S : Finset α) (out : List Bool) :
    Finset (List Bool)

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.suffix_out_mem_outSuffixes
items.statement:
lemma suffix_out_mem_outSuffixes {w : List Bool} (h : w <:+ out) :
    w ∈ outSuffixes encOut f S out

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.mem_outSuffixes
items.statement:
lemma mem_outSuffixes {w : List Bool} {a : α} (ha : a ∈ S) (h : w <:+ encOut (f a)) :
    w ∈ outSuffixes encOut f S out

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.suffix_mem_outSuffixes
items.doc: The set of suffixes is closed under taking suffixes.
items.statement:
lemma suffix_mem_outSuffixes {v w : List Bool} (h : w ∈ outSuffixes encOut f S out) (hv : v <:+ w) :
    v ∈ outSuffixes encOut f S out

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.tail_mem_outSuffixes
items.statement:
lemma tail_mem_outSuffixes {w : List Bool} (h : w ∈ outSuffixes encOut f S out) :
    w.tail ∈ outSuffixes encOut f S out

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.encOut_mem_outSuffixes
items.doc:
If the encoded output is the default output outside of `S`, then every encoded output occurs
among the suffixes.
items.statement:
lemma encOut_mem_outSuffixes (h : ∀ a ∉ S, encOut (f a) = out) (a : α) :
    encOut (f a) ∈ outSuffixes encOut f S out

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.AlmostConstState
items.doc:
The states of the machine `almostConstTM`: either the prefix of the input read so far, or the
part of the output that still has to be emitted.
items.statement:
abbrev AlmostConstState (encIn : α ↪ List Bool) (encOut : β ↪ List Bool) (f : α → β)
    (S : Finset α) (out : List Bool) : Type

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.encodedFun
items.doc:
The function `f`, transported along the encodings of its domain and codomain: it maps the
encoding of an element of `S` to the encoding of its value under `f`, and every other list to the
default output.
items.statement:
noncomputable def encodedFun (encIn : α ↪ List Bool) (encOut : β ↪ List Bool) (f : α → β)
    (S : Finset α) (out : List Bool) (p : List Bool) : List Bool

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.encodedFun_enc
items.statement:
lemma encodedFun_enc {a : α} (ha : a ∈ S) :
    encodedFun encIn encOut f S out (encIn a) = encOut (f a)

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.encodedFun_enc_of_notMem
items.statement:
lemma encodedFun_enc_of_notMem {a : α} (ha : a ∉ S) :
    encodedFun encIn encOut f S out (encIn a) = out

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.encodedFun_mem_outSuffixes
items.statement:
lemma encodedFun_mem_outSuffixes (p : List Bool) :
    encodedFun encIn encOut f S out p ∈ outSuffixes encOut f S out

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.almostConstTM
items.doc:
The machine computing a function that is constant outside of `S`. It has no work tapes.

While reading the input it remembers the prefix read so far. Once this prefix cannot be extended
to the encoding of an element of `S` anymore, or the blank behind the input is reached, it
switches to the state that holds the encoded output, which it then emits one symbol per step
before halting.
items.statement:
noncomputable def almostConstTM (encIn : α ↪ List Bool) (encOut : β ↪ List Bool) (f : α → β)
    (S : Finset α) (out : List Bool) :
    MultiTapeTM 0 Bool (AlmostConstState encIn encOut f S out)

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.runFrom_read
items.doc: The configuration reached after `j` steps of reading the input.
items.statement:
lemma runFrom_read (a : α) {j : ℕ} (hj : j ≤ (encIn a).length)
    (hmem : (encIn a).take j ∈ encPrefixes encIn S) :
    (almostConstTM encIn encOut f S out).runFrom
        ((almostConstTM encIn encOut f S out).initCfg (encIn a)) j =
      { state := some (Sum.inl ⟨(encIn a).take j, hmem⟩),
        inputPos := ⟨1 + j, by omega⟩,
        workTapes := fun _ _ => none,
        workTapePos := fun _ => 0,
        output := [] }

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.runFrom_write
items.doc:
The configuration reached after having emitted the first `i` symbols of `w`, starting from a
configuration that is about to emit `w`.
items.statement:
lemma runFrom_write {input : List Bool} (pos : Fin (input.length + 2)) (o : List Bool)
    {w : List Bool} (hw : w ∈ outSuffixes encOut f S out) {i : ℕ} (hi : i ≤ w.length) :
    (almostConstTM encIn encOut f S out).runFrom
        { state := some (Sum.inr ⟨w, hw⟩), inputPos := pos, workTapes := fun _ _ => none,
          workTapePos := fun _ => 0, output := o } i =
      { state := some (Sum.inr ⟨w.drop i, suffix_mem_outSuffixes hw (w.drop_suffix i)⟩),
        inputPos := pos,
        workTapes := fun _ _ => none,
        workTapePos := fun _ => 0,
        output := o ++ w.take i }

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.runFrom_write_halted
items.doc:
Starting from a configuration that is about to emit `w`, the machine halts after `w.length + 1`
steps, having emitted `w`.
items.statement:
lemma runFrom_write_halted {input : List Bool} (pos : Fin (input.length + 2)) (o : List Bool)
    {w : List Bool} (hw : w ∈ outSuffixes encOut f S out) :
    (almostConstTM encIn encOut f S out).runFrom
        { state := some (Sum.inr ⟨w, hw⟩), inputPos := pos, workTapes := fun _ _ => none,
          workTapePos := fun _ => 0, output := o } (w.length + 1) =
      { state := none,
        inputPos := pos,
        workTapes := fun _ _ => none,
        workTapePos := fun _ => 0,
        output := o ++ w }

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.almostConstTime
items.doc: A constant time bound for the machine `almostConstTM`.
items.statement:
public def almostConstTime (encIn : α ↪ List Bool) (encOut : β ↪ List Bool) (f : α → β)
    (S : Finset α) (out : List Bool) : ℕ

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.length_le_sup_of_mem_encPrefixes
items.statement:
lemma length_le_sup_of_mem_encPrefixes {p : List Bool} (h : p ∈ encPrefixes encIn S) :
    p.length ≤ S.sup fun a => (encIn a).length + (encOut (f a)).length

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.reaches_write
items.doc:
The machine reaches the state in which it starts emitting the encoded output after a number
of steps that is bounded independently of the input.
items.statement:
lemma reaches_write (h : ∀ a ∉ S, encOut (f a) = out) (a : α) :
    ∃ (j : ℕ) (hj : j ≤ (encIn a).length),
      j + (encOut (f a)).length ≤
        out.length + S.sup (fun a => (encIn a).length + (encOut (f a)).length) ∧
      (almostConstTM encIn encOut f S out).runFrom
          ((almostConstTM encIn encOut f S out).initCfg (encIn a)) (j + 1) =
        { state := some (Sum.inr ⟨encOut (f a), encOut_mem_outSuffixes h a⟩),
          inputPos := ⟨1 + j, by omega⟩,
          workTapes := fun _ _ => none,
          workTapePos := fun _ => 0,
          output := [] }

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.computesFunInTimeAndSpace_almostConstTM
items.doc: The machine `almostConstTM` computes `f` in at most `almostConstTime` steps and no space.
items.statement:
lemma computesFunInTimeAndSpace_almostConstTM (h : ∀ a ∉ S, encOut (f a) = out) :
    (almostConstTM encIn encOut f S out).ComputesFunInTimeAndSpace encIn encOut f
      (fun _ => almostConstTime encIn encOut f S out) (fun _ => 0)

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.computableInTimeAndSpace_almostConstTime
items.doc:
Every function whose encoded output is constant outside of a finite set is computable in time
`almostConstTime` and zero space.
items.statement:
public theorem computableInTimeAndSpace_almostConstTime
    (f : α → β) (S : Finset α) (out : List Bool) (h : ∀ a ∉ S, encOut (f a) = out) :
    ComputableInTimeAndSpace f encIn encOut
      (fun _ => almostConstTime encIn encOut f S out) (fun _ => 0)

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.computableInTimeAndSpace_of_exists_finite_ne
items.doc: Every almost constant function is computable in constant time and zero space.
items.statement:
public theorem computableInTimeAndSpace_of_exists_finite_ne
    {f : α → β} (h : ∃ b : β, {a : α | f a ≠ b}.Finite) :
    ∃ c, ComputableInTimeAndSpace f encIn encOut (fun _ => c) (fun _ => 0)

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.computableInTimeAndSpace_of_const
items.doc: Every constant function is computable in constant time and zero space.
items.statement:
public theorem computableInTimeAndSpace_of_const {α β : Type*}
    {encIn : α ↪ List Bool} {encOut : β ↪ List Bool} (b : β) :
    ∃ c, ComputableInTimeAndSpace (Function.const α b) encIn encOut
      (fun _ => c) (fun _ => 0)

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.finiteFunTime
items.doc: A constant time bound for functions on a finite type.
items.statement:
public noncomputable def finiteFunTime {α β : Type*} [Finite α] (encIn : α ↪ List Bool)
    (encOut : β ↪ List Bool) (f : α → β) : ℕ

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.computableInTimeAndSpace_finiteFunTime
items.doc: Every function on a finite type is computable in time `finiteFunTime` and zero space.
items.statement:
public theorem computableInTimeAndSpace_finiteFunTime {α β : Type*} [Finite α]
    {encIn : α ↪ List Bool} {encOut : β ↪ List Bool} (f : α → β) :
    ComputableInTimeAndSpace f encIn encOut
      (fun _ => finiteFunTime encIn encOut f) (fun _ => 0)

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.computableInTimeAndSpace_of_finite
items.doc: Every function on a finite type is computable in constant time and zero space.
items.statement:
public theorem computableInTimeAndSpace_of_finite {α β : Type*} [Finite α]
    {encIn : α ↪ List Bool} {encOut : β ↪ List Bool}
    (f : α → β) :
    ∃ c, ComputableInTimeAndSpace f encIn encOut (fun _ => c) (fun _ => 0)

modules.title: Complexity of the identity function
modules.doc:
A machine with a single state and no work tapes scans the input from left to right, copying each
symbol to the output tape, and halts on the blank at the right end of the input. On input `w` it
outputs `w` after `w.length + 1` steps, and having no work tapes it uses zero space.

## Main results

* `Turing.MultiTapeTM.computableInTimeAndSpace_id`: the identity is computable in one step per
  input symbol and zero space.

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.copy
items.doc:
The copy machine: a single state and no work tapes. It copies every input symbol to the output
tape while moving right, and halts on reading the blank at the right end of the input.
items.statement: def copy : MultiTapeTM 0 Symbol Unit

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.Copy.cfg
items.doc:
The configuration of the copy machine in state `q` after copying the first `n` input symbols
to the output: the input head is over cell `n + 1` (capped at the right end marker) and there are
no work tapes. `input` is explicit because it only occurs in the type.
items.statement: def cfg (input : List Symbol) (q : Option Unit) (n : ℕ) : Cfg 0 Symbol Unit input

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.Copy.step_scan
items.doc: Over an input symbol, the copy machine emits it and moves right.
items.statement:
lemma step_scan {n : ℕ} (hn : n < input.length) :
    copy.step (cfg input (some ()) n) = cfg input (some ()) (n + 1)

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.Copy.step_halt
items.doc: On the blank at the right end of the input, the copy machine halts in place.
items.statement:
lemma step_halt :
    copy.step (cfg input (some ()) input.length) = cfg input none input.length

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.Copy.runFrom_scan
items.doc: After `n ≤ input.length` steps, the copy machine has copied the first `n` input symbols.
items.statement:
lemma runFrom_scan (n : ℕ) (hn : n ≤ input.length) :
    copy.runFrom (copy.initCfg input) n = cfg input (some ()) n

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.Copy.runFrom_full
items.doc:
The complete run: after `input.length + 1` steps the copy machine has halted with the input
copied to the output.
items.statement:
lemma runFrom_full (input : List Symbol) :
    copy.runFrom (copy.initCfg input) (input.length + 1) = cfg input none input.length

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.Copy.computesInTimeAndSpace
items.doc: The copy machine outputs its input unchanged, in `input.length + 1` steps and zero space.
items.statement:
theorem computesInTimeAndSpace (input : List Symbol) :
    ComputesInTimeAndSpace copy input input (input.length + 1) 0

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.computableInTimeAndSpace_id
items.doc: The identity function is computable in one step per input symbol and zero space.

modules.title: Bounds on the number of reachable configurations in bounded space
modules.doc:
A multi-tape Turing machine that uses at most `s` cells of work-tape space can only reach a number
of configurations that differ in their storage content (state and work tapes) that is bounded
exponentially in `s`. Together with the `n + 2` possible positions of the input head this bounds
the number of configurations the machine can be in, disregarding the write-only output tape.

## Important Definitions

The results are layered, from the purely combinatorial to the machine-specific:

* `MultiTapeTM.encard_fitsIn_le` is a counting statement about the type `Storage` alone and does
  not mention Turing machines: a memory whose non-blank cells and heads stay within per-tape
  windows of total size `s` can hold at most `storageBound Symbol State k s` different values.
* `MultiTapeNTM.ComputationPath.storage_fitsIn` is the geometric input: the storage at the end of a
  computation path stays within the windows given by the per-tape space of the path.
* `MultiTapeTM.encard_storages_le` combines the two: a machine bounded by space `s` passes through
  at most `storageBound Symbol State k s` storages *during its whole run*, no matter how long it
  runs and how long its input is. This is the form needed for arguments below logarithmic space,
  where the number of storages is much smaller than the number of input head positions.
* `MultiTapeTM.encard_cores_le` adds the input head position, giving the bound
  `(n + 2) * storageBound Symbol State k s` on the number of reachable *cores* (`Cfg.core`,
  a configuration without its output tape) for an input of length `n`.
* `MultiTapeTM.storageBound_le_base_mul_pow` restates `storageBound Symbol State k s` as
  `storageBoundBase Symbol State k * 2 ^ (storageBoundExp Symbol k * s)`, so that the bounds can
  be used to time-bound space-bounded machines.

## Design

The write-only output tape is never read by `step`, so it can be dropped: what a machine can still
react to is its `Cfg.core`, the pair of the input head position and the `Storage`. The input head
position, in contrast, *is* read, so it cannot be dropped and has to be counted, which is where
the factor `n + 2` comes from (the input head may move one step off the input in either direction).

Starting from the all-blank tapes with every head at `0` and moving by at most one cell per step,
a computation in which tape `i` has visited at most `sᵢ` cells keeps that tape's head position and
every non-blank cell within the per-tape window `[-sᵢ, sᵢ]`.

Hence a storage is determined by finite data over these windows, and counting it gives the
per-tape product `∏ᵢ (2 sᵢ + 1) · (|Symbol| + 1)^(2 sᵢ + 1)`. Since the tapes share the total space
budget (`∑ᵢ sᵢ ≤ s`), this collapses to an expression with the *total* space (`2s + k`) as the
alphabet exponent.

We lose a factor of `2 * k` by simplifying the windows to `[-sᵢ, sᵢ]` instead of the actually used
area, but this is absorbed by the `O(s)` exponent in the final bound.

The windows for a whole run are available because the computation paths of a deterministic
machine are prefixes of one another, so the one visiting the most cells contains the windows of
every other (`MultiTapeNTM.ComputationPath.spaceUsedByTape_le_of_space_le`).

items.note:
## Storage

Defines the core data structure for this file, `Storage`, which contains the state and the work
tapes of a multi-tape Turing machine, with the work tape cells indexed over all of `ℤ`. It is
thus equivalent to a projection of `Cfg`.

Then `BoundedStorage` is introduced, which restricts the cells and the head position of each tape
to a window `[-s, s]` (with a different `s` for each tape) and is therefore a finite type. It is
proven that the restriction map is injective on those `Storage`s whose non-blank cells and head
positions all lie inside the `[-s, s]` windows, so that counting `BoundedStorage` bounds the
number of such `Storage`s.

items.name: Turing.Storage
items.doc: The state and work-tape data of a machine.
items.statement:
structure Storage (Symbol State : Type*) (k : ℕ) where
  /-- the state of the TM (cf. `Cfg.state`) -/
  state : Option State
  /-- the contents of work tape `i` (cf. `Cfg.workTapes`) -/
  workTapes (i : Fin k) : ℤ → Option Symbol
  /-- the position of the head on work tape `i` (cf. `Cfg.workTapePos`) -/
  workTapePos (i : Fin k) : ℤ

items.name: Turing.BoundedStorage
items.doc:
A bounded storage: the state and work-tape data of a machine, but with the cells and the head
position of tape `i` restricted to the finite window `[-(w i), w i]`.
items.statement: abbrev BoundedStorage (Symbol State : Type*) {k : ℕ} (w : Fin k → ℕ)

items.name: Turing.Storage.FitsIn
items.doc:
A storage fits in the per-tape windows `w`: on each tape `j`, the head position and every
non-blank cell have absolute value `≤ w j`.
items.statement:
structure Storage.FitsIn (x : Storage Symbol State k) (w : Fin k → ℕ) : Prop where
  /-- the head position on every tape lies within its window -/
  pos_le : ∀ j, (x.workTapePos j).natAbs ≤ w j
  /-- every non-blank cell on every tape lies within its window -/
  cell_le : ∀ j z, x.workTapes j z ≠ none → z.natAbs ≤ w j

items.name: Turing.Storage.FitsIn_mono
items.doc: If a `Storage` fits in a smaller window, it also fits in the larger window.
items.statement: lemma Storage.FitsIn_mono {x : Storage Symbol State k} : Monotone x.FitsIn

items.name: Turing.Storage.toBounded
items.doc:
Restriction of a storage to the finite windows `w` (with heads outside their window
clamped to `0`).
items.statement:
def Storage.toBounded (x : Storage Symbol State k) (w : Fin k → ℕ) :
    BoundedStorage Symbol State w

items.name: Turing.Storage.toBounded_injOn
items.doc: The restriction is injective on storages that fit in the windows.
items.statement:
lemma Storage.toBounded_injOn (w : Fin k → ℕ) :
    Set.InjOn (Storage.toBounded (Symbol := Symbol) (State := State) · w) {x | x.FitsIn w}

items.note:
## Counting storages

This section is purely combinatorial: it counts how many values a `Storage` restricted to given
windows can take, without reference to a machine or a run.

items.name: Turing.storageBound
items.doc:
An upper bound on the number of storages a `k`-tape machine can be in while using
at most `s` cells of total work-tape space, over the given alphabet and state set. The `(2s + 1)^k`
factor counts the possible head positions; the dominant factor `(|Symbol| + 1)^(2s + k)` uses the
*total* space `s` in the exponent (the `k` tapes share the space budget).
items.statement: def storageBound (Symbol State : Type*) [Fintype Symbol] [Fintype State] (k s : ℕ) : ℕ

items.name: Turing.card_boundedStorage_le
items.doc:
The number of bounded storages is at most `storageBound`. Counting the tapes separately gives
the per-tape product `∏ᵢ (2 wᵢ + 1) · (|Symbol| + 1) ^ (2 wᵢ + 1)`; each tape uses at most the
total space `s`, and the tapes together use at most `s`, which collapses the alphabet exponent
to `2s + k`.
items.statement:
lemma card_boundedStorage_le [Fintype Symbol] [Fintype State]
    {w : Fin k → ℕ} {s : ℕ} (hsum : ∑ i, w i ≤ s) :
    Fintype.card (BoundedStorage Symbol State w) ≤ storageBound Symbol State k s

items.name: Turing.encard_fitsIn_le
items.doc:
The counting result at the heart of this file: a `Storage` whose non-blank cells and head
positions stay within per-tape windows of total size at most `s` can take at most
`storageBound Symbol State k s` different values.
items.statement:
theorem encard_fitsIn_le [Fintype Symbol] [Fintype State]
    {w : Fin k → ℕ} {s : ℕ} (hsum : ∑ i, w i ≤ s) :
    {x : Storage Symbol State k | x.FitsIn w}.encard
      ≤ storageBound Symbol State k s

items.note:
### The exponential form of `storageBound`

This proves that `storageBound` is exponential in the space `s`.

items.name: Turing.storageBoundBase
items.doc: The base factor in the resulting exponential form of `storageBound`.
items.statement: def storageBoundBase (Symbol State : Type*) [Fintype Symbol] [Fintype State] (k : ℕ) : ℕ

items.name: Turing.storageBoundExp
items.doc: The factor in the exponent of the exponential form of `storageBound`.
items.statement: def storageBoundExp (Symbol : Type*) [Fintype Symbol] (k : ℕ) : ℕ

items.name: Turing.storageBound_le_base_mul_pow
items.doc:
`storageBound` grows at most exponentially in the space `s`, with a constant factor and a
factor in the exponent that only depend on the machine's alphabet, state set and tape count.
items.statement:
lemma storageBound_le_base_mul_pow [Fintype Symbol] [Fintype State] (s : ℕ) :
    storageBound Symbol State k s
      ≤ storageBoundBase Symbol State k * 2 ^ (storageBoundExp Symbol k * s)

items.name: Turing.storageBound_le_pow
items.doc:
`storageBound` grows at most exponentially in the space `s`: there exist constants `a` and `c`
(depending on the machine's alphabet, state set and tape count) with
`storageBound Symbol State k s ≤ a * 2 ^ (c * s)` for all `s`.
items.statement:
lemma storageBound_le_pow [Fintype Symbol] [Fintype State] :
    ∃ a c : ℕ, ∀ s : ℕ, storageBound Symbol State k s ≤ a * 2 ^ (c * s)

items.note:
## The storage and the core of a configuration

Now we relate `Cfg` and `Storage` by giving the projection.

items.name: Turing.Cfg.storage
items.doc:
This function maps a `Cfg` to `Storage`, forgetting the input head position and the
write-only output tape.
items.statement: def Cfg.storage (c : Cfg k Symbol State input) : Storage Symbol State k

items.name: Turing.Cfg.core
items.doc:
The part of a configuration that the machine can still read: the input head position together
with the `Storage`, i.e. the configuration without the write-only output tape.
items.statement:
def Cfg.core (c : Cfg k Symbol State input) :
    Fin (input.length + 2) × Storage Symbol State k

items.note:
## The storages and cores of a space-bounded run

These are the main results giving upper bounds on the number of storages and configuration cores
reachable in bounded space.

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.ComputationPath.storage_fitsIn
items.doc:
The storage at the end of a computation path fits in the windows given by its per-tape space:
the tapes start blank, with every head at `0`.
items.statement:
lemma ComputationPath.storage_fitsIn {ntm : MultiTapeNTM k Symbol State}
    (p : ntm.ComputationPath input) : p.last.storage.FitsIn p.spaceUsedByTape

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.encard_storages_le
items.doc:
A machine that uses at most `s` cells of work-tape space at every point in time passes through
at most `storageBound Symbol State k s` different storages during its whole run — independently of
the length of the input and of how long it runs.
items.statement:
theorem encard_storages_le [Fintype Symbol] [Fintype State] {s : ℕ}
    (hs : tm.RunsInSpace input s) :
    (Set.range fun p : tm.ComputationPath input => p.last.storage).encard
      ≤ storageBound Symbol State k s

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.encard_cores_le
items.doc:
The number of configuration cores that a machine bounded by space `s` can reach is at most
`(n + 2) * storageBound Symbol State k s`, where `n` is the length of the input.
items.statement:
theorem encard_cores_le [Fintype Symbol] [Fintype State] {s : ℕ}
    (hs : tm.RunsInSpace input s) :
    (Set.range fun p : tm.ComputationPath input => p.last.core).encard
      ≤ (input.length + 2) * storageBound Symbol State k s

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.encard_storages_le_pow
items.doc:
The storage bound in exponential form: the number of storages a space-`s`-bounded machine
passes through is at most `2 ^ (O(s))`, with constants depending only on the machine.
items.statement:
theorem encard_storages_le_pow [Finite Symbol] [Finite State] :
    ∃ a c : ℕ, ∀ (input : List Symbol) (s : ℕ),
      tm.RunsInSpace input s →
      (Set.range fun p : tm.ComputationPath input => p.last.storage).encard ≤ a * 2 ^ (c * s)

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.encard_cores_le_pow
items.doc:
The core bound in exponential form: the number of cores a space-`s`-bounded machine can reach
is at most `(n + 2) * 2 ^ (O(s))`, with constants depending only on the machine and not on the
input.
items.statement:
theorem encard_cores_le_pow [Finite Symbol] [Finite State] :
    ∃ a c : ℕ, ∀ (input : List Symbol) (s : ℕ),
      tm.RunsInSpace input s →
      (Set.range fun p : tm.ComputationPath input => p.last.core).encard
        ≤ (input.length + 2) * a * 2 ^ (c * s)

modules.authors: Christian Reitwiessner, Samuel Schlesinger, Aviv Bar Natan
modules.title: Configurations of Multi-Tape Turing Machines
modules.doc:
Configurations of a multi-tape Turing machine with a read-only input tape, `k` work tapes and one
write-only output tape, together with what a single transition does to a configuration.

The configurations are used by both deterministic and nondeterministic multi-tape Turing machines
and give instantaneous descriptions of their state. An `Action` describes how one configuration
transitions to the next. It records which way the input head moves, what is written and where the
work heads move, which symbol is emitted and which state follows. `Action.apply` carries out the
action on a configuration.

## Design

Configurations and actions are defined independently of a machine.

The output tape is part of the configuration, so the string emitted along a run can be read off
