`ComputesFunTidilyInTimeAndSpace tm encIn encOut f t s`: for every `a`, the machine computes
`encOut (f a)` from `encIn a` tidily, within `t a` steps and `s a` cells.
items.statement:
def ComputesFunTidilyInTimeAndSpace (tm : MultiTapeTM k Symbol State)
    (encIn : α ↪ List Symbol) (encOut : β ↪ List Symbol) (f : α → β) (t s : α → ℕ) : Prop

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.ComputesFunTidilyInTimeAndSpace.mono
items.doc: Resource bounds can be weakened independently on every input.
items.statement:
theorem ComputesFunTidilyInTimeAndSpace.mono {encIn : α ↪ List Symbol} {encOut : β ↪ List Symbol}
    {f : α → β} {t s t' s' : α → ℕ} (h : ComputesFunTidilyInTimeAndSpace tm encIn encOut f t s)
    (ht : ∀ a, t a ≤ t' a) (hs : ∀ a, s a ≤ s' a) :
    ComputesFunTidilyInTimeAndSpace tm encIn encOut f t' s'

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.ComputableTidilyInTimeAndSpace
items.doc:
Some machine with binary alphabet and finitely many states computes `f` tidily within the
bounds `t` and `s`. The bounds include the cost of restoring the tapes.
items.statement:
def ComputableTidilyInTimeAndSpace (f : α → β) (encIn : α ↪ List Bool) (encOut : β ↪ List Bool)
    (t s : α → ℕ) : Prop

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.ComputableTidilyInTimeAndSpaceOfLength
items.doc:
`Turing.MultiTapeTM.ComputableTidilyInTimeAndSpace` with the bounds `t` and `s` evaluated at the
length of the encoded input: the tidy analog of
`Turing.MultiTapeTM.ComputableInTimeAndSpaceOfLength`.
items.statement:
abbrev ComputableTidilyInTimeAndSpaceOfLength (f : α → β) (encIn : α ↪ List Bool)
    (encOut : β ↪ List Bool) (t s : ℕ → ℕ) : Prop

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.ComputableTidilyInTimeAndSpace.mono
items.doc: Tidy computability is monotone in the resource bounds.

modules.title: Machines as transformers of tape words
modules.doc:
The interface through which combinators use machines: a machine reads words from its work tapes
and leaves words on them. A combinator composing such machines talks about words only, never about
individual cells, head positions or the set of tapes a machine has touched.

Configurations are described by *equalities*: `wordsCfg input q ws out` is the configuration whose
work tape `i` holds exactly the word `ws i` (contents `tapeOfList (ws i)`, head at the start), with
the input head at the start of the input and output `out`. A specification
`TransformsTapes tm P Q t s` says: started on word-holding tapes satisfying `P`, the machine has a
run path to the halted *normal form* `wordsCfg input none ws' (out ++ emitted)` (every head reset
to its initial position, tapes blank outside their words, the word `emitted` appended to the
output it was handed), with the new words related to the old ones by `Q`, taking at most `t` steps
and visiting at most `s` work-tape cells. The time and space are those of the path, so
specifications compose by joining their paths.
Requiring this normal form is what lets specifications compose by rewriting: the halting
configuration of one machine is already a valid start for the next, so which words survived a step
is read off the equation, not re-established cell by cell.

The output is described as the word the machine *appends*, never as an absolute value, so that a
specification is insensitive to the output it is handed — which is what lets specifications
compose: along a sequence the emitted words concatenate.

## Main definitions

* `Turing.MultiTapeTM.TransformsTapes`: the specification format described above.
* `Turing.MultiTapeTM.nop`: the machine that does nothing.

## Main results

* `Turing.MultiTapeTM.TransformsTapes.imp`: strengthen the precondition, weaken the postcondition
  and raise the bounds.
* `Turing.MultiTapeTM.transformsTapes_iff_nil_output`: the generality in the ambient output is
  free, so a concrete machine need only be run with no prior output.
* `Turing.MultiTapeTM.transformsTapes_nop`: `nop` leaves every word as it was, the first machine of
  the interface and the check that the format is inhabited as intended.

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.TransformsTapes
items.doc:
`TransformsTapes tm P Q t s`: started in its initial state on tapes holding words `ws` that
satisfy the precondition `P`, the machine has a run path of at most `t` steps, visiting at most `s`
work-tape cells, to the halted configuration whose tapes hold words `ws'` and which has appended
`emitted` to the output it was handed, with `Q input ws ws' emitted`.

The bounds are numbers; a specification whose bounds depend on the data is a *family*
`∀ j, TransformsTapes tm (P j) (Q j) (t j) (s j)` over one fixed machine.
items.statement:
def TransformsTapes (tm : MultiTapeTM k Symbol State)
    (P : (input : List Symbol) → (Fin k → List Symbol) → Prop)
    (Q : (input : List Symbol) → (Fin k → List Symbol) → (Fin k → List Symbol) →
      List Symbol → Prop)
    (t s : ℕ) : Prop

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.TransformsTapes.imp
items.doc:
A `TransformsTapes` statement can be read with a stronger precondition, a weaker postcondition
and larger bounds.

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.TransformsTapes.mono
items.doc: A `TransformsTapes` statement can be read with larger bounds.

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.transformsTapes_iff_nil_output
items.doc:
**The ambient output is a concern of sequencing, not of machines.** A specification holds for
every prior output as soon as it holds for none, because a machine never reads what it has already
written. This is where that generality is discharged, once, rather than by every caller: a concrete
machine enters the interface by proving the right-hand side.

The only consumer of the generality is `Turing.MultiTapeTM.transformsTapes_seq`, which runs the
second machine after the first has emitted.
items.statement:
theorem transformsTapes_iff_nil_output {tm : MultiTapeTM k Symbol State}
    {P : (input : List Symbol) → (Fin k → List Symbol) → Prop}
    {Q : (input : List Symbol) → (Fin k → List Symbol) → (Fin k → List Symbol) →
      List Symbol → Prop} {t s : ℕ} :
    TransformsTapes tm P Q t s ↔ ∀ input ws, P input ws → ∃ ws' emitted, Q input ws ws' emitted ∧
      ∃ p : tm.RunPath input, p.head = wordsCfg input (some tm.q₀) ws [] ∧
        p.last = wordsCfg input none ws' emitted ∧ p.time ≤ t ∧ p.space ≤ s

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.nop
items.doc:
The machine that does nothing: it halts on its first step, leaving the configuration
unchanged.
items.statement: def nop (k : ℕ) (Symbol : Type*) : MultiTapeTM k Symbol Unit

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.step_nop
items.doc: A single step of `nop` halts and leaves the words alone.
items.statement:
lemma step_nop (ws : Fin k → List Symbol) (out : List Symbol) :
    (nop k Symbol).step (wordsCfg input (some ()) ws out) = wordsCfg input none ws out

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.runFrom_nop_one
items.doc: `nop` reaches its halting configuration after exactly one step.
items.statement:
lemma runFrom_nop_one (ws : Fin k → List Symbol) (out : List Symbol) :
    (nop k Symbol).runFrom (wordsCfg input (some ()) ws out) 1 = wordsCfg input none ws out

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeTM.transformsTapes_nop
items.doc:
**The machine that does nothing** halts in one step, leaving every word as it was and emitting
nothing. Its heads never move, so it visits one cell per tape. This is the first machine of the
interface: it checks that the specification format is inhabited exactly as intended.
items.statement:
theorem transformsTapes_nop (k : ℕ) (Symbol : Type*) :
    TransformsTapes (nop k Symbol) (fun _ _ => True)
      (fun _ ws ws' emitted => ws' = ws ∧ emitted = []) 1 k

modules.title: Tapes holding words and configurations of such tapes
modules.doc:
The normal form in which "tape transformer" machines (cf. `TransformsTapes.lean`) start and finish:
every work tape holds a word in the cells `0, 1, …` and is blank everywhere else, with every head
at the start.

## Main definitions

* `Turing.tapeOfList`: the tape holding exactly a given word.
* `Turing.wordsCfg`: the configuration whose tapes hold given words.

items.name: Turing.tapeOfList
items.doc: A tape containing exactly the symbols of `xs` at positions `0, ..., xs.length - 1`.
items.statement: def tapeOfList (xs : List Symbol) : ℤ → Option Symbol

items.name: Turing.tapeOfList_ofNat
items.statement: lemma tapeOfList_ofNat (xs : List Symbol) (n : ℕ) : tapeOfList xs n = xs[n]?

items.name: Turing.tapeOfList_negSucc
items.statement:
lemma tapeOfList_negSucc (xs : List Symbol) (n : ℕ) :
    tapeOfList xs (.negSucc n) = none

items.name: Turing.tapeOfList_append_single
items.doc: Appending one symbol writes precisely the cell after the existing word.
items.statement:
lemma tapeOfList_append_single (xs : List Symbol) (x : Symbol) :
    tapeOfList (xs ++ [x]) = Function.update (tapeOfList xs) (xs.length : ℤ) (some x)

items.name: Turing.tapeOfList_eq_none_iff
items.doc: A cell of `tapeOfList xs` is blank exactly outside the positions `0, …, xs.length - 1`.
items.statement:
lemma tapeOfList_eq_none_iff (xs : List Symbol) (z : ℤ) :
    tapeOfList xs z = none ↔ z < 0 ∨ (xs.length : ℤ) ≤ z

items.name: Turing.tapeOfList_nil
items.doc: The blank tape holds the empty word.
items.statement: lemma tapeOfList_nil : tapeOfList ([] : List Symbol) = fun _ => none

items.name: Turing.tapeOfList_zero
items.doc: The cell at position `0` holds the first symbol of the word.
items.statement: lemma tapeOfList_zero (xs : List Symbol) : tapeOfList xs 0 = xs.head?

items.name: Turing.wordsCfg
items.doc:
The configuration whose work tape `i` holds exactly the word `ws i` with its head at the
start, whose input head is at the start of the input, in state `q` with output `out`.
items.statement:
def wordsCfg (input : List Symbol) (q : Option State)
    (ws : Fin k → List Symbol) (out : List Symbol) : Cfg k Symbol State input

items.name: Turing.mapState_wordsCfg
items.doc: Remapping the state of a `wordsCfg` remaps its state and leaves the words alone.
items.statement:
lemma mapState_wordsCfg {State' : Type*} (φ : Option State → Option State')
    (input : List Symbol) (q : Option State) (ws : Fin k → List Symbol) (out : List Symbol) :
    (wordsCfg input q ws out).mapState φ = wordsCfg input (φ q) ws out

items.name: Turing.withState_wordsCfg
items.doc: Changing the state of a `wordsCfg` leaves the words alone.
items.statement:
lemma withState_wordsCfg {State' : Type*} (input : List Symbol) (q : Option State)
    (ws : Fin k → List Symbol) (out : List Symbol) (q' : Option State') :
    (wordsCfg input q ws out).withState q' = wordsCfg input q' ws out

items.name: Turing.prependOutput_wordsCfg
items.doc: Prepending a word to the output of a `wordsCfg` prepends it to the output word.
items.statement:
lemma prependOutput_wordsCfg (input : List Symbol) (q : Option State)
    (ws : Fin k → List Symbol) (out pre : List Symbol) :
    (wordsCfg input q ws out).prependOutput pre = wordsCfg input q ws (pre ++ out)

items.name: Turing.Cfg.init_eq_wordsCfg
items.doc: The initial configuration is the word configuration with blank tapes and no output.
items.statement:
lemma Cfg.init_eq_wordsCfg (q₀ : State) (input : List Symbol) :
    Cfg.init (k := k) q₀ input = wordsCfg input (some q₀) (fun _ => []) []

modules.authors: Christian Reitwiessner, Samuel Schlesinger, Aviv Bar Natan
modules.title: Space usage of multi-tape Turing machines
modules.doc:
Defines the space used by a run path of a multi-tape Turing machine. Space usage counts the
positions visited by each work-tape head along the path and sums over the tapes.

`MultiTapeNTM.RunPath.InWindow` says that every head of a run path stays within the window
`[-s, s]`, which bounds the space of the path.

`MultiTapeNTM.RunPath.space_map_le` bounds the space of a run path mapped by `RunPath.map` through
the head positions of the original path.

## Design

The input tape is read-only with bounded head movement, and the output tape is write-only, so we
ignore both for space usage. A work-tape cell is visited when its head occupies that position in any
configuration of the path, including the initial and final configurations. Each cell counts once,
regardless of repeated visits.

Instead of considering the cells _visited_ by the work tape heads, some textbooks
(including [AroraBarak09]) only consider the number of cells that contain
a non-blank symbol at some point in the execution or the number of cells written to. This allows
work tape heads to freely move at no cost as long as they do not write. It is
important to note that this causes `DSPACE(1)` to include `DSPACE(log log n)`, a class that
contains e.g. the non-regular language `{0^n 1^n | n ∈ ℕ}` (it is accepted by a TM that writes a
single marker on the work tape and then counts the number of symbols by work tape head movement
without writing).
Defining space usage via "cells visited" thus yields the more fine-grained "complexity world" in
which `DSPACE(1)` is exactly the class of regular languages.

## References

* [S. Arora, B. Barak, *Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach*][AroraBarak09]

items.name: Turing.window
items.doc: The window `[-s, s]` of tape positions allotted to a tape that uses `s` cells.
items.statement: def window (s : ℕ) : Finset ℤ

items.name: Turing.mem_window
items.statement: lemma mem_window {s : ℕ} {z : ℤ} : z ∈ window s ↔ z.natAbs ≤ s

items.name: Turing.card_window
items.statement: lemma card_window (s : ℕ) : (window s).card = 2 * s + 1

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.RunPath.visitedByTapeHead
items.doc: The set of positions visited by the head of work tape `i` along a run path.
items.statement: def visitedByTapeHead (p : ntm.RunPath input) (i : Fin k) : Finset ℤ

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.RunPath.spaceUsedByTape
items.doc: The number of positions visited by the head of work tape `i` along a run path.
items.statement: def spaceUsedByTape (p : ntm.RunPath input) (i : Fin k) : ℕ

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.RunPath.space
items.doc: The number of work tape cells visited along a run path.
items.statement: def space (p : ntm.RunPath input) : ℕ

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.RunPath.spaceUsedByTape_le_card
items.doc: A set containing every position of a head along a path bounds the space used by its tape.
items.statement:
lemma spaceUsedByTape_le_card (p : ntm.RunPath input) {i : Fin k} {S : Finset ℤ}
    (h : ∀ c ∈ p, c.workTapePos i ∈ S) : p.spaceUsedByTape i ≤ S.card

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.RunPath.space_le_sum_card
items.doc:
Sets containing every position of the heads along a path bound its space by their total
size.
items.statement:
lemma space_le_sum_card (p : ntm.RunPath input) {S : Fin k → Finset ℤ}
    (h : ∀ c ∈ p, ∀ i, c.workTapePos i ∈ S i) : p.space ≤ ∑ i, (S i).card

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.RunPath.space_le_of_subset
items.doc: A path whose configurations all lie on another path visits no more cells.
items.statement: lemma space_le_of_subset {p q : ntm.RunPath input} (h : ∀ c ∈ q, c ∈ p) : q.space ≤ p.space

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.RunPath.mem_visitedByTapeHead
items.doc: A path visits exactly the head positions of its configurations.
items.statement:
lemma mem_visitedByTapeHead (p : ntm.RunPath input) {i : Fin k} {z : ℤ} :
    z ∈ p.visitedByTapeHead i ↔ ∃ c ∈ p, c.workTapePos i = z

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.RunPath.visitedByTapeHead_take_subset
items.doc: A prefix of a path visits only cells that the path visits.
items.statement:
lemma visitedByTapeHead_take_subset (p : ntm.RunPath input) (j : Fin (p.length + 1)) (i : Fin k) :
    visitedByTapeHead (p.take j) i ⊆ p.visitedByTapeHead i

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.RunPath.visitedByTapeHead_snoc
items.doc: Extending a path by a configuration visits its head positions as well.
items.statement:
lemma visitedByTapeHead_snoc (p : ntm.RunPath input) (c : Cfg k Symbol State input)
    (h : ntm.Step p.last c) (i : Fin k) :
    visitedByTapeHead (p.snoc c h) i = insert (c.workTapePos i) (p.visitedByTapeHead i)

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.RunPath.InWindow
items.doc: Every head stays within the window `[-s, s]` along the path.
items.statement: def InWindow (p : ntm.RunPath input) (s : ℕ) : Prop

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.RunPath.InWindow.space_le
items.doc: A path whose heads stay within `[-s, s]` visits at most `2 * s + 1` cells on each tape.
items.statement:
lemma InWindow.space_le {p : ntm.RunPath input} {s : ℕ} (h : p.InWindow s) :
    p.space ≤ k * (2 * s + 1)

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.RunPath.InWindow.smash
items.doc: Joining two paths whose heads stay within `[-s, s]` keeps them there.
items.statement:
lemma InWindow.smash {p q : ntm.RunPath input} {h : p.last = q.head} {s : ℕ}
    (hp : p.InWindow s) (hq : q.InWindow s) : InWindow (p.smash q h) s

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.RunPath.visitedByTapeHead_map
items.doc:
If the head of tape `i'` of a mapped path follows the head of tape `i` of the source path, the
two tapes visit the same cells.
items.statement:
lemma visitedByTapeHead_map (p : ntm.RunPath input)
    (f : (ntm.stepRel input).Hom (ntm'.stepRel input')) {i : Fin k} {i' : Fin k'}
    (h : ∀ c ∈ p, (f c).workTapePos i' = c.workTapePos i) :
    (p.map f).visitedByTapeHead i' = p.visitedByTapeHead i

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.RunPath.space_map_le
items.doc:
**Space of a mapped path.** If tape `e j` of the mapped path follows tape `j` of `p`, and every
other tape `l` stays in `window l`, the mapped path uses the space of `p` plus the cells of
`window l` for every other tape `l`.
items.statement:
lemma space_map_le (p : ntm.RunPath input) (f : (ntm.stepRel input).Hom (ntm'.stepRel input'))
    (e : Fin k ↪ Fin k') (window : Fin k' → Finset ℤ)
    (hfollow : ∀ c ∈ p, ∀ j, (f c).workTapePos (e j) = c.workTapePos j)
    (hwindow : ∀ c ∈ p, ∀ l ∉ Set.range e, (f c).workTapePos l ∈ window l) :
    (p.map f).space ≤ p.space + ∑ l ∈ (Finset.univ.map e)ᶜ, (window l).card

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.ComputationPath.spaceUsedByTape
items.doc: The number of positions visited by the head of work tape `i` along a computation path.
items.statement: def ComputationPath.spaceUsedByTape (p : ntm.ComputationPath input) (i : Fin k) : ℕ

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.ComputationPath.space
items.doc: The number of work tape cells visited along a computation path.
items.statement: def ComputationPath.space (p : ntm.ComputationPath input) : ℕ

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.RunsInSpace
items.doc:
Every computation prefix on `input` visits at most `s` work-tape cells, regardless of its
outcome.
items.statement: def RunsInSpace (ntm : MultiTapeNTM k Symbol State) (input : List Symbol) (s : ℕ) : Prop

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.RunsInSpace.mono
items.doc: A space bound can be increased.
items.statement:
lemma RunsInSpace.mono {s s' : ℕ} (h : ntm.RunsInSpace input s) (hs : s ≤ s') :
    ntm.RunsInSpace input s'

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.RunsInSpace.exists_space_max
items.doc: A machine running in space `s` has a computation path visiting the most cells.
items.statement:
lemma RunsInSpace.exists_space_max {s : ℕ} (hs : ntm.RunsInSpace input s) :
    ∃ p : ntm.ComputationPath input, ∀ q : ntm.ComputationPath input, q.space ≤ p.space

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.runsInSpace_zero_tapes
items.doc: A machine without work tapes satisfies every space bound.
items.statement:
lemma runsInSpace_zero_tapes (ntm : MultiTapeNTM 0 Symbol State) (input : List Symbol) (s : ℕ) :
    ntm.RunsInSpace input s

modules.title: Head movement along run paths
modules.doc:
This file collects how a step moves the work-tape heads and changes the work tapes, and what this
implies for the cells visited along a run path: a head moves by at most one cell per step, so it
visits every cell between its first and last positions, and a cell changes only under its head.

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.Step.workTapePos_le
items.doc: A work-tape head moves by at most one cell in a single step.
items.statement:
lemma Step.workTapePos_le {c c' : Cfg k Symbol State input} (h : ntm.Step c c') (i : Fin k) :
    |c'.workTapePos i - c.workTapePos i| ≤ 1

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.Step.workTapes_eq_of_ne
items.doc: A step does not change a work-tape cell away from its head.
items.statement:
lemma Step.workTapes_eq_of_ne {c c' : Cfg k Symbol State input} (h : ntm.Step c c') {i : Fin k}
    {z : ℤ} (hz : z ≠ c.workTapePos i) : c'.workTapes i z = c.workTapes i z

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.RunPath.uIcc_workTapePos_subset_visitedByTapeHead
items.doc:
Every position between the first and the last position of a head along a path is visited,
since the head moves by at most one cell per step.
items.statement:
lemma uIcc_workTapePos_subset_visitedByTapeHead (p : ntm.RunPath input) (i : Fin k) :
    Finset.uIcc (p.head.workTapePos i) (p.last.workTapePos i) ⊆ p.visitedByTapeHead i

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.RunPath.mem_visitedByTapeHead_of_workTapes_ne
items.doc:
A work-tape cell that differs between the first and the last configuration of a path was
visited by its head.
items.statement:
lemma mem_visitedByTapeHead_of_workTapes_ne (p : ntm.RunPath input) {i : Fin k} {z : ℤ}
    (h : p.last.workTapes i z ≠ p.head.workTapes i z) : z ∈ p.visitedByTapeHead i

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.RunPath.natAbs_le_spaceUsedByTape_of_mem_visited
items.doc: Every position visited by a head lies within the space of its tape from its first position.

items.name: Turing.MultiTapeNTM.RunPath.inWindow_of_space_le
items.doc:
A path that starts with every head at cell `0` and visits at most `s` cells keeps its heads
within `[-s, s]`.
items.statement:
lemma inWindow_of_space_le {p : ntm.RunPath input} {s : ℕ} (h0 : ∀ i, p.head.workTapePos i = 0)
    (hs : p.space ≤ s) : p.InWindow s

items.name: Cslib.Computability.Turing.SingleTape.TrLabel
items.doc: The transition labels used by a single-tape Turing Machine.
items.statement:
inductive TrLabel (Symbol : Type*)
  /-- Read `x` from the tape. -/
  | read (x : Symbol)
  /-- Write `x` on the tape. -/
  | write (x : Symbol)
  /-- Move the head of the tape. -/
  | move (d : Turing.Dir)
  /-- Do nothing. -/
  | skip

items.name: Cslib.Computability.Turing.SingleTape.TrLabel.applyToTape
items.doc:
Applies a transition label to a tape, returning `none` if it is not possible.
The input is taken as an `Option` to make the function composable.
items.statement:
def TrLabel.applyToTape [DecidableEq Symbol]
    (otape : Option (Turing.BiTape Symbol)) (μ : TrLabel Symbol) :
    Option (Turing.BiTape Symbol)

items.name: Cslib.Computability.Turing.SingleTape.TrLabel.applyToTape_isSome
items.statement:
theorem TrLabel.applyToTape_isSome [DecidableEq Symbol] {μ : TrLabel Symbol}
    {ot : Option (Turing.BiTape Symbol)} (h : (μ.applyToTape ot).isSome) : ot.isSome

items.name: Cslib.Computability.Turing.SingleTape.TrLabel.applyToTape_foldl_isSome
items.statement:
theorem TrLabel.applyToTape_foldl_isSome [DecidableEq Symbol] {μs : List (TrLabel Symbol)}
    {ot : Option (Turing.BiTape Symbol)} (h : (μs.foldl applyToTape ot).isSome) : ot.isSome

modules.authors: Bolton Bailey, Pim Spelier, Daan van Gent
modules.title: Single-Tape Turing Machines
modules.doc:
Defines a single-tape Turing machine for computing functions on `List Symbol`
for finite alphabet `Symbol`.

## Design

Here are some design choices made in this file:

These machines have access to a single bidirectionally-infinite tape (`BiTape`)
which uses symbols from `Option Symbol`.

The transition function of the machine takes a state
and a tape alphabet character under the read-head (i.e. an `Option Symbol`)
and returns a `Stmt` describing the tape action to take,
as well as an optional new state to transition to (where `none` means halt).

We do not make the "halting state" a member of the state type for a few reasons:

* To avoid the need for passing a subtype of "non-halting states" to the transition function.
* To make clear that TMs are not expected to continue on after entering this special state
  (in contrast to, say, a DFA entering/leaving an accepting state).
* To make it simpler to match on halting when modifying a machine.

We also include the possibility for non-movement actions,
for convenience in composition of machines.

## Important Declarations

We define a number of structures related to Turing machine computation:

* `Stmt`: the write and movement operations a TM can do in a single step.
* `SingleTapeTM`: the TM itself.
* `Cfg`: the configuration of a TM, including internal and tape state.
* `TimeComputable f`: a TM for computing `f`, packaged with a bound on runtime.
* `PolyTimeComputable f`: `TimeComputable f` packaged with a polynomial bound on runtime.

We also provide ways of constructing polynomial-runtime TMs

* `PolyTimeComputable.id`: computes the identity function
* `PolyTimeComputable.comp`: computes the composition of polynomial time machines
* `TimeComputable.withMonotoneBound`, `PolyTimeComputable.withMonotoneBound`: replace the time
  bound with a monotone one (its `partialSups`) without changing the machine

## TODOs

- Encoding of types in lists to represent computations on arbitrary types.
- Add `∘` notation for `compComputer`.

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.Stmt
items.doc:
A Turing machine "statement" is just a `Option`al command to move left or right,
and write a symbol (i.e. an `Option Symbol`, where `none` is the blank symbol) on the `BiTape`
items.statement:
structure Stmt (Symbol : Type) where
  /-- The symbol to write at the current head position -/
  symbol : Option Symbol
  /-- The direction to move the tape head -/
  movement : Option Dir
deriving Inhabited

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM
items.doc:
A single-tape Turing machine
over the alphabet of `Option Symbol` (where `none` is the blank `BiTape` symbol).
items.statement:
structure SingleTapeTM Symbol [Inhabited Symbol] [Fintype Symbol] where
  /-- type of state labels -/
  (State : Type)
  /-- finiteness of the state type -/
  [stateFintype : Fintype State]
  /-- Initial state -/
  (q₀ : State)
  /-- Transition function, mapping a state and a head symbol to a `Stmt` to invoke,
  and optionally the new state to transition to afterwards (`none` for halt) -/
  (tr : State → Option Symbol → SingleTapeTM.Stmt Symbol × Option State)

items.note:
## Configurations of a Turing Machine

This section defines the configurations of a Turing machine,
the step function that lets the machine transition from one configuration to the next,
and the intended initial and final configurations.

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.inhabitedStmt
items.statement: instance inhabitedStmt : Inhabited (Stmt Symbol)

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.Cfg
items.doc:
The configurations of a Turing machine consist of:
an `Option`al state (or none for the halting state),
and a `BiTape` representing the tape contents.
items.statement:
structure Cfg : Type where
  /-- the state of the TM (or none for the halting state) -/
  state : Option tm.State
  /-- the BiTape contents -/
  BiTape : BiTape Symbol
deriving Inhabited

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.step
items.doc: The step function corresponding to a `SingleTapeTM`.
items.statement: def step : tm.Cfg → Option tm.Cfg

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.initCfg
items.doc:
The initial configuration corresponding to a list in the input alphabet.
Note that the entries of the tape constructed by `BiTape.mk₁` are all `some` values.
This is to ensure that distinct lists map to distinct initial configurations.
items.statement: def initCfg (tm : SingleTapeTM Symbol) (s : List Symbol) : tm.Cfg

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.haltCfg
items.doc:
The final configuration corresponding to a list in the output alphabet.
(We demand that the head halts at the leftmost position of the output.)
items.statement: def haltCfg (tm : SingleTapeTM Symbol) (s : List Symbol) : tm.Cfg

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.Cfg.spaceUsed
items.doc: The space used by a configuration is the space used by its tape.
items.statement: def Cfg.spaceUsed (tm : SingleTapeTM Symbol) (cfg : tm.Cfg) : ℕ

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.Cfg.spaceUsed_initCfg
items.statement:
lemma Cfg.spaceUsed_initCfg (tm : SingleTapeTM Symbol) (s : List Symbol) :
    (tm.initCfg s).spaceUsed = max 1 s.length

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.Cfg.spaceUsed_haltCfg
items.statement:
lemma Cfg.spaceUsed_haltCfg (tm : SingleTapeTM Symbol) (s : List Symbol) :
    (tm.haltCfg s).spaceUsed = max 1 s.length

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.Cfg.spaceUsed_step
items.statement:
lemma Cfg.spaceUsed_step {tm : SingleTapeTM Symbol} (cfg cfg' : tm.Cfg)
    (hstep : tm.step cfg = some cfg') : cfg'.spaceUsed ≤ cfg.spaceUsed + 1

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.TransitionRelation
items.doc:
The `TransitionRelation` corresponding to a `SingleTapeTM Symbol`
is defined by the `step` function,
which maps a configuration to its next configuration, if it exists.
items.statement: def TransitionRelation (tm : SingleTapeTM Symbol) (c₁ c₂ : tm.Cfg) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.Outputs
items.doc: A proof of `tm` outputting `l'` on input `l`.
items.statement: def Outputs (tm : SingleTapeTM Symbol) (l l' : List Symbol) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.OutputsWithinTime
items.doc: A proof of `tm` outputting `l'` on input `l` in at most `m` steps.
items.statement: def OutputsWithinTime (tm : SingleTapeTM Symbol) (l l' : List Symbol) (m : ℕ)

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.output_length_le_input_length_add_time
items.doc:
This lemma bounds the size blow-up of the output of a Turing machine.
It states that the increase in length of the output over the input is bounded by the runtime.
This is important for guaranteeing that composition of polynomial time Turing machines
remains polynomial time, as the input to the second machine
is bounded by the output length of the first machine.
items.statement:
lemma output_length_le_input_length_add_time (tm : SingleTapeTM Symbol) (l l' : List Symbol) (t : ℕ)
    (h : tm.OutputsWithinTime l l' t) :
    l'.length ≤ max 1 l.length + t

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.idComputer
items.doc: A Turing machine computing the identity.
items.statement: def idComputer : SingleTapeTM Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.compComputer
items.doc:
A Turing machine computing the composition of two other Turing machines.

If f and g are computed by Turing machines `tm1` and `tm2`
then we can construct a Turing machine which computes g ∘ f by first running `tm1`
and then, when `tm1` halts, transitioning to the start state of `tm2` and running `tm2`.
items.statement: def compComputer (tm1 tm2 : SingleTapeTM Symbol) : SingleTapeTM Symbol

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.compComputer_q₀_eq
items.statement: lemma compComputer_q₀_eq : (compComputer tm1 tm2).q₀ = Sum.inl tm1.q₀

items.note:
## Time Computability

This section defines the notion of time-bounded Turing Machines

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.TimeComputable
items.doc:
A Turing machine + a time function +
a proof it outputs `f` in at most `time(input.length)` steps.
items.statement:
structure TimeComputable (f : List Symbol → List Symbol) where
  /-- the underlying bundled SingleTapeTM -/
  tm : SingleTapeTM Symbol
  /-- a bound on runtime -/
  timeBound : ℕ → ℕ
  /-- proof this machine outputs `f` in at most `timeBound(input.length)` steps -/
  outputsFunInTime (a) : tm.OutputsWithinTime a (f a) (timeBound a.length)

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.TimeComputable.id
items.doc: The identity map on Symbol is computable in constant time.
items.statement: def TimeComputable.id : TimeComputable (Symbol := Symbol) id

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.TimeComputable.comp
items.doc:
Time bounds for `compComputer`.

The `compComputer` of two machines which have time bounds is bounded by

* The time taken by the first machine on the input size
* added to the time taken by the second machine on the output size of the first machine
  (which is itself bounded by the time taken by the first machine)

Note that we require the time function of the second machine to be monotone;
this is to ensure that if the first machine returns an output
which is shorter than the maximum possible length of output for that input size,
then the time bound for the second machine still holds for that shorter input to the second machine.
items.statement:
def TimeComputable.comp {f g : List Symbol → List Symbol}
    (hf : TimeComputable f) (hg : TimeComputable g)
    (h_mono : Monotone hg.timeBound) :
    (TimeComputable (g ∘ f))

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.TimeComputable.withMonotoneBound
items.doc:
Convert a `TimeComputable` to one with a monotone time bound, by replacing the time bound `t`
with `partialSups t`, i.e. `n ↦ max (t 0) ⋯ (t n)`. The underlying machine is unchanged.
items.statement:
def TimeComputable.withMonotoneBound {f : List Symbol → List Symbol}
    (hf : TimeComputable f) : TimeComputable f

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.TimeComputable.withMonotoneBound_timeBound_monotone
items.statement:
lemma TimeComputable.withMonotoneBound_timeBound_monotone {f : List Symbol → List Symbol}
    (hf : TimeComputable f) : Monotone hf.withMonotoneBound.timeBound

items.note:
## Polynomial Time Computability

This section defines polynomial time computable functions on Turing machines,
and proves that:

* The identity function is polynomial time computable
* The composition of two polynomial time computable functions is polynomial time computable

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.PolyTimeComputable
items.doc:
A Turing machine + a polynomial time function +
a proof it outputs `f` in at most `time(input.length)` steps.
items.statement:
structure PolyTimeComputable (f : List Symbol → List Symbol) extends TimeComputable f where
  /-- a polynomial time bound -/
  poly : Polynomial ℕ
  /-- proof that this machine outputs `f` in at most `time(input.length)` steps -/
  bounds : ∀ n, timeBound n ≤ poly.eval n

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.PolyTimeComputable.id
items.doc: A proof that the identity map on Symbol is computable in polytime.
items.statement: noncomputable def PolyTimeComputable.id : PolyTimeComputable (Symbol := Symbol) id

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.PolyTimeComputable.withMonotoneBound
items.doc:
Convert a `PolyTimeComputable` to one with a monotone time bound.
The polynomial bound is unchanged, since polynomial evaluation over `ℕ` is monotone.
items.statement:
noncomputable def PolyTimeComputable.withMonotoneBound {f : List Symbol → List Symbol}
    (hf : PolyTimeComputable f) : PolyTimeComputable f

items.name: Cslib.Turing.SingleTapeTM.PolyTimeComputable.comp
items.doc:
A proof that the composition of two polytime computable functions is polytime computable.

The time bound of `hg` is first replaced by a monotone one via `withMonotoneBound`,
so that no monotonicity assumption is required of the caller.

modules.title: Single-Tape Nondeterministic Turing Machines (NTMs)
modules.doc:
Nondeterministic Turing Machines (NTMs), defined as nondeterministic automata (`NA`) that act on a
bidirectional tape (`BiTape`).

## References

* [M. Sipser, *Introduction to Theory of Computation*][Sipser2013]

items.name: Cslib.Computability.Turing.SingleTape.SingleTapeNTM
items.doc:
A (single-tape) Nondeterministic Turing Machine (NTM) is a nondeterministic automaton equipped
with a set of accepting halting states.
items.statement:
structure SingleTapeNTM (State Symbol : Type*)
    extends NA State (TrLabel Symbol) where
  /-- The set of accepting states. -/
  accept : Set State
  /-- Proof that all accepting states are halting states. -/
  accept_halting (hmem : s ∈ accept) : ¬∃ μ s', Tr s μ s'

items.name: Cslib.Computability.Turing.SingleTape.SingleTapeNTM.Yields
items.doc:
An NTM yields a small-step operational semantics on configurations, which codifies an execution
step. This formalises the 'yields' relation from [Sipser2013].
items.statement:
def Yields (m : SingleTapeNTM State Symbol)
    (c c' : Cfg State Symbol) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.Computability.Turing.SingleTape.SingleTapeNTM.yields_tr
items.statement:
theorem yields_tr {m : SingleTapeNTM State Symbol} :
    m.Yields c c' ↔ ∃ μ, m.Tr c.state μ c'.state ∧ μ.applyToTape c.tape = c'.tape

items.name: Cslib.Computability.Turing.SingleTape.SingleTapeNTM.MYields
items.doc:
Multistep execution of an NTM, defined as the reflexive and transitive closure of one-step
execution.
items.statement: def MYields (m : SingleTapeNTM State Symbol)

items.name: Cslib.Computability.Turing.SingleTape.SingleTapeNTM.mYields_mTr
items.doc: Characterisation of executions in terms of multistep transitions.
items.statement:
theorem mYields_mTr {m : SingleTapeNTM State Symbol} :
    m.MYields c c' ↔ ∃ μs, m.MTr c.state μs c'.state ∧
    μs.foldl TrLabel.applyToTape (some c.tape) = c'.tape

items.name: Cslib.Computability.Turing.SingleTape.SingleTapeNTM.AcceptsInSteps
items.doc: The NTM `m` accepts `xs` in `n` execution steps.
items.statement: def AcceptsInSteps (m : SingleTapeNTM State Symbol) (xs : List Symbol) (n : ℕ) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.Computability.Turing.SingleTape.SingleTapeNTM.AcceptsInAtMostSteps
items.doc: The NTM `m` accepts `xs` in at most `n` execution steps.
items.statement: def AcceptsInAtMostSteps (m : SingleTapeNTM State Symbol) (xs : List Symbol) (n : ℕ) : Prop

modules.title: Boolean functions on the hypercube
modules.doc:
A Boolean function is a map `{0,1}ⁿ → {0,1}`, shared across the library as
`Cslib.BooleanFunction` on `Cslib.BitString n`. This file sets up block flips, which are the moves
of sensitivity and block sensitivity, and partial assignments. The complexity measures are built in
`Measures.lean`.

## Main definitions

- `BitString.flipBlock B x`: `x` with every coordinate of `B` flipped.
- `Block n`: a set of coordinates.
- `PartialAssignment n`: a partial assignment, fixing some coordinates and leaving others free.
- `restrict x S`: the partial assignment reading off `x` on the coordinates in `S`.
- `Agrees`: An input is consistent with a partial assignment.

## References

* [S. Arora, B. Barak, *Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach*][AroraBarak09],
  Chapter 12 (Decision Trees); the notions defined here underpin Sections 12.2 and 12.5.1.
* [H. Buhrman, R. de Wolf, *Complexity measures and decision tree complexity:
  a survey*][BuhrmanDeWolf2002]

items.name: Cslib.BitString.flipBlock
items.doc: `x` with every coordinate of `B` flipped.
items.statement: def flipBlock (B : Finset (Fin n)) (x : BitString n) : BitString n

items.name: Cslib.BitString.flipBlock_eq_piecewise
items.doc: Flipping `B` splices the negation of `x` into `x` on `B`.
items.statement:
theorem flipBlock_eq_piecewise (B : Finset (Fin n)) (x : BitString n) :
    flipBlock B x = B.piecewise (fun j => !(x j)) x

items.name: Cslib.BitString.flipBlock_apply_of_mem
items.statement:
theorem flipBlock_apply_of_mem {B : Finset (Fin n)} {x : BitString n} {j : Fin n} (h : j ∈ B) :
    flipBlock B x j = !(x j)

items.name: Cslib.BitString.flipBlock_apply_of_notMem
items.statement:
theorem flipBlock_apply_of_notMem {B : Finset (Fin n)} {x : BitString n} {j : Fin n} (h : j ∉ B) :
    flipBlock B x j = x j

items.name: Cslib.BitString.flipBlock_empty
items.doc: Flipping no coordinates does nothing.
items.statement: theorem flipBlock_empty (x : BitString n) : flipBlock ∅ x = x

items.name: Cslib.BitString.flipBlock_flipBlock
items.doc: Flipping the same block twice does nothing.
items.statement:
theorem flipBlock_flipBlock (B : Finset (Fin n)) (x : BitString n) :
    flipBlock B (flipBlock B x) = x

items.name: Cslib.BitString.flipBlock_involutive
items.doc: Flipping a block is an involution.
items.statement: theorem flipBlock_involutive (B : Finset (Fin n)) : Function.Involutive (flipBlock B)

items.name: Cslib.BitString.flipBlock_singleton
items.doc: Flipping the block `{i}` is flipping the single bit `i`.
items.statement:
theorem flipBlock_singleton (i : Fin n) (x : BitString n) :
    flipBlock {i} x = Function.update x i (!x i)

items.name: Cslib.BitString.flipBlock_erase
items.doc: Flipping `B \ {i}` is flipping `B` and then restoring bit `i ∈ B`.
items.statement:
theorem flipBlock_erase {B : Finset (Fin n)} {i : Fin n} (hi : i ∈ B) (x : BitString n) :
    flipBlock (B.erase i) x = Function.update (flipBlock B x) i (x i)

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.Block
items.doc: A block: a set of coordinates.
items.statement: abbrev Block (n : ℕ) : Type

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.PartialAssignment
items.doc: `C i = some b` fixes coordinate `i` to `b`; `C i = none` leaves it free.
items.statement: abbrev PartialAssignment (n : ℕ) : Type

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.support
items.doc: The coordinates the partial assignment fixes.
items.statement: def support (C : PartialAssignment n) : Finset (Fin n)

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.mem_support
items.doc: A coordinate lies in the support if and only if the partial assignment fixes it.
items.statement:
lemma mem_support {C : PartialAssignment n} {i : Fin n} :
    i ∈ support C ↔ (C i).isSome

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.size
items.doc: How many coordinates the partial assignment fixes.
items.statement: def size (C : PartialAssignment n) : ℕ

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.Agrees
items.doc: `x` agrees with `C` when it matches `C` on every fixed coordinate.
items.statement: def Agrees (C : PartialAssignment n) (x : BitString n) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.ofBitString
items.doc: The total assignment reading off every coordinate of `x`.
items.statement: def ofBitString (x : BitString n) : PartialAssignment n

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.agrees_ofBitString_iff
items.doc: A total assignment read off `x` is agreed with by `x` alone.
items.statement: theorem agrees_ofBitString_iff {x y : BitString n} : Agrees (ofBitString x) y ↔ y = x

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.size_ofBitString
items.doc: Reading off the whole input fixes all `n` coordinates.
items.statement: theorem size_ofBitString (x : BitString n) : size (ofBitString x) = n

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.restrict
items.doc: The partial assignment reading off `x` on the coordinates only in `S`.
items.statement: def restrict (x : BitString n) (S : Finset (Fin n)) : PartialAssignment n

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.agrees_restrict_iff
items.doc: An input agrees with `restrict x S` if and only if it matches `x` on `S`.
items.statement:
theorem agrees_restrict_iff {x y : BitString n} {S : Finset (Fin n)} :
    Agrees (restrict x S) y ↔ ∀ i ∈ S, y i = x i

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.support_restrict
items.doc: `restrict x S` fixes exactly the coordinates in `S`.
items.statement: theorem support_restrict (x : BitString n) (S : Finset (Fin n)) : support (restrict x S) = S

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.eq_restrict_support
items.doc: A partial assignment consistent with `x` is `x` restricted to its support.
items.statement:
theorem eq_restrict_support {C : PartialAssignment n} {x : BitString n} (h : Agrees C x) :
    C = restrict x (support C)

modules.title: Boolean function complexity measures
modules.doc:
Sensitivity `s(f)`, block sensitivity `bs(f)` and certificate complexity `C(f)`, together with
the chain `s(f) ≤ bs(f) ≤ C(f)`. Notation follows [AroraBarak09]; the pointwise measures
`s(f, x)`, `bs(f, x)`, `C(f, x)` are those of [Jukna, Section 14.3][Jukna2012].

## Main definitions

- `BitString.sensitivity`: `s(f)`, the maximum over inputs of the number of sensitive coordinates.
- `blockSensitivity`: `bs(f)`, the maximum over inputs of the maximum number of disjoint sensitive
  blocks.
- `IsCertificate`: a set of coordinates whose values at `x` pin down `f x`, as in
  [Jukna, Section 14.3][Jukna2012].
- `Forces`: a partial assignment forces the value `b`, as in [BuhrmanDeWolf2002]. At a fixed input
  an assignment consistent with `x` is determined by its support, so the pointwise measure needs no
  bit values.
- `certificateComplexity`: `C(f)`, the maximum over inputs of the smallest certificate size.

## Main results

- `sensitivity_le_blockSensitivity`: `s(f) ≤ bs(f)`.
- `blockSensitivity_le_certificateComplexity`: `bs(f) ≤ C(f)`.
- `isCertificate_iff_forces_restrict`, `forces_iff_isCertificate_support`: `IsCertificate` and
  `Forces` agree at a fixed input.
- `certificateComplexityAt_eq_inf'_size`: `C(f, x)` is the minimum size of a forcing assignment
  consistent with `x`.
- `|B| ≤ s(f)` for a minimal sensitive block `B`.

## References

* [S. Arora, B. Barak, *Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach*][AroraBarak09],
  Section 12.2 (Certificate Complexity) and Section 12.5.1 (Sensitivity).
* [H. Buhrman, R. de Wolf, *Complexity measures and decision tree complexity:
  a survey*][BuhrmanDeWolf2002]
* [S. Jukna, *Boolean Function Complexity: Advances and Frontiers*][Jukna2012], Section 14.3.

items.name: Cslib.BitString.IsSensitiveCoord
items.doc: Coordinate `i` is sensitive for `f` at `x` when flipping it flips `f`.
items.statement: def IsSensitiveCoord (f : BooleanFunction n) (x : BitString n) (i : Fin n) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.BitString.sensitiveCoords
items.doc: The set of coordinates sensitive for `f` at `x`.
items.statement: def sensitiveCoords (f : BooleanFunction n) (x : BitString n) : Finset (Fin n)

items.name: Cslib.BitString.mem_sensitiveCoords
items.doc: The bridge between the predicate and the `Finset` it cuts out.
items.statement:
lemma mem_sensitiveCoords {f : BooleanFunction n} {x : BitString n} {i : Fin n} :
    i ∈ sensitiveCoords f x ↔ IsSensitiveCoord f x i

items.name: Cslib.BitString.sensitivityAt
items.doc: The number of sensitive coordinates in input `x`, usually denoted `s(f, x)`.
items.statement: def sensitivityAt (f : BooleanFunction n) (x : BitString n) : ℕ

items.name: Cslib.BitString.sensitivity
items.doc: The maximum sensitivity over all inputs, denoted `s(f)`.
items.statement: def sensitivity (f : BooleanFunction n) : ℕ

items.name: Cslib.BitString.card_le_sensitivityAt
items.doc: Lower-bound rule for `s(f, x)`: exhibit a set of sensitive coordinates.
items.statement:
lemma card_le_sensitivityAt {f : BooleanFunction n} {x : BitString n} {S : Finset (Fin n)}
    (h : ∀ i ∈ S, IsSensitiveCoord f x i) : S.card ≤ sensitivityAt f x

items.name: Cslib.BitString.sensitivityAt_le_sensitivity
items.doc: The sensitivity at a single input is at most the sensitivity of `f`: `s(f, x) ≤ s(f)`.
items.statement:
lemma sensitivityAt_le_sensitivity (f : BooleanFunction n) (x : BitString n) :
    sensitivityAt f x ≤ sensitivity f

items.name: Cslib.BitString.card_le_sensitivity_of_forall_isSensitiveCoord
items.doc: Lower-bound rule for `s(f)`: sensitive coordinates at any input suffice.
items.statement:
lemma card_le_sensitivity_of_forall_isSensitiveCoord {f : BooleanFunction n} {x : BitString n}
    {S : Finset (Fin n)} (h : ∀ i ∈ S, IsSensitiveCoord f x i) : S.card ≤ sensitivity f

items.name: Cslib.BitString.sensitivityAt_le_card
items.doc: `s(f, x) ≤ n`: there are only `n` coordinates.
items.statement: theorem sensitivityAt_le_card (f : BooleanFunction n) (x : BitString n) : sensitivityAt f x ≤ n

items.name: Cslib.BitString.sensitivity_le_card
items.statement: theorem sensitivity_le_card (f : BooleanFunction n) : sensitivity f ≤ n

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.IsSensitiveBlock
items.doc: Block `B` is sensitive for `f` at `x` when flipping all bits of `B` flips `f`.
items.statement: def IsSensitiveBlock (f : BooleanFunction n) (x : BitString n) (B : Block n) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.IsSensitiveFamily
items.doc: Every member flips `f`, and the members are pairwise disjoint.
items.statement: def IsSensitiveFamily (f : BooleanFunction n) (x : BitString n) (F : Finset (Block n)) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.sensitiveFamilies
items.doc: All sensitive families.
items.statement: def sensitiveFamilies (f : BooleanFunction n) (x : BitString n) : Finset (Finset (Block n))

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.mem_sensitiveFamilies
items.statement:
lemma mem_sensitiveFamilies {f : BooleanFunction n} {x : BitString n} {F : Finset (Block n)} :
    F ∈ sensitiveFamilies f x ↔ IsSensitiveFamily f x F

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.blockSensitivityAt
items.doc:
The block sensitivity of `f` at `x`: the largest number of pairwise disjoint blocks of
coordinates such that flipping every coordinate of any one block flips `f`. Usually denoted
`bs(f, x)`.
items.statement: def blockSensitivityAt (f : BooleanFunction n) (x : BitString n) : ℕ

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.blockSensitivity
items.doc: The maximum block sensitivity over all inputs, denoted `bs(f)`.
items.statement: def blockSensitivity (f : BooleanFunction n) : ℕ

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.card_le_blockSensitivityAt
items.doc: Lower-bound rule for `bs(f, x)`: exhibit one sensitive family.
items.statement:
lemma card_le_blockSensitivityAt {f : BooleanFunction n} {x : BitString n} {F : Finset (Block n)}
    (h : IsSensitiveFamily f x F) : F.card ≤ blockSensitivityAt f x

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.blockSensitivityAt_le_blockSensitivity
items.doc: The block sensitivity at a single input is at most that of `f`: `bs(f, x) ≤ bs(f)`.
items.statement:
lemma blockSensitivityAt_le_blockSensitivity (f : BooleanFunction n) (x : BitString n) :
    blockSensitivityAt f x ≤ blockSensitivity f

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.card_le_blockSensitivity
items.doc: Lower-bound rule for `bs(f)`.
items.statement:
lemma card_le_blockSensitivity {f : BooleanFunction n} {x : BitString n} {F : Finset (Block n)}
    (h : IsSensitiveFamily f x F) : F.card ≤ blockSensitivity f

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.isSensitiveBlock_singleton
items.doc: A singleton block is sensitive if and only if its coordinate is.
items.statement:
lemma isSensitiveBlock_singleton {f : BooleanFunction n} {x : BitString n} {i : Fin n} :
    IsSensitiveBlock f x {i} ↔ IsSensitiveCoord f x i

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.singletonFamily
items.doc: One block per sensitive coordinate.
items.statement: def singletonFamily (f : BooleanFunction n) (x : BitString n) : Finset (Block n)

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.mem_singletonFamily
items.doc: Membership in the singleton family: one block per sensitive coordinate.
items.statement:
lemma mem_singletonFamily {f : BooleanFunction n} {x : BitString n} {B : Block n} :
    B ∈ singletonFamily f x ↔ ∃ i, IsSensitiveCoord f x i ∧ {i} = B

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.card_singletonFamily
items.doc: The singleton family has one block per sensitive coordinate, so `s(f, x)` of them.
items.statement:
lemma card_singletonFamily {f : BooleanFunction n} {x : BitString n} :
    (singletonFamily f x).card = sensitivityAt f x

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.isSensitiveFamily_singletonFamily
items.doc:
Singletons of distinct sensitive coordinates do form a sensitive family: each
flips `f`, and distinct singletons are disjoint.
items.statement:
lemma isSensitiveFamily_singletonFamily {f : BooleanFunction n} {x : BitString n} :
    IsSensitiveFamily f x (singletonFamily f x)

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.sensitivityAt_le_blockSensitivityAt
items.doc: Pointwise: `s(f, x) ≤ bs(f, x)`.
items.statement:
theorem sensitivityAt_le_blockSensitivityAt (f : BooleanFunction n) (x : BitString n) :
    sensitivityAt f x ≤ blockSensitivityAt f x

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.sensitivity_le_blockSensitivity
items.doc: Every sensitive coordinate is a sensitive block of size one, so `s(f) ≤ bs(f)`.
items.statement:
theorem sensitivity_le_blockSensitivity (f : BooleanFunction n) :
    sensitivity f ≤ blockSensitivity f

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.IsMinimalSensitiveBlock
items.doc: `B` is sensitive, and no proper subset of `B` is sensitive.
items.statement: def IsMinimalSensitiveBlock (f : BooleanFunction n) (x : BitString n) (B : Block n) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.IsMinimalSensitiveBlock.not_isSensitiveBlock_erase
items.doc: Dropping any coordinate from a minimal sensitive block breaks sensitivity.
items.statement:
lemma not_isSensitiveBlock_erase (hB : IsMinimalSensitiveBlock f x B) (hi : i ∈ B) :
    ¬ IsSensitiveBlock f x (B.erase i)

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.IsMinimalSensitiveBlock.isSensitiveCoord_flipBlock
items.doc:
Every coordinate of a minimal sensitive block is sensitive at the input which
has the minimal sensitive block flipped.
items.statement:
lemma isSensitiveCoord_flipBlock (hB : IsMinimalSensitiveBlock f x B) (hi : i ∈ B) :
    IsSensitiveCoord f (flipBlock B x) i

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.IsMinimalSensitiveBlock.card_le_sensitivity
items.doc: `|B| ≤ s(f)` for a minimal sensitive block `B`.
items.statement: theorem card_le_sensitivity (hB : IsMinimalSensitiveBlock f x B) : B.card ≤ sensitivity f

items.note:
## Certificates

A certificate for `x` is a set of coordinates whose values at `x` already determine `f x`
[Jukna, Section 14.3][Jukna2012]. The survey [BuhrmanDeWolf2002] instead works with partial
assignments that force a value; `Forces` keeps that in general form, with the forced value `b` a
parameter, and the two views agree at a fixed input.

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.IsCertificate
items.doc:
`S` is a certificate for `f` at `x`: every input agreeing with `x` on `S` takes the same
value, so `f x` can be read off from the bits of `x` in `S`.
items.statement: def IsCertificate (f : BooleanFunction n) (x : BitString n) (S : Finset (Fin n)) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.Forces
items.doc: `C` forces the value `b`: everything consistent with `C` has `f = b`.
items.statement: def Forces (f : BooleanFunction n) (C : PartialAssignment n) (b : Bool) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.isCertificate_iff_forces_restrict
items.doc: `S` is a certificate for `x` if and only if `x` restricted to `S` forces `f x`.
items.statement:
theorem isCertificate_iff_forces_restrict {f : BooleanFunction n} {x : BitString n}
    {S : Finset (Fin n)} : IsCertificate f x S ↔ Forces f (restrict x S) (f x)

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.forces_iff_isCertificate_support
items.doc:
A partial assignment consistent with `x` forces `f x` if and only if its support is a
certificate for `x`.

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.isCertificate_univ
items.doc: Reading every coordinate of `x` is a certificate.
items.statement:
lemma isCertificate_univ (f : BooleanFunction n) (x : BitString n) :
    IsCertificate f x Finset.univ

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.filter_isCertificate_nonempty
items.doc: There is always a certificate, so `C(f, x)` is a minimum over a non-empty set.
items.statement:
lemma filter_isCertificate_nonempty (f : BooleanFunction n) (x : BitString n) :
    (Finset.univ.filter (IsCertificate f x)).Nonempty

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.certificateComplexityAt
items.doc: The fewest coordinates of `x` that pin down the value of `f`, denoted `C(f, x)`.
items.statement: def certificateComplexityAt (f : BooleanFunction n) (x : BitString n) : ℕ

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.certificateComplexityAt_le
items.doc: Upper-bound rule for `C(f, x)`: exhibit one certificate.
items.statement:
lemma certificateComplexityAt_le {f : BooleanFunction n} {x : BitString n} {S : Finset (Fin n)}
    (h : IsCertificate f x S) : certificateComplexityAt f x ≤ S.card

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.le_certificateComplexityAt
items.doc: Lower-bound rule for `C(f, x)`: a bound that holds for every certificate.
items.statement:
lemma le_certificateComplexityAt {f : BooleanFunction n} {x : BitString n} {k : ℕ}
    (h : ∀ S, IsCertificate f x S → k ≤ S.card) : k ≤ certificateComplexityAt f x

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.exists_isCertificate_card_eq
items.doc: Some certificate for `x` has exactly `C(f, x)` coordinates.
items.statement:
theorem exists_isCertificate_card_eq (f : BooleanFunction n) (x : BitString n) :
    ∃ S, IsCertificate f x S ∧ S.card = certificateComplexityAt f x

items.note:
## Certificates as partial assignments

At a fixed input a forcing assignment carries no information beyond the coordinates it reads:
`Agrees C x` forces `C i = some (x i)` on the support and `none` elsewhere. So `C(f, x)` over
coordinate sets is also the minimum size of a forcing assignment consistent with `x`.

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.forcingAssignments
items.doc: Partial assignments consistent with `x` that force `f x`.
items.statement:
def forcingAssignments (f : BooleanFunction n) (x : BitString n) :
    Finset (PartialAssignment n)

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.mem_forcingAssignments
Cslib.QueryComplexity.ofBitString_mem_forcingAssignments
items.doc: Reading off all of `x` forces `f x`.
items.statement:
lemma ofBitString_mem_forcingAssignments (f : BooleanFunction n) (x : BitString n) :
    ofBitString x ∈ forcingAssignments f x

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.forcingAssignments_nonempty
items.doc: There is always a forcing assignment consistent with `x`.
items.statement:
lemma forcingAssignments_nonempty (f : BooleanFunction n) (x : BitString n) :
    (forcingAssignments f x).Nonempty

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.certificateComplexityAt_eq_inf'_size
items.doc:
`C(f, x)` over coordinate sets is the minimum size of a forcing assignment consistent with
`x`, the definition of [BuhrmanDeWolf2002].
items.statement:
theorem certificateComplexityAt_eq_inf'_size (f : BooleanFunction n) (x : BitString n) :
    certificateComplexityAt f x =
      (forcingAssignments f x).inf' (forcingAssignments_nonempty f x) size

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.certificateComplexity
items.doc: The maximum over all inputs of the smallest certificate size, denoted `C(f)`.
items.statement: def certificateComplexity (f : BooleanFunction n) : ℕ

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.certificateComplexityAt_le_certificateComplexity
items.doc: The certificate complexity at a single input is at most that of `f`: `C(f, x) ≤ C(f)`.
items.statement:
lemma certificateComplexityAt_le_certificateComplexity (f : BooleanFunction n)
    (x : BitString n) : certificateComplexityAt f x ≤ certificateComplexity f

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.certificateComplexityAt_le_card
items.doc: `C(f, x) ≤ n`: reading every coordinate pins down `f`.
items.statement:
theorem certificateComplexityAt_le_card (f : BooleanFunction n) (x : BitString n) :
    certificateComplexityAt f x ≤ n

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.certificateComplexity_le_card
items.statement: theorem certificateComplexity_le_card (f : BooleanFunction n) : certificateComplexity f ≤ n

items.note:
## `bs(f) ≤ C(f)`

A certificate for `x` must meet every block of a sensitive family. The blocks are pairwise
disjoint, so a family has at most `|S|` members.

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.sensitiveBlock_inter_nonempty
items.doc: A certificate must contain at least one coordinate of every sensitive block.

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.card_le_card_of_isSensitiveFamily
items.doc: A certificate is at least as large as any sensitive family.

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.blockSensitivityAt_le_certificateComplexityAt
items.doc: Pointwise: `bs(f, x) ≤ C(f, x)`.
items.statement:
theorem blockSensitivityAt_le_certificateComplexityAt (f : BooleanFunction n)
    (x : BitString n) : blockSensitivityAt f x ≤ certificateComplexityAt f x

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.blockSensitivity_le_certificateComplexity
items.doc: Every block of a sensitive family meets every certificate, so `bs(f) ≤ C(f)`.
items.statement:
theorem blockSensitivity_le_certificateComplexity (f : BooleanFunction n) :
    blockSensitivity f ≤ certificateComplexity f

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.blockSensitivityAt_le_card
items.doc: `bs(f, x) ≤ n`.
items.statement:
theorem blockSensitivityAt_le_card (f : BooleanFunction n) (x : BitString n) :
    blockSensitivityAt f x ≤ n

items.name: Cslib.QueryComplexity.blockSensitivity_le_card
items.doc: `bs(f) ≤ n`.
items.statement: theorem blockSensitivity_le_card (f : BooleanFunction n) : blockSensitivity f ≤ n

modules.title: URM Basic Lemmas
modules.doc:
This file contains basic lemmas and helper operations for URM types.

## Main definitions

- `Instr.IsJump`: predicate for jump instructions
- `Instr.JumpsBoundedBy`: checks if jump targets are bounded
- `Instr.capJump`: caps jump targets to a given length

## Main results

- `Regs.write_read_self`, `Regs.write_read_of_ne`: register read/write lemmas
- `State.isHalted_iff`, `State.ext`: state lemmas
- `JumpsBoundedBy.mono`: bounded jumps are monotonic in the bound
- `JumpsBoundedBy.shiftJumps`: shifting preserves bounded jumps
- `Program.mem_maxRegister`: instruction maxRegister bounded by program maxRegister

items.name: Cslib.URM.Regs.write_read_self
items.statement: theorem write_read_self (σ : Regs) (n v : ℕ) : (σ.write n v).read n = v

items.name: Cslib.URM.Regs.write_read_of_ne
items.statement:
theorem write_read_of_ne (σ : Regs) (m n v : ℕ) (h : m ≠ n) :
    (σ.write n v).read m = σ.read m

items.name: Cslib.URM.State.isHalted_iff
items.statement: theorem isHalted_iff (s : State) (p : Program) : s.isHalted p ↔ p.length ≤ s.pc

items.name: Cslib.URM.State.ext
items.doc: Extensionality for State: two states are equal iff their components are equal.
items.statement: theorem ext {s₁ s₂ : State} (hpc : s₁.pc = s₂.pc) (hregs : s₁.regs = s₂.regs) : s₁ = s₂

items.name: Cslib.URM.Instr.IsJump
items.doc: An instruction is a jump instruction.
items.statement: def IsJump : Instr → Prop

items.name: Cslib.URM.Instr.Z_nonJump
items.doc: Z instruction is not a jump.
items.statement: theorem Z_nonJump (n : ℕ) : ¬(Z n).IsJump

items.name: Cslib.URM.Instr.S_nonJump
items.doc: S instruction is not a jump.
items.statement: theorem S_nonJump (n : ℕ) : ¬(S n).IsJump

items.name: Cslib.URM.Instr.T_nonJump
items.doc: T instruction is not a jump.
items.statement: theorem T_nonJump (m n : ℕ) : ¬(T m n).IsJump

items.name: Cslib.URM.Instr.J_IsJump
items.doc: J instruction is a jump.
items.statement: theorem J_IsJump (m n q : ℕ) : (J m n q).IsJump

items.name: Cslib.URM.Instr.shiftJumps_of_nonJump
items.doc: shiftJumps is identity for non-jumping instructions.
items.statement:
theorem shiftJumps_of_nonJump {instr : Instr}
    (h : ¬instr.IsJump) (offset : ℕ) : instr.shiftJumps offset = instr

items.name: Cslib.URM.Instr.JumpsBoundedBy
items.doc:
An instruction's jump target is bounded by a given length.
Non-jump instructions trivially satisfy this.
items.statement: def JumpsBoundedBy (len : ℕ) : Instr → Prop

items.name: Cslib.URM.Instr.jumpsBoundedBy_of_nonJump
items.doc: Non-jumping instructions have bounded jumps for any length.
items.statement:
theorem jumpsBoundedBy_of_nonJump {instr : Instr} (h : ¬instr.IsJump)
    (len : ℕ) : instr.JumpsBoundedBy len

items.name: Cslib.URM.Instr.JumpsBoundedBy.mono
items.doc: JumpsBoundedBy is monotonic: if bounded for len1, then bounded for any len2 ≥ len1.

items.name: Cslib.URM.Instr.JumpsBoundedBy.shiftJumps
items.doc: shiftJumps preserves bounded jumps with adjusted bound.

items.name: Cslib.URM.Instr.capJump
items.doc: Cap a jump target to be at most `len`. Non-jump instructions are unchanged.
items.statement: def capJump (len : ℕ) : Instr → Instr

items.name: Cslib.URM.Instr.capJump_Z
items.statement: theorem capJump_Z (len n : ℕ) : (Z n).capJump len = Z n

items.name: Cslib.URM.Instr.capJump_S
items.statement: theorem capJump_S (len n : ℕ) : (S n).capJump len = S n

items.name: Cslib.URM.Instr.capJump_T
items.statement: theorem capJump_T (len m n : ℕ) : (T m n).capJump len = T m n

items.name: Cslib.URM.Instr.capJump_J
items.statement:
theorem capJump_J (len m n q : ℕ) :
    (J m n q).capJump len = J m n (min q len)

items.name: Cslib.URM.Instr.JumpsBoundedBy.capJump
items.doc: capJump always produces an instruction with bounded jump.
items.statement:
theorem JumpsBoundedBy.capJump (len : ℕ) (instr : Instr) :
    (instr.capJump len).JumpsBoundedBy len

items.name: Cslib.URM.Instr.capJump_idempotent
items.doc: capJump is idempotent: capping twice is the same as capping once.
items.statement:
theorem capJump_idempotent (len : ℕ) (instr : Instr) :
    (instr.capJump len).capJump len = instr.capJump len

items.name: Cslib.URM.Program.mem_maxRegister
items.doc: Any instruction in a program has maxRegister at most the program's maxRegister.
items.statement:
theorem mem_maxRegister {p : Program} {instr : Instr} (h : instr ∈ p) :
    instr.maxRegister ≤ p.maxRegister

modules.title: URM-Computable Functions
modules.doc:
This file defines the notion of URM-computability for partial functions on natural numbers.

## Main definitions

- `URM.Computes`: A program computes a given partial function.
- `URM.Computable`: A partial function is URM-computable if there exists a URM program that
  computes it.

## Implementation notes

Inputs are provided in registers 0, 1, ..., n-1 and output is read from register 0.

items.name: Cslib.URM.Computes
items.doc:
A program `p` computes a partial function `f : (Fin n → ℕ) → Part ℕ` if for any input,
`eval p inputs = f inputs` as partial values. This captures both:
- The program halts iff the function is defined on that input
- When both are defined, the program's output equals the function's value

Note: Inputs are provided in registers 0, 1, ..., n-1 and output is read from register 0.
items.statement: def Computes (n : ℕ) (p : Program) (f : (Fin n → ℕ) → Part ℕ) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.URM.Computable
items.doc:
A partial function `f : (Fin n → ℕ) → Part ℕ` is URM-computable if there exists a URM program
that computes it.
items.statement: def Computable (n : ℕ) (f : (Fin n → ℕ) → Part ℕ) : Prop

modules.title: URM Core Definitions
modules.doc:
This file contains the core definitions for Unlimited Register Machines (URMs):
instructions, register state, programs, and machine configurations.

## Main definitions

- `URM.Instr`: The four URM instructions (Z, S, T, J)
- `URM.Regs`: Register contents as a function `ℕ → ℕ`
- `URM.Program`: A finite sequence of instructions
- `URM.State`: Machine state (program counter + registers)

## References

* [N.J. Cutland, *Computability: An Introduction to Recursive Function Theory*][Cutland1980]
* [J.C. Shepherdson and H.E. Sturgis,
  *Computability of Recursive Functions*][ShepherdsonSturgis1963]

items.name: Cslib.URM.Instr
items.doc:
URM instructions.
- `Z n`: Set register n to zero
- `S n`: Increment register n by one
- `T m n`: Transfer (copy) the contents of register m to register n
- `J m n q`: If registers m and n have equal contents, jump to instruction q;
             otherwise proceed to the next instruction
items.statement:
inductive Instr : Type where
  | Z : ℕ → Instr
  | S : ℕ → Instr
  | T : ℕ → ℕ → Instr
  | J : ℕ → ℕ → ℕ → Instr
deriving DecidableEq, Repr

items.name: Cslib.URM.Instr.readsFrom
items.doc: The registers read by an instruction.
items.statement: def readsFrom : Instr → Finset ℕ

items.name: Cslib.URM.Instr.writesTo
items.doc: The register written to by an instruction, if any.
items.statement: def writesTo : Instr → Option ℕ

items.name: Cslib.URM.Instr.maxRegister
items.doc: The maximum register index referenced by an instruction.
items.statement: def maxRegister : Instr → ℕ

items.name: Cslib.URM.Instr.shiftJumps
items.doc:
Shift all jump targets in an instruction by `offset`.
Used when concatenating programs to maintain correct jump destinations.
items.statement: def shiftJumps (offset : ℕ) : Instr → Instr

items.name: Cslib.URM.Instr.shiftRegisters
items.doc:
Shift all register references in an instruction by `offset`.
Used to isolate register usage when composing programs.
items.statement: def shiftRegisters (offset : ℕ) : Instr → Instr

items.name: Cslib.URM.Regs
items.doc:
Register contents: maps register indices to natural number contents.

Uses the functional representation `ℕ → ℕ` for efficiency with rewrites,
following the advice from the `grind` tactic documentation.
items.statement: abbrev Regs

items.name: Cslib.URM.Regs.zero
items.doc: The zero registers where all registers contain 0.
items.statement: def zero : Regs

items.name: Cslib.URM.Regs.read
items.doc: Read the contents of register n.
items.statement: def read (σ : Regs) (n : ℕ) : ℕ

items.name: Cslib.URM.Regs.write
items.doc: Write value v to register n.
items.statement: def write (σ : Regs) (n : ℕ) (v : ℕ) : Regs

items.name: Cslib.URM.Regs.ofInputs
items.doc:
Initialize registers with input values in registers 0, 1, ..., k-1.
Registers beyond the inputs are initialized to 0.
items.statement: def ofInputs (inputs : List ℕ) : Regs

items.name: Cslib.URM.Regs.output
items.doc: Extract output from register 0.
items.statement: def output (σ : Regs) : ℕ

items.name: Cslib.URM.Program
items.doc: A URM program is a list of instructions.
items.statement: abbrev Program

items.name: Cslib.URM.Program.maxRegister
items.doc: The maximum register index referenced by any instruction in the program.
items.statement: def maxRegister (p : Program) : ℕ

items.name: Cslib.URM.Program.shiftJumps
items.doc:
Shift all jump targets in a program by `offset`.
Used when concatenating programs: the second program's jumps must be adjusted
by the length of the first program.
items.statement: def shiftJumps (p : Program) (offset : ℕ) : Program

items.name: Cslib.URM.Program.shiftRegisters
items.doc:
Shift all register references in a program by `offset`.
Used to isolate register usage when composing programs.
items.statement: def shiftRegisters (p : Program) (offset : ℕ) : Program

items.name: Cslib.URM.State
items.doc: Machine state: program counter (0-indexed) and register contents.
items.statement:
structure State where
  /-- Program counter (0-indexed). -/
  pc : ℕ
  /-- Register contents. -/
  regs : Regs

items.name: Cslib.URM.State.init
items.doc:
Initial state for a program with given inputs.
The program counter starts at 0, and inputs are loaded into registers 0, 1, ....
items.statement: def init (inputs : List ℕ) : State

items.name: Cslib.URM.State.isHalted
items.doc: A state is halted if the program counter is at or beyond the program length.
items.statement: def isHalted (s : State) (p : Program) : Prop

modules.title: URM Execution Semantics
modules.doc:
Single-step and multi-step execution semantics for URMs.

## Main definitions

- `URM.Step`: Single-step execution relation
- `URM.Steps`: Multi-step execution (reflexive-transitive closure of `Step`)
- `URM.Halts`: A program halts on given inputs
- `URM.Diverges`: A program diverges on given inputs
- `URM.HaltsWithResult`: A program halts on given inputs with a specific result

Bridge lemmas:
- `isHalted_iff_normal`: `s.isHalted p ↔ Relation.Normal (Step p) s`
- `halts_iff_normalizable`: `Halts p inputs ↔ Relation.Normalizable (Step p) (State.init inputs)`
- `step_confluent`: The step relation is confluent (follows from determinism)

## Notation (scoped to `URM` namespace)

Standard computability theory notation:
- `p ↓ inputs` — program `p` halts on inputs
- `p ↑ inputs` — program `p` diverges on inputs
- `p ↓ inputs ≫ result` — program `p` halts on inputs with result in R[0]

## Main results

- `Step.deterministic`: The step relation is deterministic
- `step_confluent`: The step relation is confluent (from determinism)
- `haltsWithResult_iff_eval`: `p ↓ inputs ≫ result ↔ eval p inputs = Part.some result`

items.name: Cslib.URM.Step
items.doc:
Single-step execution relation for URMs.

Each constructor corresponds to one of the four instruction types:
- `zero`: Execute `Z n` (set register n to 0)
- `succ`: Execute `S n` (increment register n)
- `transfer`: Execute `T m n` (copy register m to register n)
- `jump_eq`: Execute `J m n q` when registers m and n are equal (jump to q)
- `jump_ne`: Execute `J m n q` when registers m and n differ (proceed to next)
items.statement:
inductive Step : State → State → Prop where
  | zero {s : State} {n : ℕ}
      (h : p[s.pc]? = some (Instr.Z n)) :
      Step s ⟨s.pc + 1, s.regs.write n 0⟩
  | succ {s : State} {n : ℕ}
      (h : p[s.pc]? = some (Instr.S n)) :
      Step s ⟨s.pc + 1, s.regs.write n (s.regs.read n + 1)⟩
  | transfer {s : State} {m n : ℕ}
      (h : p[s.pc]? = some (Instr.T m n)) :
      Step s ⟨s.pc + 1, s.regs.write n (s.regs.read m)⟩
  | jump_eq {s : State} {m n q : ℕ}
      (h : p[s.pc]? = some (Instr.J m n q))
      (heq : s.regs.read m = s.regs.read n) :
      Step s ⟨q, s.regs⟩
  | jump_ne {s : State} {m n q : ℕ}
      (h : p[s.pc]? = some (Instr.J m n q))
      (hne : s.regs.read m ≠ s.regs.read n) :
      Step s ⟨s.pc + 1, s.regs⟩

items.name: Cslib.URM.Steps
items.doc: Multi-step execution: the reflexive-transitive closure of `Step`.
items.statement: abbrev Steps : State → State → Prop

items.name: Cslib.URM.Step.deterministic
items.doc: The step relation is deterministic: each state has at most one successor.
items.statement: theorem deterministic : Relator.RightUnique (Step p)

items.name: Cslib.URM.Step.no_step_of_halted
items.doc: A halted state has no successor in the step relation.
items.statement: theorem no_step_of_halted {s s' : State} (hhalted : s.isHalted p) : ¬Step p s s'

items.name: Cslib.URM.Step.preserves_register
items.doc:
A single step preserves registers not written to by the current instruction.

This is a fundamental property of URM execution: each instruction modifies at most
one register (Z, S, T write to one register; J writes to none).
items.statement:
theorem preserves_register {s s' : State} {r : ℕ}
    (hstep : Step p s s')
    (hr : ∀ instr, p[s.pc]? = some instr → instr.writesTo ≠ some r) :
    s'.regs.read r = s.regs.read r

items.name: Cslib.URM.isHalted_iff_normal
items.doc: A state is halted iff it is normal (has no successor) in the reduction system.
items.statement:
theorem isHalted_iff_normal {p : Program} {s : State} :
    s.isHalted p ↔ Relation.Normal (Step p) s

items.name: Cslib.URM.step_confluent
items.doc: The step relation is confluent.
items.statement: theorem step_confluent (p : Program) : Relation.Confluent (Step p)

items.name: Cslib.URM.Steps.preserves_register
items.doc: Multi-step execution preserves registers not written by any executed instruction.
items.statement:
theorem preserves_register {s s' : State} {r : ℕ}
    (hsteps : Steps p s s')
    (hr : ∀ instr, instr ∈ p → instr.writesTo ≠ some r) :
    s'.regs.read r = s.regs.read r

items.name: Cslib.URM.Steps.eq_of_halts
items.doc:
If two halted states are reachable from the same start, they are equal.

This follows from confluence: since `Step p` is confluent and both `s₁` and `s₂`
are normal forms reachable from `init`, they must be equal.

items.name: Cslib.URM.Halts
items.doc:
A program halts on given inputs if execution reaches a halted state.

This is equivalent to `(Step p).Normalizable (State.init inputs)` —
see `halts_iff_normalizable`.
items.statement: def Halts (inputs : List ℕ) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.URM.halts_iff_normalizable
items.doc: Halting is equivalent to normalizability in the reduction system.
items.statement:
theorem halts_iff_normalizable {p : Program} {inputs : List ℕ} :
    Halts p inputs ↔ Relation.Normalizable (Step p) (State.init inputs)

items.name: Cslib.URM.Diverges
items.doc: A program diverges on given inputs if it does not halt.
items.statement: def Diverges (inputs : List ℕ) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.URM.HaltsWithResult
items.doc: A program halts on given inputs with a specific result in R[0].
items.statement: def HaltsWithResult (inputs : List ℕ) (result : ℕ) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.URM.HaltsWithResult.toHalts
items.doc: If a program halts with a result, it halts.
items.statement:
theorem toHalts {inputs : List ℕ} {result : ℕ}
    (h : p ↓ inputs ≫ result) : p ↓ inputs

items.name: Cslib.URM.evalState
items.doc: Evaluation returning the full halting state.
items.statement: noncomputable def evalState (inputs : List ℕ) : Part State

items.name: Cslib.URM.evalState_spec
items.doc: Specification: the state from evalState satisfies Steps and isHalted.
items.statement:
theorem evalState_spec {inputs : List ℕ} (h : (evalState p inputs).Dom) :
    let s := (evalState p inputs).get h
    Steps p (State.init inputs) s ∧ s.isHalted p

items.name: Cslib.URM.Halts.toHaltsWithResult
items.doc: If a program halts, it halts with the output of the final state.
items.statement:
theorem toHaltsWithResult {inputs : List ℕ} (h : p ↓ inputs) :
    p ↓ inputs ≫ ((evalState p inputs).get h).regs.output

items.name: Cslib.URM.eval
items.doc:
Evaluation as a partial function using `Part`.
Defined when the program halts, returning the value in register 0.
items.statement: noncomputable def eval (inputs : List ℕ) : Part ℕ

items.name: Cslib.URM.haltsWithResult_iff_eval
items.doc: A program halts with result `a` iff evaluation returns `Part.some a`.
items.statement:
theorem haltsWithResult_iff_eval {inputs : List ℕ} {result : ℕ} :
    p ↓ inputs ≫ result ↔ eval p inputs = Part.some result

items.name: Cslib.URM.ProgramEquiv
items.doc: Two programs are equivalent if they produce the same result for all inputs.
items.statement: def ProgramEquiv (p q : Program) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.URM.ProgramEquiv.equivalence
items.doc: Program equivalence is an equivalence relation.
items.statement: theorem ProgramEquiv.equivalence : Equivalence ProgramEquiv

modules.title: Standard Form Programs
modules.doc:
This file defines standard-form programs (those with bounded jump targets)
and proves their execution properties.

## Main definitions

- `Program.IsStandardForm`: all jump targets are bounded by program length
- `Program.toStandardForm`: convert a program to standard form

## Main results

- `straight_line_IsStandardForm`: straight-line programs are standard form
- `Halts.toStandardForm_iff`: halting equivalence with normalized programs

items.name: Cslib.URM.Program.IsStandardForm
items.doc:
A program is in standard form if all jump targets are bounded by the program length.
Jumps can target any instruction (0..length-1) or the "virtual halt" position (length).
items.statement: def IsStandardForm (p : Program) : Prop

items.name: Cslib.URM.Program.toStandardForm
items.doc: Convert a program to standard form by capping all jump targets at the program length.
items.statement: def toStandardForm (p : Program) : Program

items.name: Cslib.URM.Program.toStandardForm_length
items.doc: toStandardForm preserves program length.
items.statement: theorem toStandardForm_length (p : Program) : p.toStandardForm.length = p.length

items.name: Cslib.URM.Program.toStandardForm_isStandardForm
items.doc: toStandardForm produces a standard form program.
items.statement:
theorem toStandardForm_isStandardForm (p : Program) :
    p.toStandardForm.IsStandardForm

items.name: Cslib.URM.Program.getElem?_toStandardForm
items.doc: Accessing an instruction in toStandardForm gives the capJump'd instruction.
items.statement:
theorem getElem?_toStandardForm (p : Program) (i : ℕ) :
    p.toStandardForm[i]? = (p[i]?).map (Instr.capJump p.length)

items.name: Cslib.URM.Program.toStandardForm_idempotent
items.doc: toStandardForm is idempotent: applying it twice equals applying it once.
items.statement:
theorem toStandardForm_idempotent (p : Program) :
    p.toStandardForm.toStandardForm = p.toStandardForm

items.name: Cslib.URM.straight_line_IsStandardForm
items.doc: Straight-line programs are in standard form.
items.statement:
theorem straight_line_IsStandardForm {p : Program} (hsl : p.IsStraightLine) :
    p.IsStandardForm

items.note:
## Bisimulation

`p` and `p.toStandardForm` are bisimilar: each step in one program corresponds to a
step in the other that either reaches the same state or reaches a halted state with the
same registers. This bisimulation implies functional equivalence (`eval_toStandardForm`).
The key insight is that jumps with target `q > p.length` land in halted states in both
programs.

items.name: Cslib.URM.Step.toStandardForm
items.doc:
Forward step correspondence: if p steps from s to s', then either:
(1) p.toStandardForm steps from s to s' (same step), or
